karty.g: Information that shows the player what their current goals are.
karty.nz: They must give accurate, timely information about goals and progress toward them, in a form players can read at a glance. The information must connect to something players can act on.
karty.yr: A quest log or marker that is vague, outdated or hidden, so players still don't know what to do or how close they are.
karty.rk: how much detail is shown; how precise (exact vs vague); how often it is updated
karty.ik: <circle cx="30" cy="34" r="22"/><circle cx="30" cy="34" r="13"/><circle cx="30" cy="34" r="4" fill="#e85d4f"/><path d="M30 34L56 8" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M50 6l8 0 0 8" stroke-width="3"/>

karty.g: Goal: after finishing earlier goals, the character sets new ones for themselves.
karty.nz: Goals must be measurable from game state and link into chains, so finishing one opens the next, with a way for the agent to pick from them. For computer agents this needs detailed encoded conditions and benefits.
karty.yr: A character whose 'new goals' are scripted text or a changed title, while behaviour and choices stay the same.
karty.rk: how many chained goals; how much choice among next goals; how closely goals depend on past outcomes
karty.ik: <path d="M6 58h14V44h14V30h14V16h10" /><circle cx="13" cy="34" r="5"/><path d="M6 54c0-8 3-11 7-11s7 3 7 11z" fill="#2f6b8f" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M46 6v10M42 10l4-4 4 4" stroke="#4fa83a" stroke-width="4"/>

karty.g: An interface element showing where the player is currently acting on the game.
karty.nz: A pointer that works anywhere in the world and is unaffected by it, with actions tied to what it selects or points at. The input handling must be responsive and the available actions clear.
karty.yr: A cursor that appears but can only click menus, or one that merely shows position without letting players act on the world.
karty.rk: which actions the pointer allows; selection modes; its range and precision
karty.ik: <path d="M26 30V10a4 4 0 0 1 8 0v20l8 2c4 1 6 4 6 8l-2 14H24l-8-14c-2-3 1-6 4-5l6 4z" fill="#fff"/><path d="M6 54h10M52 54h6" stroke="#2f6b8f" stroke-dasharray="2 6"/><circle cx="50" cy="14" r="5" fill="#c9a24a" stroke-width="3"/>

karty.g: The world is shown without being tied to any object inside it.
karty.nz: A camera players can move freely over the world, independent of units, with enough detail to be useful. Decide what stays hidden (fog of war) so there is still uncertainty.
karty.yr: A zoomed-out camera that is actually locked to a character or a fixed spot, so the player still sees only what that character sees.
karty.rk: camera freedom and zoom range; how much is hidden by fog of war; number of display modes
karty.ik: <path d="M4 22c10-8 20-12 28-12s18 4 28 12"/><ellipse cx="32" cy="20" rx="7" ry="5" fill="#c9a24a" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M10 56l10-22h24l10 22z" fill="#4fa83a"/><path d="M32 34v22M15 45h34" stroke-width="2.5"/>

karty.g: Game characters pass information to each other by word of mouth.
karty.nz: Information in the world must be uncertain, so statements can be true, false or partial and players can't instantly check them. Someone must actually pass messages along, and acting on them must matter.
karty.yr: Idle chatter lines that repeat facts already known or never affect any decision, so it is flavour text only.
karty.rk: who talks to whom; how reliable the information is; what topics it covers

karty.g: Rewards for repeating the same action many times.
karty.nz: A counter requires many repetitions of an action, set high enough to reflect real dedication but still reachable by persevering. Repeated tasks should vary or be meaningful or they are only chores.
karty.yr: A threshold so low it's reached by accident, or one that counts something players already do constantly, so it marks no extra effort.
karty.rk: required count; whether tasks must differ or be the same; how visible the progress is

karty.g: Repeating simple actions many times to get resources or complete a goal.
karty.nz: The game needs a need for resources or progress that can only be met by repeating a simple, low-challenge action many times, with rewards that don't advance the player too much. Players must choose or feel pushed to repeat it.
karty.yr: A repeating task that is quick and varied enough that players don't feel repetition, or one the player never needs to do.
karty.rk: amount needed; drop rates; how repetitive and easy the action is

karty.g: Goal: keep other players or elements away from certain zones or objects.
karty.nz: There must be something worth guarding and real opponents trying to get it, with ways for the guard to fail. The guard needs means to watch and block, either passive (traps, alarms) or active (combat).
karty.yr: An objective marked 'defend' that nobody ever attacks, or that cannot be lost.
karty.rk: what is guarded; how strong and how frequent the threats are; what means of defence are available

karty.g: The game makes the player act by making them feel pangs of conscience.
karty.nz: Players need real connections with other players (teams, guilds, reciprocity) and a situation where their action or inaction visibly hurts or helps someone. Social dilemmas or requests for help create it.
karty.yr: A pop-up message saying 'your friends need you' with no real person affected and no connection, so nobody feels anything.
karty.rk: strength of social bonds; how visible others' needs or losses are; reciprocity rules

karty.g: A reward for a goal completed while voluntarily making the game harder.
karty.nz: The restriction must really raise difficulty, such as limited weapons or time limits, and be optional, with the achievement recorded and visible. It needs a base game strong enough to support the harder play.
karty.yr: A 'challenge' whose handicap is trivial or cosmetic and makes no difference to how you play.
karty.rk: kind and severity of the restriction; which goals it applies to
karty.ik: <path d="M18 8h28v16c0 9-6 14-14 14s-14-5-14-14z" fill="#c9a24a"/><path d="M32 38v8M22 52h20"/><path d="M8 60l48-8" stroke="#e85d4f"/><circle cx="54" cy="52" r="5" fill="#2a2a2a" stroke-width="3"/>

karty.g: Rules that make the game easier or harder for individual players to even out their chances.
karty.nz: The adjustments must change real quantities, such as resources, health, abilities or head starts, in proportion to the skill gap. Players must accept them, whether voluntary or enforced.
karty.yr: A 'difficulty' setting that only renames levels or tweaks a number too small to feel, so strong and weak players still have very unequal chances.
karty.rk: size of advantage or penalty; which attribute is changed; voluntary vs enforced
karty.ik: <path d="M32 12v38M20 56h24M6 28l52-10"/><path d="M6 28l-3 12h12zM58 18l-3 12h12z" stroke-width="2" stroke="none"/><path d="M2 40h14c0 5-3 7-7 7s-7-2-7-7z" fill="#c9a24a" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M48 30h14c0 5-3 7-7 7s-7-2-7-7z" fill="#c9a24a" stroke-width="3"/><rect x="49" y="20" width="12" height="8" fill="#e85d4f" stroke-width="3"/>

karty.g: Nicknames by which players and their achievements are recognized.
karty.nz: Names or symbols need to be tied to records or accounts and shown where others see them (scores, chat, over avatars). Decide how they are chosen and moderated.
karty.yr: A name field that is never shown or saved anywhere, or auto-generated names everyone ignores.
karty.rk: length and format; free vs preset choice; where they are displayed
karty.ik: <rect x="6" y="14" width="52" height="36" rx="4"/><circle cx="22" cy="28" r="6" fill="#2f6b8f"/><path d="M12 44c0-6 4-9 10-9s10 3 10 9" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M38 26h14M38 36h10" stroke-width="4"/>

karty.g: A set of game elements of a certain kind that a player currently holds.
karty.nz: Players must hold hidden elements they can pick between, with a size limit and a clear way to refill. The elements held need to matter enough that choosing among them is a real decision.
karty.yr: A hand where the next play is forced or all cards are identical or visible, so holding them gives no choice.
karty.rk: hand size; refill rule; whether hands are secret or open
karty.ik: <rect x="8" y="14" width="22" height="34" rx="3" transform="rotate(-18 19 31)" fill="#fff"/><rect x="20" y="10" width="22" height="34" rx="3" fill="#fff"/><rect x="32" y="14" width="22" height="34" rx="3" transform="rotate(18 43 31)" fill="#e85d4f"/><path d="M6 58h52"/>

karty.g: A measure of how much damage a character can take before serious penalties.
karty.nz: Damage must reduce the value and reaching zero or thresholds must have real consequences. Sources of damage and ways to restore it need to be balanced so the number matters.
karty.yr: A health bar that never drops meaningfully or refills freely, so damage has no effect on play.
karty.rk: maximum health; damage amounts; healing availability
karty.ik: <rect x="6" y="20" width="52" height="24" rx="4"/><rect x="10" y="24" width="28" height="16" rx="2" fill="#e85d4f" stroke="none"/><path d="M32 6v8M28 10h8" stroke="#4fa83a" stroke-width="4"/>

karty.g: Characters not controlled by players who help the player.
karty.nz: Decide what each helper can do and where or when it appears, so the help matches a real moment of need, such as a puzzle, a shortage, or a lack of information. The help must be useful enough to rely on but limited enough that players still have to make their own choices.
karty.yr: A character stands in the world with a friendly name and model but only repeats flavor lines, so players gain nothing and never need to consult it.
karty.rk: how much and what kind of help they give; how often, where and when they are available; what it costs the player to use them
karty.ik: <circle cx="22" cy="20" r="8"/><path d="M8 58c0-14 6-20 14-20s14 6 14 20z" fill="#4fa83a"/><path d="M44 8v22" stroke-width="5"/><circle cx="44" cy="40" r="3" fill="#2a2a2a" stroke="none"/><path d="M36 16a8 8 0 0 1 16 0c0 6-8 6-8 14" fill="none"/>

karty.g: Situations in which the player cannot change anything themselves.
karty.nz: Players must be able to see the game going on while having no useful input, and the state needs a clear end (a timer, a rescue by others, or the situation resolving). Without a way out or a clear duration it just feels broken.
karty.yr: A brief animation or stun where the player can still steer, act, or skip ahead, so nothing about their choices is actually removed.
karty.rk: how long the state lasts; what ends it (timer, rescue, none)
karty.ik: <rect x="14" y="8" width="36" height="50" rx="3"/><path d="M26 8v50M38 8v50"/><circle cx="32" cy="34" r="8" fill="#e85d4f"/><path d="M4 58h56"/>

karty.g: Goal: bring objects to a needed place not by moving them directly but by acting through others.
karty.nz: The herded elements need their own movement and a limited set of ways for players to nudge them (pushing, luring, blocking), with a clear destination. The herded things must be able to go the wrong way so steering takes real effort.
karty.yr: Elements that just follow the player or a fixed path to the goal, so the player never has to handle their independent movement.
karty.rk: how stubborn or erratic the herded things are; how strong the player's influence is; distance to the goal
karty.ik: <ellipse cx="18" cy="34" rx="10" ry="7" fill="#fff"/><ellipse cx="36" cy="46" rx="9" ry="6" fill="#fff"/><path d="M8 14l16 4M8 14l4 14" stroke="#c9a24a" stroke-width="4"/><path d="M40 26h12M46 20l6 6-6 6" stroke="#4fa83a" stroke-width="4"/><path d="M54 56V40l8 4-8 4" stroke="none"/>

karty.g: Each player brings their own game elements to a new game.
karty.nz: Components must differ enough in function that choosing and combining them matters, and the sets must be balanced or limited so that having more or rarer pieces does not decide the game. Players also need time and means to build and tune their own sets.
karty.yr: Players bring their own pieces but all pieces are functionally the same or one set is clearly best, so ownership changes nothing in play.
karty.rk: how much the elements differ in power; limits on set size or cost; how much players can customise
karty.ik: <rect x="4" y="22" width="16" height="16" rx="2" fill="#e85d4f"/><circle cx="32" cy="14" r="8" fill="#c9a24a"/><path d="M44 38h16L52 24z" fill="#2f6b8f"/><path d="M12 44v8h40v-8M32 24v24" stroke-width="3"/>

karty.g: Places in the game where a person or thing can be hidden.
karty.nz: Seekers must truly be less able to notice things in them, and there must be enough, well-placed spots to make concealment a real option without making it trivial. Players should be able to judge how good a spot is.
karty.yr: Decorative crates or bushes that do not block sight or detection, so hiding in them is no safer than standing in the open.
karty.rk: number, size and placement of hiding spots; how well they hide; how clearly players can tell they are hidden
karty.ik: <path d="M10 58V26L32 6l22 20v32z" fill="#d5d9e0"/><rect x="24" y="34" width="16" height="24"/><circle cx="32" cy="42" r="2" fill="#2a2a2a" stroke="none"/><path d="M27 22h10" stroke-width="3"/>

karty.g: Results are saved after a game so they can be compared.
karty.nz: Results must be saved and shown where players will see them, be comparable across attempts, and be ordered fairly with ties handled. Someone must care about the comparison, whether themselves, friends, or the world.
karty.yr: A list that resets on exit, is hidden in a menu, or is full of unreachable or fake entries so no one tries to beat it.
karty.rk: how many entries are kept; who can see them (local, friends, global); time-limited versus all-time lists
karty.ik: <rect x="10" y="6" width="44" height="52" rx="4"/><path d="M30 16h18M30 30h18M30 44h18" stroke-width="4"/><circle cx="20" cy="16" r="4" fill="#c9a24a"/><circle cx="20" cy="30" r="4" fill="#d5d9e0"/><circle cx="20" cy="44" r="4" fill="#e85d4f"/>

karty.g: As the game goes on, the stages that get completed become more and more significant.
karty.nz: Later achievements must be bigger in stakes, rarity, and effect than earlier ones, supported by gating, rising difficulty, or goal hierarchies, and checked in playtests. Late moments need to feel meaningfully more important, not just harder.
karty.yr: Later goals are just the same task with bigger numbers, so finishing them feels no more significant than the first one.
karty.rk: how much importance or reward grows per stage; spacing and gating of milestones
karty.ik: <path d="M4 58h14V46h14V34h14V22h14"/><path d="M4 58h14V46H4zM18 46h14V34H18zM32 34h14V22H32z" fill="#d5d9e0" stroke="none"/><path d="M50 22V6l10 4-10 4" fill="#e85d4f" stroke-width="3"/>

karty.g: Players take turns sitting at one interface and making their moves.
karty.nz: There must be a clear rule for when control changes hands, and the waiting players need something to do or to watch so the wait is tolerable. If secrecy matters, players must not see each other's turns.
karty.yr: Several players nominally share a device but the game never enforces turns, so they just crowd around or one person plays.
karty.rk: what triggers a handover (turn end, death, level end); turn length or time limit

karty.g: An upcoming event that the player can clearly see in advance.
karty.nz: Players must be able to see a specific upcoming outcome and have reason to care, and it needs time to loom (a timer, a delay, a visible progress). The outcome must remain uncertain or influenceable.
karty.yr: An outcome shown in the interface that is unavoidable, trivial, or too hidden to notice, so nobody feels any suspense.
karty.rk: how visible the pending outcome is; how long the delay is; how much stands to be gained or lost
karty.ik: <path d="M8 56h48"/><path d="M32 6l-10 8v8l10 8 10-8v-8z" fill="#e85d4f" stroke="none"/><circle cx="32" cy="20" r="8" fill="#c9a24a"/><path d="M32 30v14M26 44l6 8 6-8z" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M22 56l10-8 10 8" stroke-width="3"/>

karty.g: Information and action buttons are shown over the picture of the world, as if on glass before the eyes.
karty.nz: It must show the information players need at the moments they need it without cluttering the view, and update reliably with the game state. What it includes should match what the design wants players to track.
karty.yr: A screen overlay with decorative or redundant elements that tell the player nothing useful for decisions.
karty.rk: what information is shown; how large and prominent; whether it fits the game world
karty.ik: <rect x="4" y="8" width="56" height="48" rx="4"/><rect x="9" y="13" width="22" height="7" rx="2" fill="#e85d4f" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="50" cy="18" r="5" fill="#c9a24a" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M10 50l14-14 8 8 10-12 12 18" stroke="#4fa83a" stroke-width="3"/>

karty.g: The game is played at once in a real place and in a virtual or abstract one.
karty.nz: There must be a real link between physical places and virtual ones (sensors, overlays, or rules), so that where the player physically is changes what happens in the game. Both parts of the space need to matter for play.
karty.yr: A game set in a real location that only uses it as a backdrop, where the virtual part ignores where players actually are.
karty.rk: how strongly physical position affects the virtual state; the sensing or overlay method; size of the real area
karty.ik: <path d="M4 54h28V24L18 6 4 24z" fill="#4fa83a"/><path d="M32 22h28v32H32z" fill="#fff"/><path d="M38 30h6v6h-6zM48 40h6v6h-6zM38 46h6M48 28h6" stroke="#2f6b8f" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M32 22v32"/>

karty.g: The world looks more spacious than it really is: there are fewer playable zones than it seems.
karty.nz: The unreachable scenery must look credible, be consistent with the setting, and be blocked in ways players do not easily notice. It breaks down if the blocks are obvious or conflict with the theme.
karty.yr: A flat backdrop or map edge that obviously ends, so players see the limit at once and the world does not feel bigger.
karty.rk: how much unreachable scenery is shown; how the blocks are disguised; level of detail of distant areas
karty.ik: <rect x="6" y="8" width="52" height="48" rx="3"/><path d="M6 36h52M6 36l14-14M58 36L44 22M32 36V22" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M24 22h16" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M8 56L26 38M56 56L38 38" stroke="#e85d4f" stroke-width="3"/>

karty.g: Rewards that do not help with goals and improve nothing.
karty.nz: The reward must still feel like a recognition to players, through look, status, information, or social value, even though it gives no gameplay benefit. Players need some reason to want it.
karty.yr: A reward that changes the game state after all, or one so dull that no one notices or wants it.
karty.rk: how attractive or visible the reward is; how hard it is to earn; how much social or story value it carries
karty.ik: <path d="M32 8l6 12 13 2-9 10 2 13-12-6-12 6 2-13-9-10 13-2z" fill="#c9a24a" fill-opacity=".45" stroke-dasharray="4 4"/><path d="M18 56h28"/><path d="M24 56l-4 4M40 56l4 4" stroke-width="3"/>

karty.g: An ability the player already has starts working more effectively.
karty.nz: The improvement must noticeably change what actions achieve, be tied to progress or rewards, and be paced so it does not erase challenge. Players should be able to feel the difference.
karty.yr: A level-up that raises a stat so slightly or so evenly with enemy scaling that play feels exactly the same.
karty.rk: size of each improvement; how often and by what route it is gained; whether players choose
karty.ik: <path d="M10 36l22-24 22 24H42v22H22V36z" fill="#4fa83a"/><path d="M6 12h12M12 6v12" stroke="#c9a24a" stroke-width="4"/>

karty.g: Places in the world that can be seen but not visited.
karty.nz: The areas must be visible and be blocked by a believable barrier, and the blocking must be reliable. If players are meant to get in later, a visible condition for access helps.
karty.yr: An area that looks blocked but can be reached by an exploit, or that is blocked with no visible reason so it feels like an arbitrary wall.
karty.rk: how much of the world is blocked; what blocks it; whether and how access is later unlocked
karty.ik: <rect x='6' y='8' width='52' height='48' rx='3'/><path d='M8 54l16-24 10 12 8-10 14 22z' fill='#4fa83a' stroke-width='3'/><path d='M20 8v46M32 8v46M44 8v46' stroke-width='3'/>

karty.g: Goal: two or more goals that cannot be completed together because they exclude each other.
karty.nz: The goals must truly exclude each other in play, either for one player or between players, and be known to those pursuing them. Players need to feel the cost of choosing one over another.
karty.yr: Goals that are described as conflicting but can all be completed in the same game, so no choice has to be made.
karty.rk: how many goals clash; whether they clash for one player or between players; how soon the conflict is visible

karty.g: The further the game progresses, the bigger or better the rewards.
karty.nz: Rewards must really grow in value that players can use or see, paced against rising difficulty or costs so they keep up. The growth should be noticeable between stages.
karty.yr: Rewards that are labelled bigger but are worth the same, or are cancelled out by matching cost increases so nothing feels better.
karty.rk: growth rate per stage; reward type (resources or abilities); match to rising difficulty
karty.ik: <circle cx='12' cy='48' r='5' fill='#c9a24a'/><circle cx='28' cy='38' r='8' fill='#c9a24a'/><circle cx='47' cy='22' r='12' fill='#c9a24a'/><path d='M4 60h56'/>

karty.g: A penalty that affects only one of the players.
karty.nz: The penalty must hit only the player who earned it and be meaningful enough to affect their choices. How it interacts with shared rewards or teams should be clear.
karty.yr: A penalty so small or so easy to dodge that the player ignores it, or one that spreads to others anyway.
karty.rk: size and type of the penalty; what triggers it; who chooses the target

karty.g: A reward that goes to only one player.
karty.nz: The reward must go to a single player and matter enough that others want it for themselves. It creates competition only if players can compete for it.
karty.yr: A reward given to one player that has no value or is quietly shared with everyone, so it makes no difference who gets it.
karty.rk: size of the reward; who qualifies; how contested the winning is

karty.g: One character gives another information that can affect how the game goes.
karty.nz: The information must change what players know or can do (a new goal, a clue, a better choice), and delivered through a channel such as dialogue or eavesdropping. It must be reliable or deliberately unreliable.
karty.yr: Characters talk but say only flavour text, so players learn nothing that affects their decisions.
karty.rk: how much and how useful the information is; how it is delivered; whether it can be false
karty.ik: <rect x='6' y='24' width='52' height='34' rx='3'/><path d='M6 26l26 18 26-18'/><circle cx='32' cy='44' r='4' fill='#c9a24a' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M12 16c10-10 30-10 40 0' stroke='#2f6b8f'/><path d='M44 18l8-2-3-8' stroke='#2f6b8f' stroke-width='3'/>

karty.g: The ability of agents to act on their own, not only in response to events.
karty.nz: Agents must be able to start actions that are not simply triggered by something the player did, and these actions must affect play. Players need to notice that the agent chose to act.
karty.yr: Agents that only react to player actions or follow a script that looks spontaneous, so they never start anything.
karty.rk: how often agents act on their own; what range of actions they can start

karty.g: Large tools in the world that the player cannot move or carry away.
karty.nz: They must give actions that are better or different from those available elsewhere, and be placed where players would want to go. Limits like cooldowns or cost keep them from dominating.
karty.yr: A large fixed object in the scenery that offers nothing that could not be done elsewhere, so no one needs to use it.
karty.rk: where they are placed; what they offer; cooldown or cost of use
karty.ik: <path d='M6 12h44c0 8-6 12-14 12v10h10v22H18V34h10V24C16 24 8 20 6 12z' fill='#d5d9e0'/><path d='M24 5v4M32 3v5' stroke='#e85d4f' stroke-width='3'/><path d='M8 60h48'/>

karty.g: Parts of the world are created for a particular group of players when they are needed.
karty.nz: The system must create isolated copies on demand with a set group size, and the content must be worth entering as a group. Access conditions (group size, timing) should be clear.
karty.yr: A zone called an instance that everyone still shares, so crowding and interference are the same as before.
karty.rk: group size required; how often and when instances open; content and difficulty inside
karty.ik: <circle cx='18' cy='18' r='11'/><circle cx='46' cy='18' r='11'/><circle cx='32' cy='46' r='11'/><circle cx='18' cy='18' r='3.5' fill='#c9a24a' stroke-width='2'/><circle cx='46' cy='18' r='3.5' fill='#c9a24a' stroke-width='2'/><circle cx='32' cy='46' r='3.5' fill='#c9a24a' stroke-width='2'/>

karty.g: Goal: other players or the game itself can speed up, slow down or break its completion.
karty.nz: Other agents need actual actions that can hamper the goal, and a reason to use them. Players should be able to tell who might interfere.
karty.yr: A goal others could theoretically interfere with, but no action in the game lets them, so it is effectively safe.
karty.rk: what actions interfere; who can interfere; how visible the goal and threat are
karty.ik: <rect x='6' y='44' width='26' height='14' fill='#c9a24a'/><rect x='6' y='30' width='26' height='14' fill='#c9a24a'/><rect x='8' y='14' width='26' height='14' fill='#c9a24a' transform='rotate(-14 21 21)'/><circle cx='50' cy='22' r='8' fill='#e85d4f'/>

karty.g: Desired actions get in each other's way: progress in one costs you in another.
karty.nz: The goals must be of similar appeal, with consequences players can foresee or learn, so that choosing one really costs another. Choices should be hard to take back.
karty.yr: Several goals offered where one is plainly the best or all can be done anyway, so there is nothing to agonise over.
karty.rk: how many incompatible options; how equal their appeal; how reversible the choice is

karty.g: The opponent or competitor is in the same social group as you.
karty.nz: Players must belong to a shared group while having goals that conflict, and the rules should keep the conflict from ending in outright elimination. The group's norms or limited actions keep it ongoing.
karty.yr: Teammates labelled rivals but with fully aligned goals, so no one ever works against another.
karty.rk: how strongly individual and group goals diverge; what actions are allowed against rivals

karty.g: The game's design lets one player step out for a while without spoiling the game for others.
karty.nz: Stopping must not harm the player or others, which means saving state, pausing time, or having others covered by AI when someone leaves. It works only if the rest of the system also copes.
karty.yr: A pause or save option that still costs the player progress, or that wrecks the game for other players.
karty.rk: where and how often saves/pauses are allowed; what covers an absent player
karty.ik: <rect x='4' y='14' width='56' height='36' rx='10'/><rect x='18' y='20' width='28' height='24' rx='2' fill='#d5d9e0'/><path d='M28 27v10M36 27v10' stroke='#e85d4f'/>

karty.g: An action can be broken off before it has fully taken effect.
karty.nz: Actions must have a delay or build-up in which others can respond, and there must be a means to stop them. The window should be long enough to react to.
karty.yr: An action that has a wind-up animation but cannot actually be stopped, so the wind-up is just decoration.
karty.rk: length of the interruption window; what can interrupt; cost to the interrupted
karty.ik: <path d='M4 32h24M22 25l7 7-7 7'/><rect x='38' y='8' width='9' height='48' rx='4' fill='#e85d4f'/><path d='M54 32h6' stroke-dasharray='1 5'/>

karty.g: A place where everything a character carries is stored.
karty.nz: It needs limits (space, weight) and real actions (use, drop, equip, trade) so that managing items is a choice. The limits must be tight enough to force choosing.
karty.yr: An item list with no limit and no actions beyond viewing, so carrying anything is free and no decision arises.
karty.rk: capacity; what actions are available; how items are sorted and accessed
karty.ik: <path d='M24 18v-4a8 8 0 0 1 16 0v4'/><rect x='12' y='18' width='40' height='40' rx='12' fill='#2f6b8f'/><rect x='22' y='38' width='20' height='14' rx='3' fill='#c9a24a'/><path d='M12 32h40'/>

karty.g: A player gives up resources for a time for gain later, not knowing how it will turn out.
karty.nz: Resources must be spent with the payoff delayed and uncertain, and the payoff must be worth the wait. Players need enough knowledge to weigh the risk.
karty.yr: Spending resources that return immediately or with certainty, so it is just a purchase.
karty.rk: cost; delay before payoff; size and certainty of the return

karty.g: Barriers that stop you from passing but do not stop you from looking.
karty.nz: Collision must reliably stop movement at the edge while the view carries beyond it, and placement should be where players do not expect to go. The more natural the edge looks, the less it breaks immersion.
karty.yr: A boundary players can walk through, or one that is obvious and unexplained so it simply looks like a bug.
karty.rk: where the walls are placed; how much is visible beyond; how they are disguised
karty.ik: <rect x='20' y='6' width='24' height='52' rx='2' fill='#2f6b8f' fill-opacity='.2' stroke-dasharray='5 5'/><path d='M26 20l12-10M26 40l12-14' stroke-width='3'/><circle cx='9' cy='44' r='5' fill='#c9a24a'/><path d='M47 54l6-13 6 13z' fill='#4fa83a' stroke-width='3'/>

karty.g: Actions by which a player calls new people into the game, sometimes earning a reward for it.
karty.nz: The game needs a way to reach people outside it (online link, share feature) and must let newcomers join a running game or world. A reward or social reason for inviting helps players actually use it.
karty.yr: An invite button exists but newcomers cannot join anyway, or nobody has a reason to press it, so no one ever arrives.
karty.rk: what the inviter gets as reward; how many invites are allowed; how easily invitees can join
karty.ik: <path d='M6 16h52v10a6 6 0 0 0 0 12v10H6V38a6 6 0 0 0 0-12z' fill='#c9a24a'/><path d='M22 20v24' stroke-dasharray='1 6'/><path d='M40 32h12M46 26v12' stroke='#4fa83a' stroke-width='5'/>

karty.g: The ability to take no harm from attacks and other dangers.
karty.nz: Decide which damage types are blocked, for whom, and whether the immunity is permanent or timed. It only matters if the dangers it blocks are otherwise real, and if some others lack it so it is a privilege.
karty.yr: An entity is labeled immune but the threats it ignores never occur, or everyone has it, so it changes no decisions.
karty.rk: which damage types are covered; who has it; how long it lasts
karty.ik: <circle cx='32' cy='32' r='26' fill='#2f6b8f' fill-opacity='.2'/><circle cx='32' cy='26' r='7'/><path d='M20 50c0-9 5-14 12-14s12 5 12 14z' fill='#fff'/><path d='M60 4L48 14' stroke='#e85d4f' stroke-width='3'/>

karty.g: Events whose consequences cannot be undone in the game.
karty.nz: No other rule or action may push that part of the state back, and the game must be able to enforce this (system or facilitator). Players must also understand that it cannot be undone.
karty.yr: The event is called permanent but a later action, undo, reload or house rule quietly reverses it.
karty.rk: which events are made permanent; how often they happen; how clearly players are warned

karty.g: Right after a kill, the player is shown a replay of it.
karty.nz: The game must record the moments before a death and show them right away, with a clear camera choice and view style. The replay must show enough to explain how the death happened.
karty.yr: A replay plays but from a useless angle or too late, so the player learns nothing about what killed them.
karty.rk: when the replay triggers; how long it is; camera angle; full screen or small inset
karty.ik: <rect x='6' y='8' width='52' height='38' rx='4'/><circle cx='32' cy='27' r='9' stroke='#e85d4f'/><path d='M32 13v8M32 33v8M18 27h8M38 27h8' stroke='#e85d4f' stroke-width='3'/><path d='M22 58h20M32 46v12'/>

karty.g: Goal: take a desirable position in the game and hold it while others try to take it away.
karty.nz: Several players must want the same hold-the-spot condition that only one can have, with holding rewarded over time. The holder needs some edge or pressure so the position matters and the others are pushed to contest it.
karty.yr: A marked zone exists but holding it gives nothing, or nobody can contest it, so people ignore it.
karty.rk: time required to hold; how fast score builds; advantage or penalty for the holder

karty.g: A player cannot win themselves but decides which of the others wins.
karty.nz: It arises when positions are clear and a hopeless player still has influence over others, as with early elimination or a predictable winner. A designer avoids it by keeping outcomes uncertain, hiding information, or giving losing players reasons to keep playing.
karty.yr: A player is called a kingmaker but their choice has no real effect on who wins, so nothing happens.
karty.rk: how early outcomes become clear; how much hidden information there is; how much a trailing player can still affect others

karty.g: Noticeable objects in the game world that make it easier to find your way.
karty.nz: Objects must stand out and be visible from many places so players can use them to orient. They must be spread across the space and be distinguishable from each other.
karty.yr: Many similar tall objects or decorations that look alike, so players still get lost.
karty.rk: how many; how large and distinctive; where placed; how often visible
karty.ik: <path d='M6 18h10M48 18h10' stroke='#c9a24a'/><path d='M24 58l4-34h8l4 34z' fill='#fff'/><polygon points='26 34 38 34 39 44 25 44' fill='#e85d4f' stroke-width='3'/><rect x='26' y='12' width='12' height='12' fill='#c9a24a'/><path d='M24 12h16l-8-8z' fill='#e85d4f'/><path d='M10 58h44'/>

karty.g: All movement follows a few set routes, which makes the game more predictable.
karty.nz: The map must offer a small fixed set of routes between areas, such as bases, and make leaving them hard or pointless. The lanes must lead to real choices and meetings between opponents.
karty.yr: Paths are drawn but players can walk anywhere, so the lanes are ignored.
karty.rk: number of lanes; their width and length; how blocked the space between lanes is
karty.ik: <rect x='4' y='6' width='56' height='14' fill='#d5d9e0'/><rect x='4' y='25' width='56' height='14' fill='#d5d9e0'/><rect x='4' y='44' width='56' height='14' fill='#d5d9e0'/><circle cx='16' cy='13' r='4' fill='#e85d4f'/><circle cx='44' cy='32' r='4' fill='#e85d4f'/><circle cx='28' cy='51' r='4' fill='#e85d4f'/>

karty.g: Goal: knock out rivals until you are the only surviving player or team.
karty.nz: Players must be able to eliminate each other (lives, health, or removal) with goals that conflict. The game ends or moves on when only one remains, and it should handle what eliminated players do.
karty.yr: Players are called survivors but cannot really remove each other, so the winner is decided by something else.
karty.rk: how easily players are eliminated; how many lives; whether alliances or surrender are allowed

karty.g: The game lets you join at any moment without waiting for someone else's start.
karty.nz: The system must be able to insert a new player into a running game, with spawning, a fair starting state, and some answer to the balance problems newcomers cause. It needs players to actually arrive at different times.
karty.yr: A join button exists but latecomers start so far behind or ahead that they cannot take part in a meaningful way.
karty.rk: how late one can join; what starting resources a newcomer gets; whether bots fill empty slots

karty.g: The results of one game permanently change the conditions of later games.
karty.nz: The rules must specify lasting changes, such as new components or rules, that carry to later sessions, while a core of fixed rules keeps it the same game. Players must be able to track the changes.
karty.yr: A campaign log or score is kept but nothing in the next session actually differs.
karty.rk: how big and how frequent the permanent changes are; how much of the rule set stays fixed

karty.g: A part of the game where all the action takes place until a goal or end condition is reached.
karty.nz: Each level needs boundaries, a goal or end condition, and real differences in content or play, not only looks. The number and order of levels shape pacing.
karty.yr: Levels differ only in colors or theme, while the play stays the same.
karty.rk: number of levels; how they differ; how much randomness; length of each
karty.ik: <path d='M6 58V46h14V34h14V22h14V10h10v48z' fill='#2f6b8f'/><circle cx='13' cy='40' r='5' fill='#c9a24a'/>

karty.g: A punishment the player receives upon losing a life.
karty.nz: The game needs Lives and a clear trigger for losing one, either a direct hit or full damage. Losing a life must move the player closer to game end, with respawn in between.
karty.yr: A life counter drops but players can regain lives freely or ignore it, so failure costs nothing.
karty.rk: what triggers a life loss; how many lives exist; whether lives can be regained

karty.g: One game element must be able to see another directly.
karty.nz: The world needs things that block sight and actions that depend on seeing, such as shooting, stealth or detection. The blockers must be placed so that position matters.
karty.yr: A sight rule is declared but the map has almost no blockers, so everything can always see everything.
karty.rk: how much cover or obstruction exists; sight range; which actions need sight
karty.ik: <path d='M3 30c4-6 9-9 14-9s10 3 14 9c-4 6-9 9-14 9s-10-3-14-9z'/><circle cx='17' cy='30' r='3.5' fill='#2a2a2a' stroke='none'/><path d='M36 30h14' stroke-dasharray='1 6'/><circle cx='55' cy='30' r='5' fill='#e85d4f'/><rect x='40' y='42' width='8' height='16' fill='#d5d9e0'/>

karty.g: A role-playing game where participants physically act out their heroes.
karty.nz: Players must act in person, in character, with believable props and costumes, and communicate in-world. The design must handle gaps between what players know and what characters know.
karty.yr: People wear costumes but talk and act as themselves, so it is just a normal tabletop game in costume.
karty.rk: how much in-character play is demanded; how real the props are; rules for out-of-game talk

karty.g: The number of attempts a player has before the game ends.
karty.nz: Failure must remove a life but not end the game at once, and running out must end it. Dangers must be real enough that lives are actually lost.
karty.yr: Players have a number of lives but gain them so easily, or are so seldom hit, that losing one never matters.
karty.rk: starting number of lives; how often they are lost; how they can be regained

karty.g: Game tips that are shown while the game is loading.
karty.nz: There must be waiting moments, and the hints must be useful, correct and varied enough to be read. They should connect to what the player will do next.
karty.yr: Vague or repeated tips, or generic lore lines, that teach nothing about play.
karty.rk: how many hints; how they are chosen; how long they display
karty.ik: <rect x='14' y='6' width='36' height='28' rx='4' fill='#c9a24a'/><path d='M21 16h22M21 24h12' stroke-width='3'/><rect x='6' y='44' width='52' height='12' rx='6'/><rect x='6' y='44' width='30' height='12' rx='6' fill='#4fa83a'/>

karty.g: Abilities are available only in certain places in the game world.
karty.nz: Certain spots must give real, useful abilities that are not available elsewhere, and be limited or contestable. Movement rules should let players choose to reach them.
karty.yr: Special spots exist but give weak bonuses or nobody needs them, so players walk past.
karty.rk: how strong the ability is; how many such places; who can control them

karty.g: Items, usually random, that the player finds in the world as a reward.
karty.nz: Defeating or searching things must yield items with some randomness and enough variety that players want to check. Items must matter to later play, and distribution among players needs handling.
karty.yr: Enemies drop items that are always the same or worthless, so killing them gives no reason to look.
karty.rk: drop rate; spread of item quality; what kinds of items can drop; how it is shared

karty.g: The drive to keep your word and support a person, group or cause within the game.
karty.nz: There must be a character, faction or cause to be loyal to, with a cost for breaking it and tempting reasons to do so. Without that choice it is only background story.
karty.yr: The story says you serve a faction but nothing in play rewards or punishes staying with it.
karty.rk: what penalties follow betrayal; how many competing loyalties; how tempting the alternatives are
karty.ik: <circle cx='22' cy='46' r='11' stroke='#c9a24a' stroke-width='6'/><circle cx='42' cy='46' r='11' stroke='#c9a24a' stroke-width='6'/><path d='M32 30C20 22 20 10 27 10c3 0 5 2 5 5 0-3 2-5 5-5 7 0 7 12-5 20z' fill='#e85d4f'/>

karty.g: The feeling that random events are not fully random and tend to work out in the player's favor.
karty.nz: Random outcomes with visible uncertainty, plus ways for players to feel they may influence them, such as choosing when to roll or risking something. The outcome reveal needs to be noticeable.
karty.yr: Random results occur but are hidden or happen without the player's involvement, so they never feel lucky.
karty.rk: how random the outcomes are; how visible the roll is; how much the player can bet or choose

karty.g: A player can guess the correct answer to a problem by chance.
karty.nz: The puzzle or choice must have several options that can simply be tried with quick feedback. Few options and cheap retries make guessing likely.
karty.yr: A puzzle looks like it could be guessed but the choices are so many or penalties so harsh that guessing never works.
karty.rk: number of options; cost of a wrong try; how quickly feedback comes
karty.ik: <circle cx='28' cy='36' r='22'/><circle cx='28' cy='36' r='12'/><circle cx='28' cy='36' r='4' fill='#e85d4f'/><path d='M56 8L30 34'/><path d='M50 8h8v8' stroke-width='3'/>

karty.g: Stretches of the game when players do not need to rush their actions.
karty.nz: The game must have stretches with no urgent threats, such as gaps between waves, and not force fast actions. Players need to know it is safe for the break to feel relaxing.
karty.yr: A break is announced but threats keep coming or timers keep running, so no relaxation occurs.
karty.rk: length of breaks; how often they come; whether threats are fully absent

karty.g: Game elements the story revolves around and that drive the narrative forward.
karty.nz: A chosen object or character must be what goals such as capture, deliver or protect point to, so story and play both depend on it. It need not be detailed, only important to the goals.
karty.yr: The story mentions a special object but no goal or action in the game involves it.
karty.rk: which goals refer to it; how present it is in the world; how its importance is shown
karty.ik: <path d='M24 24v-8a4 4 0 0 1 4-4h8a4 4 0 0 1 4 4v8'/><rect x='8' y='24' width='48' height='32' rx='5' fill='#c9a24a'/><path d='M8 38h48'/><rect x='27' y='33' width='10' height='10' rx='2' fill='#fff' stroke-width='3'/>

karty.g: Goal that shows the player which challenges to take on and gives motivation to play.
karty.nz: The game must state the overarching aim clearly and tie play actions to reaching it. Completing it should be how one wins or finishes.
karty.yr: A stated goal exists but other activities are more rewarding, so players ignore it.
karty.rk: how many main goals; whether all are required; how clearly they are shown
karty.ik: <circle cx='28' cy='38' r='22'/><circle cx='28' cy='38' r='11' fill='#e85d4f'/><circle cx='28' cy='38' r='3' fill='#2a2a2a' stroke='none'/><path d='M28 38L56 8M56 8h-9M56 8v9' stroke-width='3'/>

karty.g: Goal of completing a task whose completion wins the game.
karty.nz: One overarching quest must organize the main story and places, with side quests supporting it. Its completion should be what wins or concludes the game.
karty.yr: A quest is labeled main but can be skipped without consequence, and players never need it.
karty.rk: length of the quest chain; how many places and characters it touches; whether finishing ends the game

karty.g: Goal of a task that must be completed in order to move forward.
karty.nz: The game must make it truly required for completion, with the requirement known to players. Any bypass undermines it.
karty.yr: A goal is marked required but a shortcut lets players finish without it.
karty.rk: how many goals are required; whether all or a subset must be done
karty.ik: <rect x='12' y='10' width='40' height='48' rx='3'/><rect x='24' y='5' width='16' height='10' rx='3' fill='#c9a24a'/><path d='M20 36l8 8 16-18' stroke='#e85d4f' stroke-width='6'/>

karty.g: Controlling the movement of objects in real-time games.
karty.nz: Real-time movement with consequences for bad control, such as obstacles, enemies or timing. Speed and number of hazards decide the difficulty, and players need a good view of space.
karty.yr: Players can steer, but nothing needs avoiding or reaching, so movement is empty.
karty.rk: speed; number of obstacles; control sensitivity; penalty for collisions

karty.g: Games where hundreds or thousands of players live and communicate in one world at the same time.
karty.nz: A server infrastructure, support for joining and leaving at any time, and communication tools. Enough players need to be online and reasons to return so social play appears.
karty.yr: A big shared world exists but players hardly meet or affect each other, so it is solo play in a crowd.
karty.rk: player capacity per world; how much players interact; how often content is updated

karty.g: The game uses data from other players' sessions, but everyone plays separately.
karty.nz: Servers must carry other players' results, such as scores, ghosts or gifts, into each person's game in a visible way. Players need to notice and react to this input.
karty.yr: A leaderboard exists but sits in a menu and never changes how anyone plays.
karty.rk: what data is shared between players; how visible it is; how much players can help each other
karty.ik: <circle cx='32' cy='28' r='8' fill='#2f6b8f'/><path d='M18 60c0-12 6-18 14-18s14 6 14 18z' fill='#2f6b8f'/><circle cx='9' cy='11' r='5' fill='#d5d9e0'/><circle cx='55' cy='11' r='5' fill='#d5d9e0'/><path d='M13 15l11 9M51 15l-11 9' stroke-dasharray='1 6'/>

karty.g: Players act in the game and communicate with each other through a technical system.
karty.nz: The design needs a game system or server that takes player input, decides what it means, and decides what each player gets to see. The designer must choose what the system shows, hides and delays.
karty.yr: A game that runs on a computer or network but lets players see and change everything directly, so the system filters or interprets nothing.
karty.rk: how much the system filters and delays what players see and do

karty.g: The story is built so the player or viewer knows more than any character.
karty.nz: The game must show events from several viewpoints or add commentary, and this extra knowledge must change how the player reads what the character does. The perspective shifts have to be large enough to matter.
karty.yr: A game with several playable characters or a wide camera that shows the player nothing beyond what the current character already knows.
karty.rk: how often the viewpoint switches; how much the player is told beyond the character

karty.g: Content or items earned in the game that remain available after it ends.
karty.nz: The game needs a durable item, such as a kept component or a produced record, tied to a specific game instance and actually handed to the player. It must carry some value in memory, status or later use.
karty.yr: A generic souvenir or a stats screen that nobody keeps, shows or cares about, and that is not tied to anything that happened in play.
karty.rk: what is kept; how scarce or personal it is; whether it has use in later games
karty.ik: <path d='M6 16h52v10a6 6 0 0 0 0 12v10H6V38a6 6 0 0 0 0-12z' fill='#c9a24a'/><path d='M42 16v32' stroke-dasharray='3 5'/><path d='M16 32h16'/>

karty.g: It benefits the player to remember facts about the game or its state.
karty.nz: Information must be shown briefly or only once, and later decisions must depend on recalling it. It must not be easy to look up again, and there must be enough variation that memory beyond one session helps.
karty.yr: A game with facts to remember, but the interface always shows them again or they never affect any decision.
karty.rk: how long information stays visible; how much has to be remembered; whether it can be looked up again
karty.ik: <rect x='5' y='14' width='24' height='36' rx='3' fill='#fff'/><circle cx='17' cy='32' r='7' fill='#e85d4f'/><rect x='35' y='14' width='24' height='36' rx='3' fill='#2f6b8f'/><path d='M42 24l10 16M52 24L42 40' stroke='#fff' stroke-width='2.5'/>

karty.g: Game characters remember important past events and show that they do.
karty.nz: The design needs a way to detect and record significant events, and then characters must refer to them later in speech or behavior at fitting moments. The recall has to be specific to what the player did.
karty.yr: Characters say a generic scripted line that sounds like remembering but is identical whatever the player did.
karty.rk: how many event types are tracked; how long they are kept; how visibly characters react

karty.g: Games built on the results and consequences of other games.
karty.nz: Results must carry over and be comparable between games, through scores, rankings or tournament structure. Players need a reason to care about this layer.
karty.yr: A leaderboard or achievement list that is displayed but changes no decisions and which nobody pursues or compares.
karty.rk: what carries between games; how results are compared or rewarded
karty.ik: <rect x='6' y='6' width='36' height='36' rx='2'/><path d='M18 6v36M30 6v36M6 18h36M6 30h36' stroke-width='2.5'/><circle cx='44' cy='44' r='14' fill='#c9a24a'/><circle cx='44' cy='44' r='6'/>

karty.g: Servers that assign players to game servers and store shared data about them.
karty.nz: The service must really connect players to game servers, remember their data across sessions and offer features like friend lookup. It needs enough players to make the routing worthwhile.
karty.yr: A server list or login screen that only lists servers and neither routes players nor stores anything across sessions.
karty.rk: what the server stores and offers: matchmaking, friend lists, global rankings
karty.ik: <rect x='18' y='5' width='28' height='14' rx='3' fill='#c9a24a'/><path d='M32 19v8M10 27h44M10 27v6M32 27v6M54 27v6'/><rect x='3' y='33' width='14' height='20' rx='3'/><rect x='25' y='33' width='14' height='20' rx='3'/><rect x='47' y='33' width='14' height='20' rx='3'/>

karty.g: Agreed poses and gestures convey information about the game without breaking character.
karty.nz: The gestures must be few, easy to learn, clearly different from each other and visible without breaking the fiction. Everyone must know the meanings.
karty.yr: A list of gestures on paper that players forget or ignore, so they keep speaking out of character anyway.
karty.rk: how many gestures; how distinct and how visible they are

karty.g: In role-playing, players tell each other something without passing it on to their characters.
karty.nz: The game must give players actual methods for signaling about rules or desired direction without speaking through characters, and players must be taught and use them. The method must suit the fiction.
karty.yr: A rule that says players may communicate out of character but gives no actual technique, so it is just ordinary talking.
karty.rk: which technique types are offered; how intrusive they are

karty.g: All stages of the game between the beginning and the end.
karty.nz: The game needs recognizable phases, so the middle must have its own goals and kinds of action, such as expanding or building, different from the opening and the end. Rules like balancing effects can be tied to it.
karty.yr: A game whose phases are named in the manual but play feels the same throughout, with no real shift in goals or actions.
karty.rk: how long the middle lasts; what shifts in goals and rules separate it from other phases
karty.ik: <rect x='4' y='20' width='16' height='24' rx='2' fill='#d5d9e0'/><rect x='24' y='20' width='16' height='24' rx='2' fill='#e85d4f'/><rect x='44' y='20' width='16' height='24' rx='2' fill='#d5d9e0'/><path d='M4 54h56'/>

karty.g: Sensors judge how accurately the player copies movements, and this is part of the game.
karty.nz: The sensors must measure real physical movement and the game must score how well it is done. Tolerance should be tuned so players can learn gradually.
karty.yr: A game with a themed controller, such as a plastic guitar, where pressing buttons gives the same result and the physical action is not really measured.
karty.rk: how strictly the performance is judged; how tolerant the early levels are
karty.ik: <rect x='22' y='8' width='20' height='48' rx='6' fill='#fff'/><circle cx='32' cy='22' r='4' fill='#e85d4f'/><path d='M27 36h10M27 44h10'/><path d='M10 20c-4 8-4 16 0 24M54 20c4 8 4 16 0 24' stroke-width='3'/>

karty.g: A small map showing the game world in broad outline.
karty.nz: The map must show the player's position and relevant things in the world in a readable way, and the world must be big enough that overview is needed. What it shows or hides should be chosen deliberately.
karty.yr: A small map that is too vague or too cluttered to read, or a world so small that nobody ever looks at it.
karty.rk: how much it shows: zoom, markers, hidden areas
karty.ik: <rect x='4' y='6' width='56' height='52' rx='3'/><path d='M8 50l10-16 8 10 6-6'/><rect x='34' y='12' width='20' height='20' rx='2' fill='#d5d9e0'/><path d='M38 28l5-8 5 4' stroke-width='2.5'/><circle cx='48' cy='24' r='3' fill='#e85d4f' stroke='none'/>

karty.g: A small game inside another game.
karty.nz: The small game needs its own distinct rules, and its outcome should feed back into the outer game. They should be short and different enough to bring variety.
karty.yr: A reskinned menu choice or a brief interlude with no skill or choice that changes nothing in the outer game.
karty.rk: how many there are; how long each lasts; how their results affect the main game

karty.g: The game barely gets in the way of people talking to each other during play.
karty.nz: The game must demand little attention and have natural pauses, with little bookkeeping and no long waits. Players should be able to stop and resume freely.
karty.yr: A game described as casual or social that still demands constant attention or long upkeep, so conversation suffers.
karty.rk: how much attention the game demands; how easy it is to interrupt; how much upkeep it needs

karty.g: The player can act to reduce their own risk of failure.
karty.nz: Bad luck must be possible and costly, and players need real options to reduce it, such as rerolls, known odds or a choice of action order. The options must cost something.
karty.yr: A mitigation option that is available but either always the obvious choice or so weak that it does not change outcomes.
karty.rk: how many rerolls or extra chances; how much they cost; how well the odds are known

karty.g: World elements that move, but not of their own will.
karty.nz: The tiles need clear movement rules, such as what triggers them and where they stop, and the level must be built so their movement matters, for example by carrying, blocking or opening routes.
karty.yr: Tiles that move as decoration, on a path that never affects where players can go or what they can do.
karty.rk: movement pattern, speed and what triggers it

karty.g: Action of moving game elements around the game world.
karty.nz: The game needs a space and clear rules for how elements move through it. The terrain and goals should make where and how far one moves matter.
karty.yr: Things technically move, but in a space so empty or with goals so unrelated that position never matters.
karty.rk: speed or distance per move; terrain costs; restrictions on direction
karty.ik: <circle cx='16' cy='20' r='7' fill='#2f6b8f'/><path d='M8 46c0-10 4-14 8-14s8 4 8 14z' fill='#2f6b8f'/><path d='M6 54h20'/><path d='M30 40h18' stroke-dasharray='1 7'/><path d='M50 32l10 8-10 8z' fill='#e85d4f'/>

karty.g: Changes that make moving worse than it was before.
karty.nz: Movement must already matter in the game, and the limitation must be felt in play, with players needing to plan around it. It should be tied to places, states or enemies.
karty.yr: A slowdown so small or so easily avoided that players ignore it and route exactly as before.
karty.rk: how much speed or range is lost; how long it lasts; terrain costs
karty.ik: <circle cx='14' cy='14' r='7' fill='#e85d4f'/><ellipse cx='26' cy='26' rx='3' ry='6' transform='rotate(-45 26 26)'/><ellipse cx='33' cy='33' rx='3' ry='6' transform='rotate(-45 33 33)'/><circle cx='46' cy='46' r='14' fill='#2a2a2a'/>

karty.g: Programs that take over monotonous, repetitive actions from the player.
karty.nz: The game must have repetitive tasks worth delegating, and the automation must be able to run them without the player. Limits on efficiency or risks keep it from replacing play entirely.
karty.yr: An auto-play button that does the task but is so weak or so restricted that players still do everything by hand.
karty.rk: which tasks can be automated; how efficient; what risks come with it
karty.ik: <rect x='12' y='20' width='40' height='32' rx='6' fill='#d5d9e0'/><path d='M32 20V11'/><circle cx='32' cy='8' r='3' fill='#e85d4f'/><path d='M23 32h0M41 32h0' stroke-width='6'/><path d='M24 44h16'/>

karty.g: Games in which more than one player takes part.
karty.nz: The rules must give each player a real role with consequences for the others, through competition, cooperation or communication. Players need ways to find and join each other.
karty.yr: A game that supports several players but where they play in parallel with no effect on one another.
karty.rk: number of players; competitive or cooperative; how much they affect each other

karty.g: Enjoyment from handling chaos and difficult situations together.
karty.nz: The game needs chaotic, overwhelming situations that a group faces jointly, with enough pressure that coordination matters yet manageable enough to leave a sense of getting through. Shared goals or teams help.
karty.yr: Chaos where each player is overwhelmed alone, or chaos so total that success is impossible and play is just frustrating.
karty.rk: how chaotic and pressured the challenges are; how much players depend on each other
karty.ik: <circle cx='30' cy='38' r='20' fill='#2a2a2a'/><path d='M42 22l8-10'/><circle cx='52' cy='10' r='5' fill='#c9a24a'/><path d='M20 40c4 8 14 8 18 0' stroke='#fff'/>

karty.g: Goal in which the same task faces two or more participants.
karty.nz: Players must truly succeed or fail together, with shared rewards or penalties. Added individual incentives decide whether the shared goal stays shared.
karty.yr: A team label or common objective in the text while outcomes and rewards stay individual, so players just pursue their own aims.
karty.rk: how much is shared versus individual; how big the shared reward is

karty.g: The structure of stories that the game contains or can generate.
karty.nz: Events and goals must be linked to the story so that progress moves it forward. The structure needs points of tension and closure that gameplay actually reaches.
karty.yr: A story told in intro text and cutscenes that has no link to the goals or actions, so play would be identical without it.
karty.rk: how tightly the story is tied to goals; how linear or branching it is

karty.g: After a failure, the player sees how close they or others came to the goal.
karty.nz: The game must measure closeness to success and show it clearly after a failure. It needs to be informative enough that players use it for their next attempt.
karty.yr: A generic failure message, or a near-miss display that shows the same thing whether the miss was narrow or wide.
karty.rk: how precisely the near-miss is measured and shown; how often it is displayed

karty.g: Rules that bring some game measure back toward a preset value.
karty.nz: The game must measure a part of the state, such as relative position, and apply a counter-effect strong enough to matter but not so strong that effort is pointless. It usually needs playtesting.
karty.yr: A catch-up bonus so small that leaders still win, or so large that it flips results no matter how people play.
karty.rk: how strong the correction is; what is measured; how soon it triggers

karty.g: Players themselves agree on how long the whole session will last.
karty.nz: The game must have an adjustable end condition and a point before play where players agree on it. The game must still work at different lengths.
karty.yr: A length setting that exists in the menu but is nearly always left at default, or one where a short setting breaks the game.
karty.rk: which limits players can set: time, turns or score target

karty.g: A player can influence how long they play without spoiling the game for others.
karty.nz: The game must give a meaningful experience at both short and long lengths, with natural stopping points and ways to extend or shorten play. Other players must not be harmed by the choice.
karty.yr: A game claiming flexible length while the content or progression needs a fixed time, so short sessions feel incomplete.
karty.rk: minimum and maximum session length; points where play can end

karty.g: Each person decides how long to play, and this does not spoil the session for others.
karty.nz: Players must be able to leave and return without breaking progress for themselves or others, through pauses, saves, turn breaks or drop-in play.
karty.yr: A pause or save feature that exists but penalizes leaving, or is unusable in multiplayer, so players must stay until the end.
karty.rk: how easy it is to pause or leave; how much progress is lost by stopping
karty.ik: <circle cx='32' cy='32' r='25'/><path d='M25 22v20M39 22v20' stroke='#e85d4f' stroke-width='7'/>

karty.g: Skills gained during the game that open up new actions.
karty.nz: The ability must allow an action that was not possible before and be introduced at a time that opens new options. The game must give uses for it, such as new challenges.
karty.yr: A new ability that is only a number increase or a reskin of an old action, or one with no situation that calls for it.
karty.rk: when abilities are given; how many; how different they are from existing ones

karty.g: Taking loot that the player has no right to.
karty.nz: Loot must be physically takeable by anyone nearby and ownership must not be enforced. The reward must be worth taking, and other players must be near enough to do it.
karty.yr: Loot labeled as shared or ownable that is in fact automatically assigned, so nobody can take anything from others.
karty.rk: who can pick up loot and when; how long loot stays unprotected
karty.ik: <circle cx='30' cy='30' r='20' fill='#2a2a2a'/><rect x='14' y='24' width='32' height='12' rx='6' fill='#fff'/><path d='M24 30h0M36 30h0' stroke-width='5'/><circle cx='50' cy='50' r='8' fill='#c9a24a'/>

karty.g: Games where the player barely or never directly controls what happens.
karty.nz: The rules must cut players off from changing the game state, while still giving them something to do around it, such as betting, building an agent beforehand, or setting up an initial state. Their involvement has to be real enough that they stay emotionally invested.
karty.yr: A game with only a few trivial buttons that look like input but make no difference to the result, and nothing else for players to engage with.
karty.rk: how much input players get, if any; whether they can prepare in advance or place bets
karty.ik: <rect x='10' y='10' width='44' height='44' rx='9' fill='#fff'/><path d='M22 22h0M42 22h0M32 32h0M22 42h0M42 42h0' stroke-width='6' stroke='#e85d4f'/>

karty.g: Player actions that change nothing in the game state.
karty.nz: Waiting must be a legal choice, or a forced effect, and the game state must keep changing while the player waits so that waiting has a point. Whether it is voluntary or forced determines whether it feels like a strategic choice or a punishment.
karty.yr: A pass button that is never worth using because the situation never rewards waiting, or a forced skip so rare that it never affects anyone.
karty.rk: whether no-ops are voluntary or forced; how often and how long they last

karty.g: Unused actions are given a bonus so they get chosen more often later.
karty.nz: Actions must be chosen from a shared set, and the bonus must grow enough over turns to shift the value of the neglected option. The reward type should matter to players.
karty.yr: A bonus so small or so irrelevant that unpopular actions stay ignored, or one that arrives only after the action has already become attractive for other reasons.
karty.rk: what resource is added; how much per unused turn; whether the bonus accumulates or resets
karty.ik: <ellipse cx='24' cy='50' rx='17' ry='6' fill='#c9a24a'/><ellipse cx='24' cy='40' rx='17' ry='6' fill='#c9a24a'/><ellipse cx='24' cy='30' rx='17' ry='6' fill='#c9a24a'/><path d='M52 28V10M45 17l7-7 7 7' stroke='#e85d4f'/>

karty.g: Narration in the game whose parts do not agree with each other.
karty.nz: Story elements must be repeated or contradict the game world's history, with instances or phasing isolating the inconsistency so that only the players inside it see it. It must be a deliberate trade-off for the sake of reuse or scale.
karty.yr: A story that is just sloppy and contradictory by accident, with no reuse or purpose behind it, which only breaks immersion without giving anything back.
karty.rk: how much story content is reused; how isolated each player's copy is (instancing or phasing)

karty.g: Players talk to each other as real people, not as characters of the world.
karty.nz: Players need channels and reasons to talk outside the fiction, such as shared information, social settings or non-diegetic UI. Designers who want less of it must give diegetic substitutes or remove the triggers.
karty.yr: Chat that exists but nobody uses to talk about anything outside the story, or a chat that is framed as in-world speech while players still use it for out-of-game coordination.
karty.rk: how much out-of-fiction communication is allowed or provided with channels; how much non-diegetic information the game exposes

karty.g: Parts of the game's presentation that do not fit into its fictional world.
karty.nz: The game needs a world with a fiction and then must show information that does not belong to it, such as indicators, markers or notifications. Placement and prominence decide how much they break consistency.
karty.yr: A HUD element dressed up as an in-world object so it looks diegetic, or an indicator that duplicates what the world already shows and adds nothing.
karty.rk: how much non-diegetic information is shown; how prominent it is and whether it can be hidden
karty.ik: <rect x="6" y="8" width="52" height="36" rx="3" fill="#d5d9e0"/><path d="M6 36l14-12 12 10 10-8 16 12"/><rect x="12" y="12" width="22" height="8" rx="2" fill="#c9a24a" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M24 56h16M32 44v12"/>

karty.g: Resources that are at least partly not tied to a place in the game world.
karty.nz: The game must have a world in which other things have locations, and the resources must be held as abstract counts that cannot be seen, stolen or carried in space. Designers choose which resources and whether all or only acquired instances are abstract.
karty.yr: A counter in the interface that is still tied to a physical item players must go and fetch or guard in the world, so it behaves as a located resource anyway.
karty.rk: which resources are abstract; whether all instances or only collected ones are non-localized

karty.g: Characters in the game world that players do not control.
karty.nz: The game needs a world for NPCs to live in, and each NPC needs a clear role and recognizable look. Whether they act as agents with goals or only as scenery or story devices decides how much they matter.
karty.yr: Figures standing in the world that do nothing, say nothing and affect nothing, so they are scenery with a name tag.
karty.rk: how many NPCs; what role each has; whether they have agency and goals

karty.g: The game expects people who are not playing to help the players.
karty.nz: Outsiders must know they can help, and the help must be restricted by limited actions, power and cooldowns so it does not skew balance or devalue players' own effort. Information from helpers can be unreliable to keep it risky.
karty.yr: A help feature that nobody outside the game is told about, or that gives such weak or restricted help that it never changes any outcome.
karty.rk: how strong helpers' actions are; how often they can help; how helpers are informed and admitted

karty.g: Resources whose amount does not grow during the game.
karty.nz: There must be no generation or replenishment of the resource anywhere in the game, and there must be consumers that use it up. Without consumption, players can hoard it and the scarcity never bites.
karty.yr: A resource labelled as finite but with a hidden refill, or one so plentiful for the game's length that it never runs out and never changes decisions.
karty.rk: starting amount; consumption rate; whether the limit is global or per player

karty.g: Elements that block the shortest path between two places.
karty.nz: Obstacles must sit on routes players want to take and force a detour, a wait, or some action to bypass them. Whether they can be destroyed, moved or ignored by some players defines what they mean for play.
karty.yr: Decoration placed off the routes that players take, or an object that can be walked through or around at no cost.
karty.rk: size and placement; whether they can be removed or bypassed, and by whom
karty.ik: <path d="M4 56h56"/><path d="M10 56V30M30 56V30" stroke-width="4"/><rect x="8" y="22" width="34" height="12" rx="2" fill="#e85d4f"/><path d="M46 56c0-8 4-14 10-14" stroke="#2f6b8f"/><path d="M48 38l8 4-8 4" stroke-width="3"/>

karty.g: Characters' stories turn out differently from game to game because of what happens.
karty.nz: Characters or factions need tracked state that actually changes in response to events, and endings must differ enough to be noticeable. There must be few enough distinct outcomes, each reachable by different play, for players to see the difference.
karty.yr: Several endings that are only a cosmetic text change on top of the same arc, or a branching that always converges to the same fate.
karty.rk: how many distinct endings; which characters or factions have a tracked arc; how much play affects each arc

karty.g: Some rolled values require rolling the dice again until a final result forms.
karty.nz: Certain results must trigger further rolls that add to the total, so the range has no fixed ceiling. The trigger value, the dice it applies to and any cap decide how often the extreme results happen.
karty.yr: A re-roll rule so rarely triggered, or so capped, that results never go beyond what a normal roll could give.
karty.rk: which results trigger rerolls; which dice it applies to; whether there is a cap on repeats

karty.g: Goal that need not be completed to win or finish the game.
karty.nz: The goals must be visible and worth pursuing for their own sake, and the game must not require them to win. Tracking them with a reward or penalty gives them more weight.
karty.yr: A listed side goal with no reward or interest, so nobody ever goes for it, or one that is secretly required to progress.
karty.rk: how many optional goals; whether the game tracks them; what reward or penalty they carry
karty.ik: <path d="M14 58V6"/><path d="M14 8h30l-8 9 8 9H14z" fill="#d5d9e0" stroke-dasharray="4 5"/><circle cx="46" cy="46" r="10" fill="#c9a24a"/><path d="M46 40v12M40 46h12" stroke-width="3"/>

karty.g: Rules that players themselves decide whether to use.
karty.nz: The rule set must have clearly separate modules that can be added without breaking the core game. Too many options add confusion and production cost, so a small set that is easy to explain works best.
karty.yr: An option that is listed in the rulebook but changes nothing in play, or is so entangled with the core rules that nobody can use it without breaking the game.
karty.rk: how many optional rules; when they can be chosen (before play, during play, by whom)
karty.ik: <rect x="8" y="6" width="36" height="48" rx="3"/><path d="M15 18h22M15 28h22M15 38h12"/><rect x="36" y="38" width="24" height="14" rx="7" fill="#4fa83a"/><circle cx="53" cy="45" r="4" fill="#fff" stroke-width="2.5"/>

karty.g: Entities differ in kind of abilities rather than in number: not stronger, but different.
karty.nz: Each entity must be able to do something others cannot do at all, not just do the same thing better. The differences need to matter in play so that players need the entities for their special function.
karty.yr: Units with different names, looks and stat numbers, but who all do the same kind of thing, so they are just reskins with different values.
karty.rk: how many entity types; how unique each ability is; how the sets are distributed among players
karty.ik: <circle cx="15" cy="18" r="10" fill="#e85d4f"/><rect x="38" y="8" width="20" height="20" rx="2" fill="#2f6b8f"/><path d="M6 56l18-24 18 24z" fill="#c9a24a"/><path d="M46 36v22M36 47h20" stroke-width="5"/>

karty.g: Extra signals about how an action ended, beyond its effect in the world.
karty.nz: There must be an outcome that players cannot easily read from the world itself, and the indicator must report it clearly and at the right time. The detail level can be varied to keep some uncertainty.
karty.yr: An indicator that repeats what is already obvious on screen, or one that appears too late or too vaguely to help players understand what happened.
karty.rk: what outcomes are indicated; how precise the information is; how long and when it is shown
karty.ik: <path d="M10 50a24 24 0 0 1 44 0"/><path d="M32 50l10-20" stroke="#e85d4f"/><circle cx="32" cy="50" r="4" fill="#2a2a2a"/><path d="M14 40l-4-3M32 20v-6M50 40l4-3" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M8 60h48" stroke="#4fa83a"/>

karty.g: Goal of defeating an opposing force.
karty.nz: There must be an opponent with a way to resist or act against the player, and clear rules for what counts as defeating it. The opposing force needs agency or a story that makes it feel like a force.
karty.yr: An enemy that is on the goal list but is passive and cannot resist, so defeating it is just a chore, or a victory that is announced without any real opposition.
karty.rk: what opponents are to be defeated; how many; how defeat is defined and how strong they are
karty.ik: <path d="M20 56V30" stroke-width="4"/><path d="M6 24h28M20 24V10" stroke="#2a2a2a"/><path d="M14 14l12 0" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M38 60V26l10-8 10 8v34z" fill="#d5d9e0"/><path d="M44 40h8M48 34v12" stroke="#e85d4f" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M4 60h56"/>

karty.g: Algorithm-controlled characters appear to pursue goals of their own.
karty.nz: Agents need actions towards their own goals, plus visible emotional reactions to progress, success and failure, supported by memory and context-sensitive responses. The impression must survive repeat play without obvious scripted patterns.
karty.yr: A character with a stated goal who behaves the same whatever happens and never shows any reaction to progress or setbacks.
karty.rk: how many agents have goals; how rich their emotional expression and memory are; how varied their reactions are
karty.ik: <rect x="14" y="22" width="28" height="24" rx="4" fill="#d5d9e0"/><path d="M28 22v-8"/><circle cx="28" cy="11" r="3" fill="#e85d4f"/><circle cx="22" cy="32" r="3" fill="#2a2a2a" stroke="none"/><circle cx="34" cy="32" r="3" fill="#2a2a2a" stroke="none"/><path d="M22 40h12"/><path d="M46 56V36l12 5-12 5" fill="#c9a24a" stroke-width="3"/>

karty.g: Losing one element does not stop the game, but losing all or a set number does.
karty.nz: Players must control several elements at risk at once, and losing one must hurt but not stop play. The elements should matter enough that players must decide which to protect, so threats come at them concurrently.
karty.yr: Several units where only one really matters, or ones so easily replaced that losing them never forces a choice.
karty.rk: how many elements; how much each is worth; how many must be lost to end the game

karty.g: Groups of characters acting together toward a common goal within the world.
karty.nz: Characters must need each other, for example through complementary roles, and the group must have a size limit or composition choices. The relationships among them must give real reasons for cooperating.
karty.yr: A group of characters that follow the player around but are interchangeable and contribute nothing, so the party is just a count.
karty.rk: party size and maximum; how roles are distributed; how many characters each player controls

karty.g: A save that consists of a single password.
karty.nz: The game state to save must be small enough to encode in a short code that players can write down and type in. The code must be generated from the state and accepted on entry.
karty.yr: A code that is just a level name anyone can guess, or one that does not actually restore the progress it claims to.
karty.rk: what state the password encodes; its length and format; when it is shown
karty.ik: <rect x="10" y="28" width="44" height="28" rx="4" fill="#c9a24a"/><path d="M18 28v-6a14 14 0 0 1 28 0v6"/><circle cx="32" cy="40" r="3" fill="#2a2a2a"/><path d="M32 43v7" stroke-width="3"/>

karty.g: To play, you must pay in one form or another.
karty.nz: Payment must be required to start or to continue playing, and it needs to be tied to something players want enough to pay. The price and timing have to fit what players find acceptable.
karty.yr: A payment that is optional for cosmetic extras only, so nobody actually pays to play, or one required once at purchase, which is just ownership.
karty.rk: price; when payment is demanded (entry, continue, extras); what each payment buys
karty.ik: <circle cx="22" cy="22" r="15" fill="#c9a24a"/><circle cx="22" cy="22" r="7" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M38 44h22M6 44h8"/><rect x="28" y="38" width="30" height="18" rx="3" fill="#2f6b8f"/><path d="M43 42v10" stroke="#fff" stroke-width="3"/>

karty.g: Unpleasant consequences for the player's position, progress, or abilities.
karty.nz: The effect must actually worsen the player's position, progress or abilities, and it must follow from specific events. It needs to be large enough to be felt but fair enough that it does not break the experience.
karty.yr: A penalty so small or so easily undone that players ignore it, or one that is announced but changes nothing in the game state.
karty.rk: how severe; what triggers it; whether it can be recovered from
