karty.ik: <rect x="17" y="10" width="26" height="38" rx="3" fill="#e85d4f" transform="rotate(12 30 29)"/><path d="M50 10l7-4M52 20h8M50 30l7 4" stroke-width="3"/>

karty.g: The outcome depends on how skillfully the player performs the action themselves.
karty.nz: Outcomes must depend on skill in a physical, mental or social task that varies from player to player and moment to moment. Success must not be guaranteed by simply knowing a procedure.
karty.yr: An action that looks skill-based but has a fixed outcome whatever the player does, or one so easy that everyone succeeds every time.
karty.rk: how demanding the skill task is; how much the result depends on performance versus system; tolerance for error
karty.ik: <circle cx="32" cy="32" r="26" fill="#fff"/><circle cx="32" cy="32" r="16"/><circle cx="32" cy="32" r="6" fill="#e85d4f"/><path d="M58 6L36 28" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M52 6h6v6" stroke-width="3"/>

karty.g: A character's death is irreversible and they cannot be brought back.
karty.nz: Death must truly remove the character with no respawn, and loading an earlier state must not be possible, or it loses meaning. The game must be built around the loss so it feels like a real stake.
karty.yr: A death that is advertised as permanent but can be undone by loading a save or a free revive, so it costs nothing.
karty.rk: what can permanently die; whether there are extra chances; whether saves are allowed
karty.ik: <path d="M14 58V24a18 18 0 0 1 36 0v34z" fill="#d5d9e0"/><path d="M32 28v18M24 35h16" stroke-width="5"/><path d="M4 58h56"/>

karty.g: Changes in the game world that do not revert on their own.
karty.nz: Player actions must alter the world state and that state must be kept, not reverted by resets or temporary instances. There must be ways to change the world, such as building, destroying or moving things.
karty.yr: World changes that vanish on reload or after a short time, or that are only visual and do not affect later gameplay.
karty.rk: which changes persist; for how long; whether and when the world resets
karty.ik: <path d="M4 54h56"/><path d="M8 54V34l10-8 10 8v20z" fill="#c9a24a"/><path d="M36 54V40l8-6 6 6M50 40l6 14" stroke="#2a2a2a"/><path d="M38 54l6-14 6 14z" fill="#e85d4f" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M32 10l-6 6 6 6" stroke="#2f6b8f" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M26 16h20" stroke="#2f6b8f" stroke-width="3"/>

karty.g: The world exists by itself, whether or not anyone is playing it.
karty.nz: Servers or facilitators must keep the world running continuously, with state updated even when players are absent. Characters and items must be tracked over time.
karty.yr: A world that exists only while players are logged in or that resets each session, called persistent in marketing only.
karty.rk: what state persists; how the world updates while players are away; reset schedule

karty.g: The player tries to see events through another player's or fictional character's eyes.
karty.nz: The game needs roles or characters that players must understand to act well, such as role-playing or a game master voicing characters. Rewarding choices that fit another's view makes it more likely.
karty.yr: A role-play label or character sheet that players never need to consider when deciding, so everyone just acts as themselves.
karty.rk: how much the game rewards acting from another's view; how detailed the characters or roles are

karty.g: A game that coexists with everyday activities or blends into them.
karty.nz: Gameplay must be able to happen alongside ordinary activities, through real-life actions that affect the game state, ubiquitous access and safe spots or drop-in and drop-out. It must not demand dedicated places or equipment.
karty.yr: A mobile game that is said to be played anywhere but needs focused attention and a dedicated session, so it never blends with other activities.
karty.rk: which real-life activities count; how often and when the game asks for attention; how interruptible it is
karty.ik: <rect x="4" y="26" width="22" height="34" rx="4" fill="#2f6b8f"/><path d="M12 54h6" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M30 60V30l10-8 10 8v30z" fill="#d5d9e0"/><path d="M36 60V46h8v14" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M12 20c4-6 10-6 14 0M8 14c6-10 16-10 22 0" stroke="#e85d4f"/>

karty.g: In one session, world elements are removed or changed for some players.
karty.nz: The design must define the phases, the triggers for entering and leaving them, and whether players share a phase. Gameplay must also be tied to what each phase shows, so the difference actually matters.
karty.yr: Different players see slightly different scenery, but nothing in their goals, options or story differs, so nobody notices or cares.
karty.rk: how many phases exist; what triggers entering and leaving; whether players share a phase
karty.ik: <circle cx="22" cy="32" r="18" fill="#fff"/><circle cx="42" cy="32" r="18" fill="#d5d9e0" fill-opacity=".7"/><path d="M32 16c-5 5-5 27 0 32" stroke="#2f6b8f" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M18 28h0M46 36h0" stroke-width="5"/>

karty.g: The player personally performs actions that then happen in the game.
karty.nz: The game needs a way to read or judge the body action, and a clear choice of which actions are enacted and which are abstracted. The physical demand has to be what decides outcomes.
karty.yr: A motion-controller game where a button press or tiny flick does the same job as the gesture, so the movement is just decoration.
karty.rk: which actions must be physically performed; how large and demanding the movement is; how strictly it is judged

karty.g: The player finds their way through the game environment by actually moving through space.
karty.nz: The game needs real-world goal locations, a way to confirm arrival, and obstacles that make the route matter. Designers must also decide whether speed and fitness should count.
karty.yr: Players are told to walk somewhere, but the goal could be completed from the sofa or the route never matters.
karty.rk: distance between goal locations; how arrival is verified; time pressure

karty.g: Items lying in the game world, usually picked up by touching them.
karty.nz: Items must be placed where reaching them costs something or means a choice, and they must give a gain that players care about. They should be visibly distinct so players can find and want them.
karty.yr: Items lie everywhere in such quantity or with such trivial value that players grab them on autopilot and nothing is decided.
karty.rk: how many are placed; where; how much each gives; whether they respawn and how fast

karty.g: One image or view is shown inside another.
karty.nz: The inset must show information players really need during play that the main view cannot, in a place and size that does not hide the main action. Its content should change what players decide.
karty.yr: A small window duplicates what the main view already shows, or is too tiny or cluttered to read, so nobody uses it.
karty.rk: what it shows; its size and position; whether players can move, resize or switch it
karty.ik: <rect x="4" y="6" width="56" height="44" rx="3"/><path d="M4 40l16-14 14 12 10-8 16 12"/><rect x="34" y="10" width="22" height="16" rx="2" fill="#2f6b8f"/><circle cx="45" cy="18" r="4" fill="#fff" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M22 58h20"/>

karty.g: The player can change the course of the game through their actions.
karty.nz: Choices must have visible, lasting consequences, and several options must be viable rather than one obvious best. The game must respond clearly to what the player did.
karty.yr: The game offers many buttons and options, but the result is the same whatever the player picks, or the game plays itself.
karty.rk: number and meaningfulness of choices; how strongly and visibly actions change the state
karty.ik: <path d="M18 6v34" stroke-width="4"/><circle cx="18" cy="14" r="8" fill="#e85d4f"/><rect x="6" y="40" width="24" height="8" rx="2" fill="#d5d9e0"/><path d="M36 30c4-6 8-6 10 0v-8c0-4 6-4 6 0v6c0-4 6-4 6 0v6c0-4 6-4 6 0v14c0 8-6 12-14 12s-14-6-14-10z" stroke-width="3" transform="translate(-6 4) scale(.9)" fill="#fff"/>

karty.g: Handouts with extra information about the game world or the current situation.
karty.nz: The aid must hold information players can use or react to, and be given at a well-chosen moment. Its look and material should fit the fiction.
karty.yr: A handout that only repeats what the players already know and is thrown away unread.
karty.rk: what information it holds; when it is handed out; its material and visual design

karty.g: Other players do not know who exactly is playing.
karty.nz: The game must remove or block identity cues such as names, voice and friend links, and enforce this consistently. Designers must decide whether anonymity is optional or forced.
karty.yr: Players are called 'anonymous' but use persistent handles, or can easily be recognised from chat or friend lists.
karty.rk: whether anonymity is forced or optional; which identity cues are hidden; whether communication is allowed
karty.ik: <circle cx="32" cy="20" r="12" fill="#fff"/><path d="M20 20h24" stroke-width="0"/><path d="M22 18h20v6a10 10 0 0 1-20 0z" fill="#2a2a2a" stroke="none"/><path d="M10 60c0-14 8-22 22-22s22 8 22 22z" fill="#d5d9e0"/><path d="M32 44v8" stroke="#c9a24a" stroke-width="6"/>

karty.g: Support that helps the player perform game actions better.
karty.nz: The help must truly change the success of specific actions, and must be tuned against the game's challenge. Designers must decide who gets it, so that it neither trivialises play nor feels useless.
karty.yr: An assist option exists but is so weak, or so hidden, that results are the same with or without it.
karty.rk: strength of the help; which actions it affects; who receives it
karty.ik: <path d="M10 36h44M10 36l-4-6M54 36l4-6"/><rect x="14" y="20" width="36" height="22" rx="4" fill="#d5d9e0"/><path d="M32 50V26M24 34l8-8 8 8" stroke="#4fa83a" stroke-width="5"/><path d="M18 58h28"/>

karty.g: Game design that gives everyone equal chances of success or victory.
karty.nz: Starting positions, resources and abilities must be near-equal, or any asymmetry must be offset by something else. Designers must watch for feedback loops that let an early lead decide everything, and test with real play.
karty.yr: The sides look symmetrical on paper, but one option or position wins nearly every time in practice.
karty.rk: how equal starting resources and abilities are; strength of catch-up or anti-snowball rules

karty.g: Characters the player directly controls and through whom they take part in the game.
karty.nz: The character needs its own traits, abilities and a role in the story that give the player something to act through and care about. The link between player knowledge and character knowledge needs to be handled.
karty.yr: A named figure on screen with no traits, history or effect on play, which is really just a cursor.
karty.rk: how detailed the character is; its power compared with others; how much the player can shape it

karty.g: Game elements that players make themselves for use in the game.
karty.nz: The game must offer creation tools and a way for the made elements to enter play and matter there. Designers must also handle effects on balance and on the economy.
karty.yr: Players can make things, but they stay cosmetic or are never used in actual gameplay.
karty.rk: what players may create; how much freedom they have; how created items enter the game
karty.ik: <path d="M10 8h28v14H10z" fill="#c9a24a"/><path d="M24 22v36" stroke-width="0"/><rect x="6" y="30" width="24" height="24" rx="2" fill="#fff"/><path d="M44 56l-2-14 14-26 8 4-14 26z" transform="translate(-8 0) scale(.85)" fill="#e85d4f"/><path d="M38 54l4-10 6 4z" fill="#2a2a2a" stroke-width="2"/>

karty.g: A player is forcibly removed from the game before it ends for everyone.
karty.nz: Clear elimination conditions are needed, together with a plan for what eliminated players do, such as spectating, and for how long the others keep playing. Game length must keep waiting time acceptable.
karty.yr: Players are 'out' in name but are respawned at once or keep playing, so being eliminated costs nothing.
karty.rk: how easily and how early players can be eliminated; what eliminated players can still do
karty.ik: <path d="M10 58V30l22-20 22 20v28z" fill="#d5d9e0"/><path d="M24 58V38h16v20"/><path d="M44 4l16 16M60 4L44 20" stroke="#e85d4f" stroke-width="5"/>

karty.g: A player is removed from the session by others' decision, not by the game's rules.
karty.nz: Someone must hold the power to kick, such as a moderator or a vote, with clear criteria and a defined length and scope. Without that, it will be unfair or ignored.
karty.yr: A kick button exists, but kicked players can rejoin immediately or nobody has the authority to use it.
karty.rk: who may kick; vote threshold; duration and scope of the ban

karty.g: Players are removed from active play by the deliberate actions of others.
karty.nz: Players must be able to harm each other, and the harm must be traceable to a real agent. Penalties for dying and rewards for killing have to make it a real choice.
karty.yr: Players can technically shoot each other, but death costs nothing and the victim returns at once, so it is just noise.
karty.rk: cost of dying; reward for killing; who can attack whom and where
karty.ik: <path d="M8 56L40 24" stroke-width="5"/><path d="M40 24l6-18 12 12z" fill="#d5d9e0"/><path d="M6 40l18 18" stroke="#c9a24a" stroke-width="6"/><path d="M46 40c0 6 2 8 8 8" stroke="#e85d4f" stroke-width="3"/><circle cx="50" cy="54" r="3" fill="#e85d4f" stroke="none"/>

karty.g: The game's outcome depends on how well players control their own bodies.
karty.nz: Tasks must really test strength, endurance, precision or reflexes, and be scored so that ability decides the result. The demand must be clearly measured.
karty.yr: A game labelled 'active' where physical skill makes no difference to the result.
karty.rk: how demanding the physical tasks are; time limits; how strictly performance is scored
karty.ik: <path d="M8 32h48" stroke-width="5"/><rect x="4" y="18" width="10" height="28" rx="3" fill="#e85d4f"/><rect x="50" y="18" width="10" height="28" rx="3" fill="#e85d4f"/><path d="M16 24v16M48 24v16" stroke-width="4"/><path d="M22 10l4-4M42 10l-4-4M32 8V3" stroke="#c9a24a" stroke-width="3"/>

karty.g: While it is unknown how others will act, the game's course cannot be foreseen exactly.
karty.nz: There must be several real opponents with meaningful choices, and information that is hidden or imperfect so their moves cannot be easily deduced. No single dominant strategy should exist.
karty.yr: Opponents are present but all follow the same obvious best line, so their moves are easy to predict.
karty.rk: number of opponents; how much information is hidden; how many viable strategies exist
karty.ik: <circle cx="32" cy="34" r="20" fill="#d5d9e0"/><path d="M24 28a8 8 0 1 1 11 7c-3 2-3 4-3 7" stroke-width="5"/><circle cx="32" cy="51" r="3.5" fill="#2a2a2a" stroke="none"/><path d="M12 10l6 6M52 10l-6 6" stroke="#e85d4f"/>

karty.g: Rules depend on how physically close the player is to certain objects.
karty.nz: The game needs a way to measure or verify closeness, a defined distance threshold, and events that really depend on it. The artifacts must matter to gameplay.
karty.yr: A proximity condition is claimed, but players can complete the task from anywhere or the check is never enforced.
karty.rk: distance threshold; what is triggered on entering or leaving; how long players must stay near
karty.ik: <circle cx="16" cy="20" r="7"/><path d="M4 48c0-9 5-14 12-14s12 5 12 14z" fill="#2f6b8f"/><path d="M40 34h18v16H40z" fill="#c9a24a"/><path d="M40 34l9-8 9 8"/><path d="M30 42h6" stroke-dasharray="1 5"/>

karty.g: Rules take into account how close the player and their avatar are in reality.
karty.nz: The game must track both the real position of one side and the virtual position of the other, and base events on how they relate. Both positions have to matter to play.
karty.yr: Both positions are tracked but the relation between them triggers nothing.
karty.rk: distance threshold; how long proximity must hold; what it triggers

karty.g: Characters whose creation the player was able to influence in some way.
karty.nz: Players need real options, such as traits, equipment and skills, that change how the character plays. Designers must balance the freedom against the time and knowledge it demands.
karty.yr: A long creation screen with only cosmetic choices, so every character plays the same.
karty.rk: number and depth of options; randomness in creation; when in the game customization happens
karty.ik: <circle cx="32" cy="20" r="10" fill="#fff"/><path d="M14 58c0-14 8-22 18-22s18 8 18 22z" fill="#2f6b8f"/><path d="M54 6l-18 18" stroke-width="5"/><path d="M36 24l-6 1 -1 6z" fill="#c9a24a" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M25 18h0M39 18h0" stroke-width="4"/>

karty.g: Goal where players themselves create or customize goals and subgoals in the game.
karty.nz: The game needs open systems, readable information such as scores and state, and room for varied approaches. Players must feel free to set aims beyond the official ones.
karty.yr: The game has a 'custom goal' menu that nobody uses, because the game offers no way to track or measure progress toward it.
karty.rk: how open the sandbox is; how visible scores and progress are; whether goals can be formally set up
karty.ik: <path d="M16 6v54"/><path d="M16 8h32l-8 10 8 10H16z" fill="#e85d4f"/><path d="M8 60h16"/><path d="M50 44l6 6M56 44l-6 6" stroke="#c9a24a" stroke-width="3"/>

karty.g: Rules depend on whether the player is physically near a place.
karty.nz: The game needs reliable position detection or self-reporting, defined places, and gameplay that truly depends on arriving there. The cost of travel has to be reasonable.
karty.yr: Places are listed as targets, but the player's actual position is never checked or never changes anything.
karty.rk: trigger distance; number and spacing of locations; how position is verified

karty.g: The player can plan in advance how the game's stats and objects will develop.
karty.nz: There must be several development paths with different long-term payoffs, and enough time and information for players to plan. The consequences have to carry forward.
karty.yr: A skill tree where every path ends up with the same power, so planning changes nothing.
karty.rk: number of branches; how different their payoffs are; how costly it is to change plans

karty.g: Rules depend on how close players are to each other.
karty.nz: The game must define what counts as near, which effects follow and how they are detected. It must also plan for the social contact this brings.
karty.yr: Players are told to stay close, but nothing in the rules reacts to the distance.
karty.rk: distance threshold; what is triggered when entering, keeping or breaking proximity

karty.g: The character knows about the world exactly what the player knows.
karty.nz: The interface and information rules must give the player only what the character knows, and the reverse. Any gap has to be closed on purpose.
karty.yr: The game claims the player sees through the character's eyes, but the UI shows hidden facts the character couldn't know.
karty.rk: how much information the player has beyond the character's knowledge; what the interface reveals

karty.g: An action's result depends on both the player's own skill and the character's attributes.
karty.nz: Each action's result must include a real contribution from the player's execution and from the character's attributes. Neither part should be able to cancel the other.
karty.yr: The character has stats, but the player's input decides everything, or the reverse, so one part is only for show.
karty.rk: relative weight of player skill versus character stats in outcomes
karty.ik: <circle cx="32" cy="14" r="8"/><path d="M18 54c0-10 5-16 14-16s14 6 14 16z" fill="#2f6b8f"/><path d="M6 24l14 14M10 44l-6-6" stroke-width="4"/><path d="M50 20l8 8M58 20l-8 8" stroke="#c9a24a" stroke-width="4"/><path d="M52 58V36" stroke-width="5"/><path d="M46 36h12" stroke-width="4"/>

karty.g: The player deliberately loses with their character because it is more interesting.
karty.nz: Failure must be allowed to be interesting, and players need room to roleplay and to shape their characters' fate. Rules should not wipe out a character too early, and the group should value dramatic loss.
karty.yr: Players say they will lose on purpose, but they still try to win, or losing simply ends the game with no story value.
karty.rk: how harsh the penalty for losing is; how much roleplay freedom players have; protection against early removal
karty.ik: <path d="M8 56V30h12v26M26 56V18h12v38M44 56V40h12v16" fill="#c9a24a"/><path d="M10 6v14M10 20l-5-6M10 20l5-6" stroke="#e85d4f" stroke-width="4"/><path d="M4 60h56"/>

karty.g: Hints that guide the player to important places and objects in the world.
karty.nz: The indicator must be clear and well timed, pointing at things that really matter. The game has to decide how much help it gives so it doesn't ruin exploration.
karty.yr: A marker is always on screen but is ignored, or points at things that don't matter.
karty.rk: how many things are marked; how obvious the marker is; when it appears
karty.ik: <circle cx="32" cy="32" r="24"/><path d="M32 12l7 20-7 20-7-20z" fill="#e85d4f"/><path d="M32 52l-7-20h14z" fill="#fff"/><circle cx="32" cy="32" r="2.5" fill="#2a2a2a" stroke="none"/>

karty.g: Goal of completing several challenges, each needing different skills.
karty.nz: Each event must need a different skill and have a clear result that can be combined into a final score. The mix must make players be either generalists or specialists.
karty.yr: Several events are listed, but they test the same skill, so it is really one game repeated.
karty.rk: number of events; how different their skills are; how they are weighted in the total
karty.ik: <circle cx="14" cy="20" r="10" fill="#2f6b8f"/><circle cx="32" cy="20" r="10" fill="#c9a24a" transform="translate(0 0)"/><circle cx="50" cy="20" r="10" fill="#e85d4f"/><circle cx="23" cy="34" r="10" fill="#4fa83a"/><circle cx="41" cy="34" r="10" fill="#fff"/>

karty.g: An effect reinforces itself: each next such effect is stronger than the previous one.
karty.nz: Rewards must make the next success easier or larger, with no strong caps or counter-effects. Designers must check how quickly the effect grows, or the leader runs away.
karty.yr: A bonus is given for winning, but it is so small or so capped that early leads fade and nothing compounds.
karty.rk: growth rate of the reward; strength of caps or counter-loops; how much advantage carries over
karty.ik: <path d="M32 8c14 0 24 10 24 22"/><path d="M56 30l-5-6M56 30l6-5" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M10 58a8 8 0 0 1 8-8" stroke="#e85d4f"/><circle cx="14" cy="54" r="5" fill="#c9a24a"/><circle cx="30" cy="46" r="8" fill="#c9a24a"/><circle cx="48" cy="46" r="12" fill="#c9a24a" transform="translate(0 0)"/>

karty.g: The player can choose not to reveal who they are.
karty.nz: The game must give players a way to hide their identity and must not leak it elsewhere, e.g. through cross-session statistics or friend lists. Communication has to go through masks such as handles or avatars.
karty.yr: A nickname field exists, but real names, linked accounts or public stats still reveal who the player is, so hiding changes nothing.
karty.rk: how much identity is shown; whether names, profiles and stats are linked across sessions

karty.g: The player can give up or leave without spoiling the session for others.
karty.nz: Leaving must not break the game for the others. That means handling the leaver's resources, closing kingmaker loopholes, and rebalancing or substituting an AI for the departed player.
karty.yr: A quit button exists, but leaving ends the match, ruins it for others or counts as a punishable desertion, so players stay on or ragequit.
karty.rk: what happens to the leaver's pieces and resources; whether an AI takes over; penalty for leaving
karty.ik: <path d="M14 60V8"/><path d="M14 10h34v24H14z" fill="#fff"/><path d="M14 10c10 6 22-6 34 0" stroke="none"/><path d="M24 56h28" stroke="#4fa83a"/><path d="M4 60h24"/>

karty.g: Fiddling with game resources for the sake of the activity, not for a goal.
karty.nz: Players need open-ended activities with no pressure, such as safe spaces, no hard deadlines, sorting or building tools, and freedom to set their own goals. Anything that threatens or interferes with their work must be limited.
karty.yr: A sandbox or farm exists, but constant threats, timers or mandatory objectives push players along, so nobody tinkers aimlessly.
karty.rk: amount of pressure and threat; how many self-directed activities are offered; how safe the space is

karty.g: Collectible items that immediately give a benefit or advantage.
karty.nz: Pickups must sit in places worth reaching and respawn on some schedule. Their effects have to matter for current goals and be balanced against the other players' advantages.
karty.yr: Shiny items lie around but give a negligible bonus or one that is never needed, so players ignore them.
karty.rk: spawn frequency and place; effect strength; effect duration or number of uses

karty.g: Goal set by the developers in advance, before the game starts.
karty.nz: Requirements and outcomes must be fixed in advance and visible enough for players to plan. A reward or consequence has to be attached to completing them.
karty.yr: A goal list is shown, but completing items gives nothing and changes no decisions, or players invent their own aims anyway.
karty.rk: how many goals; how they are ordered or nested; how much is revealed up front; reward size
karty.ik: <rect x="10" y="8" width="44" height="48" rx="4"/><path d="M18 20l4 4 8-8" stroke="#4fa83a" stroke-width="4"/><path d="M36 20h10"/><path d="M18 36l4 4 8-8" stroke="#4fa83a" stroke-width="4"/><path d="M36 36h10"/><circle cx="22" cy="50" r="0"/>

karty.g: The order in which the story is presented is fixed before the session begins.
karty.nz: Story beats need triggers tied to player progress, and the narrative must connect to goals, characters and clues. The designer must decide how much player choice may bend the order.
karty.yr: There are cutscenes and text, but they are skippable decoration that neither guide goals nor react to what the player does.
karty.rk: how linear the story is; how many branches; how story events are triggered
karty.ik: <path d="M6 14h14v10H6zM44 14h14v10H44zM25 40h14v10H25z" fill="#c9a24a"/><path d="M20 19h24M51 24v6L32 36v4" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M32 40l-3-5M32 40l4-4" stroke-width="3"/>

karty.g: You can estimate in advance how the game will change after actions or events.
karty.nz: Rules must be deterministic and clear enough to read, and the game must show state and effects. Little hidden information or randomness should sit between an action and its result.
karty.yr: Rules are written down, but dice, hidden effects or opaque systems make outcomes impossible to foresee, so players cannot plan.
karty.rk: amount of randomness and hidden information; clarity of feedback and previews
karty.ik: <circle cx="12" cy="20" r="6" fill="#e85d4f"/><path d="M18 20h14"/><circle cx="38" cy="20" r="6" fill="#fff"/><path d="M44 20h4"/><circle cx="54" cy="20" r="6" fill="#fff"/><path d="M6 46h52"/><path d="M6 46l4 8M6 46l4-8" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M58 46l-4 8M58 46l-4-8" stroke-width="3"/>

karty.g: During the session, players can see who will almost certainly win.
karty.nz: It emerges when snowballing mechanics, big skill gaps, readable scores and kingmaking exist without comeback tools. Designers mostly work to prevent it with uncertainty or catch-up mechanisms.
karty.yr: A leaderboard shows someone ahead, but comebacks or hidden scoring keep the result open, so nobody treats the winner as settled.
karty.rk: strength of positive vs negative feedback; hidden information; randomness; catch-up mechanisms

karty.g: Goal of stopping some other goal from being completed.
karty.nz: The target goal must be one that can be interfered with, and the blocking agent needs real means, information and time to act. Opposing goals must conflict directly.
karty.yr: Enemies exist with a blocking role, but they are too weak, too passive or unable to reach the target, so nothing is ever prevented.
karty.rk: strength and number of blockers; the information they have; time limits
karty.ik: <path d="M8 56V8M8 8h20v12H8z" fill="#4fa83a"/><rect x="34" y="20" width="24" height="36" rx="3" fill="#c9a24a"/><path d="M34 30h24M34 44h24"/><path d="M34 20l-10 10" stroke="#e85d4f"/>

karty.g: Parts of the game space directly controlled by only one player.
karty.nz: Other players' actions must truly be blocked or limited in that space. The designer decides what visitors may do and how spaces interact with the shared game.
karty.yr: Each player has a named area, but others can attack, alter or sabotage it freely, so it gives no safety.
karty.rk: who may enter or act; what visitors may do; whether the space is permanent or temporary
karty.ik: <path d="M6 30L32 8l26 22"/><path d="M12 28v28h40V28" fill="#fff"/><rect x="26" y="38" width="12" height="18" rx="2" fill="#c9a24a"/><circle cx="35" cy="48" r="1" fill="#2a2a2a"/>

karty.g: Abilities that let someone do what others cannot.
karty.nz: The ability must open genuinely different tactics or goals, and access must be defined and balanced. Skilled play should not easily make up for its absence.
karty.yr: A special power is named, but it is weak or easily imitated, so privileged and ordinary agents play the same way.
karty.rk: who gets the ability; its power; how often it can be used; how it is obtained

karty.g: A way of moving that is available to some and unavailable to others.
karty.nz: The game world needs obstacles, restricted areas or travel costs that the special movement overcomes in a meaningful way. Its effect on goals like capture or evasion must be considered.
karty.yr: A unit has a flashy movement type, but the map offers no obstacles it bypasses, so it travels the same as everyone.
karty.rk: which units can do it; what obstacles it ignores; duration or cost
karty.ik: <path d="M4 54h56"/><path d="M6 54V40h14v14M24 54V40h14v14" fill="#d5d9e0"/><path d="M10 14c10-8 26-8 36 0" stroke-dasharray="1 7"/><path d="M44 10l8 4-8 6" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M46 40c4-8 12-8 14 0z" fill="#c9a24a"/>

karty.g: Worlds built by an algorithm rather than drawn by hand by an author.
karty.nz: The generator needs good rules, parameters and randomness that produce varied yet playable worlds. Balance checks or seeds help keep results fair and reproducible.
karty.yr: Worlds are generated, but outputs look nearly identical or are broken, so the variety adds no new play.
karty.rk: generator parameters; amount of randomness; seed use; balance constraints

karty.g: Show how close the player is to finishing, beyond the arrangement of the elements themselves.
karty.nz: They must show measurements tied to real goals, at the right moment and in a readable way. The information has to help players decide what to do next.
karty.yr: A bar is on screen but is cosmetic, misleading or unrelated to actual goals, so it does not guide anything.
karty.rk: what is measured; how precisely; when it is shown; to whom
karty.ik: <rect x="4" y="22" width="56" height="20" rx="10"/><path d="M10 28h28a4 4 0 0 1 0 8H10a4 4 0 0 1 0-8z" fill="#4fa83a" stroke="none"/><path d="M46 14v6M54 14v6" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M32 50h0" stroke-width="3"/>

karty.g: In role-playing: lines that hint how to change the scene without leaving character.
karty.nz: The group needs shared, easily noticed signals that fit the fiction, learned before play. Different scenes may need different prompts.
karty.yr: Signals are listed in the rulebook, but nobody notices or uses them, so players still break character to change scenes.
karty.rk: which signals exist; how subtle they are; who may use them

karty.g: World objects that exist only for appearance and play no part in the game.
karty.nz: They need to fit the setting and be visually distinct from usable items. They work best when they also provide mood, landmarks or clues.
karty.yr: Objects are scattered randomly with no theme, or look like usable items so players waste time on them.
karty.rk: how many; where placed; how distinct from usable items
karty.ik: <path d="M10 56V28M54 56V28"/><path d="M10 28L32 6l22 22" fill="#d5d9e0"/><rect x="10" y="28" width="44" height="28" fill="none"/><path d="M10 28l22-22 22 22z" fill="#d5d9e0"/><path d="M18 56l8-8M30 56l8-8M42 56l8-8" stroke-width="3"/>

karty.g: Information about players that is easily available to everyone else.
karty.nz: Stats must be visible to others, tied to a persistent identity and connected to meaningful performance. Who can see them must be decided.
karty.yr: Stats are kept but hidden, anonymous or irrelevant, so nobody sees or cares about them.
karty.rk: what is tracked; who can see it; how long it persists
karty.ik: <rect x="6" y="8" width="52" height="36" rx="3"/><path d="M14 36V28M24 36V20M34 36V24M44 36V14" stroke="#2f6b8f" stroke-width="5"/><path d="M24 44v8M40 44v8M16 56h32"/>

karty.g: The player can spend real money to gain advantages in the game.
karty.nz: Goods must be tied to meaningful game effects, with prices and transfer rules defined. The designer must accept the effect on balance and on other players' sense of effort.
karty.yr: A shop exists, but items are cosmetic or trivially available through play, so buying gives no real edge.
karty.rk: what can be bought; prices; power of purchases; tradability

karty.g: Tasks that are solved mainly by thinking.
karty.nz: The challenge must be solvable by deduction or experiment, with clear information, fitting difficulty and no pressure that replaces thinking. Brute-force trial should be costly or impossible.
karty.yr: A puzzle is presented, but it can be solved by trying every option or by luck, so no reasoning is needed.
karty.rk: difficulty; amount of information given; number of attempts; time pressure

karty.g: The game itself, not other players, creates the challenges for the player.
karty.nz: The game needs system-controlled opponents or hazards with enough behaviour to be a real challenge. Players need reasons to team up against them.
karty.yr: Enemies exist but are passive or trivial, so there is no real challenge from the system.
karty.rk: enemy strength and number; AI behaviour; difficulty scaling
karty.ik: <circle cx="18" cy="20" r="8"/><path d="M4 58c0-14 6-22 14-22s14 8 14 22z" fill="#2f6b8f"/><path d="M38 54c0-18 6-28 12-28s10 10 10 28z" fill="#4fa83a"/><path d="M42 36l-3-6M58 36l3-6" stroke-width="3"/><circle cx="46" cy="40" r="2" fill="#2a2a2a" stroke="none"/><circle cx="54" cy="40" r="2" fill="#2a2a2a" stroke="none"/>

karty.g: Players, as individual people, directly compete against each other.
karty.nz: Players need opposed goals, ways to affect one another and roughly matched skill. Matchmaking or balancing tools help sustain it.
karty.yr: Many players share a space, but they cannot hurt or compete with each other, so it is parallel solo play.
karty.rk: how much players can harm each other; matchmaking; balance and handicap tools

karty.g: Goal of completing a task for which a reward is given.
karty.nz: Each needs a clear task, a visible reward and a way to be offered and completed. Rewards must be worth the effort and tied to the world.
karty.yr: A quest log exists, but tasks are trivial, rewards meaningless or the requirements unclear, so players ignore it.
karty.rk: number and type of quests; reward size; how they are offered; difficulty
karty.ik: <path d="M10 6h38v42H10z" fill="#fff"/><path d="M10 6c-6 0-6 8 0 8h38" fill="none"/><path d="M16 22h26M16 30h20"/><path d="M48 48c0 8 6 10 10 10" stroke="none"/><circle cx="46" cy="46" r="12" fill="#c9a24a"/><path d="M46 40v12M40 46h12" stroke-width="3"/>

karty.g: World design where returning to a point is much easier than getting there.
karty.nz: It should open only after the outward journey, so return is cheaper than getting there. It must link to places players actually revisit.
karty.yr: A shortcut exists but is as long as the original route or opens before the journey, so nothing is saved.
karty.rk: when it unlocks; how fast; which places it connects
karty.ik: <path d="M6 54h18l8-12 8 12h18"/><path d="M10 36C14 12 46 10 54 28" stroke="#4fa83a"/><path d="M54 28l-8-1M54 28l-1-8" stroke="#4fa83a" stroke-width="3"/><circle cx="10" cy="46" r="4" fill="#c9a24a"/>

karty.g: The game shows a sequence of button presses that must be performed instantly.
karty.nz: The game must be real-time, with clear prompts, fair time windows and meaningful consequences for failure. They work best where normal controls do not cover the situation.
karty.yr: Prompts appear but have no penalty or can't be failed, so they are a cutscene with a button press.
karty.rk: sequence length; time window; penalty for failure
karty.ik: <circle cx="32" cy="32" r="22"/><rect x="22" y="22" width="20" height="20" rx="4" fill="#e85d4f"/><path d="M32 3v8M32 53v8M3 32h8M53 32h8" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M32 27v10M27 32h10" stroke="#fff" stroke-width="3"/>

karty.g: Ways to reach another place in the world, skipping intermediate points.
karty.nz: Travel points must be reachable, with rules for when it works and what it costs. The world should have enough distance that the shortcut matters.
karty.yr: A map teleport exists, but the world is so small or the travel so restricted that nobody needs it.
karty.rk: where it is available; cost; unlock conditions; one-way or two-way

karty.g: A set of questions asked to players during the game.
karty.nz: Questions must fit the audience, be well written and have fair answer options. The number of questions and format should suit their role in the game.
karty.yr: Questions are shown but are so easy or guessable that knowledge makes no difference.
karty.rk: number of questions; difficulty; multiple choice or free answer

karty.g: A vague invitation that draws a person into a particular game.
karty.nz: The cryptic messages must be placed where target players will find them and be intriguing enough to follow. Several are spread over media and time since individual ones may be missed.
karty.yr: A clue is posted, but it is too obscure or in the wrong place, so nobody finds or follows it.
karty.rk: how many; where posted; how cryptic; timing

karty.g: Goal of finishing under pressure, often ahead of others or before a deadline.
karty.nz: Players need a shared target with limited time or competitors, and progress should be visible. Excluding goals and a clear end condition create the pressure.
karty.yr: A finish line or score target exists, but with no rival or time pressure players just proceed at leisure.
karty.rk: time limit; number of rivals; target distance; visibility of others' progress
karty.ik: <path d='M12 4v56'/><rect x='12' y='8' width='42' height='24' fill='#fff'/><path d='M22 8h10v8H22zM42 8h12v8H42zM12 16h10v8H12zM32 16h10v8H32zM22 24h10v8H22zM42 24h12v8H42z' fill='#2a2a2a' stroke='none'/><path d='M4 60h16' stroke='#e85d4f'/>

karty.g: A player abandons the session out of anger, without thinking how it affects others.
karty.nz: It emerges when frustration rises beyond tolerance, often from repeated failure, unfair treatment or betrayal. Designers mainly limit it through fairness, mitigation of its effects and easy exits.
karty.yr: A quit penalty exists, but players leave calmly and not out of anger, so it is plain quitting.
karty.rk: frustration level and difficulty; quit penalties; how well the game absorbs a departure
karty.ik: <circle cx='32' cy='32' r='25' fill='#e85d4f'/><path d='M32 14v16M21 21a15 15 0 1 0 22 0' stroke='#fff' stroke-width='5'/>

karty.g: Events and effects in the game cannot be predicted exactly.
karty.nz: Random outcomes must have known ranges and affect decisions that matter. The balance with player skill needs to be chosen deliberately.
karty.yr: Random rolls happen, but the results are trivial or always overridden by skill, so luck changes nothing.
karty.rk: size of the random range; which events use it; probability distribution
karty.ik: <rect x='8' y='8' width='48' height='48' rx='9' fill='#fff'/><circle cx='21' cy='21' r='3.5' fill='#2a2a2a' stroke='none'/><circle cx='43' cy='21' r='3.5' fill='#2a2a2a' stroke='none'/><circle cx='32' cy='32' r='3.5' fill='#e85d4f' stroke='none'/><circle cx='21' cy='43' r='3.5' fill='#2a2a2a' stroke='none'/><circle cx='43' cy='43' r='3.5' fill='#2a2a2a' stroke='none'/>

karty.n: Real Life Activities Affect Game State
karty.g: Ordinary life activities unrelated to the game change its state.
karty.nz: The design must pick which everyday activities count, measure them reliably, and map them to clear state changes. Players need to see the link between what they did and what the game did in response.
karty.yr: A game that only shows your steps or activity as a decorative number, while nothing in play depends on it.
karty.rk: which activities count; how they are measured and converted into game state changes

karty.g: Features of the real physical place where the game is played affect the play itself.
karty.nz: Actions must be bound to specific physical places or distances, so that moving the body matters for what you can do. Distances, boundaries and the space's features must actually be used by the rules.
karty.yr: A game played in a room or park where the place is only a backdrop and any spot would work equally well.
karty.rk: size and shape of the space; which actions are allowed only inside it or at certain spots

karty.g: Real-life knowledge about the game's subject helps the player.
karty.nz: Game decisions must depend on facts that exist outside the game, and the game must not hand those facts to everyone. Players must also differ in how much they know.
karty.yr: Trivia sits in the game's theme or flavor text, but anyone can do equally well without knowing it.
karty.rk: how much outcomes depend on outside facts; how much of that information the game supplies itself
karty.ik: <circle cx='26' cy='38' r='20' fill='#2f6b8f'/><ellipse cx='26' cy='38' rx='8' ry='20' fill='#fff' fill-opacity='.4'/><path d='M6 38h40'/><circle cx='49' cy='14' r='8' fill='#c9a24a'/><path d='M45 25h8'/>

karty.g: Game time runs at the same pace as real time.
karty.nz: The game state must update continuously on its own, with something (a computer, a timer, physics) driving it. Events must demand reaction within a short span so waiting has a cost.
karty.yr: A game with a visible clock or animation, but the state only changes when a player acts, so waiting costs nothing.
karty.rk: speed of the game clock; how long players have to react; whether pauses are allowed
karty.ik: <circle cx='28' cy='28' r='22' fill='#fff'/><path d='M28 14v14l9 6'/><circle cx='48' cy='48' r='11' fill='#4fa83a'/><path d='M45 43l8 5-8 5z' fill='#fff' stroke='none'/>

karty.g: The world's basic layout can change during a session or between sessions.
karty.nz: The world must be made of parts that can be rearranged, and either the rules or the players must actually rearrange them. Changes have to alter what choices are good, not just how things look.
karty.yr: A world that is re-skinned or has cosmetic changes, but the layout and routes play out the same every time.
karty.rk: what can change; when it changes (between games or during play); who triggers the change and how often
karty.ik: <rect x='6' y='6' width='22' height='22' rx='3'/><rect x='36' y='6' width='22' height='22' rx='3' fill='#c9a24a'/><rect x='6' y='36' width='22' height='22' rx='3' fill='#2f6b8f'/><rect x='36' y='36' width='22' height='22' rx='3' stroke-dasharray='4 6'/><path d='M47 31v10m-4-4l4 4 4-4' stroke-width='3'/>

karty.g: Goal of going around areas of the world and noticing what has changed in them.
karty.nz: Players must not know where things are and must be able to find out by spending time or effort. The information must change, so old knowledge goes stale and checking again is worth it.
karty.yr: A scouting action exists, but everything is already visible or never changes, so nobody bothers to use it.
karty.rk: how much of the world is hidden; how fast information goes stale; cost and range of observing
karty.ik: <path d='M12 32V12h12v20M40 32V12h12v20'/><circle cx='18' cy='42' r='13' fill='#2f6b8f'/><circle cx='46' cy='42' r='13' fill='#2f6b8f'/><circle cx='18' cy='42' r='5' fill='#fff'/><circle cx='46' cy='42' r='5' fill='#fff'/><path d='M30 40h4'/>

karty.g: Items or information created to confuse or distract players.
karty.nz: Decoys must look as plausible as the real clues and cost players something to check. The game must also have real uncertainty so that players cannot tell them apart at once.
karty.yr: A fake clue that is obviously irrelevant at first glance, so it is ignored and does not distract anyone.
karty.rk: ratio of false to real clues; how convincing the decoys look; cost of following a false lead
karty.ik: <ellipse cx='28' cy='32' rx='21' ry='13' fill='#e85d4f'/><path d='M47 32l13-11v22z' fill='#e85d4f'/><circle cx='16' cy='29' r='2' fill='#2a2a2a' stroke='none'/><path d='M28 22v20' stroke-width='3'/>

karty.g: Players discuss their actions with each other and think about the game together.
karty.nz: Players must depend on each other and have reasons to share knowledge, take each other's view and agree on methods. The game should give space and time for discussion and reward working it out together.
karty.yr: A chat channel or team mode exists, but no one has to talk to succeed, so nobody discusses or reflects.
karty.rk: how much team success depends on shared understanding; time and channels available for discussion

karty.g: Resources that accumulate by themselves as game time passes.
karty.nz: A clear refill rate and usually a cap must be set, and the resource must matter enough that players spend it and wait for it. Refill speed should shape pacing of play.
karty.yr: A resource that refills so quickly or so little that it never runs short, or one nobody needs, so the refill changes no decision.
karty.rk: regeneration rate; cap size; what pauses or speeds up regeneration

karty.g: Resources that are replenished in some way during the game.
karty.nz: There must be a clear way the resource comes back (spawning, producing, timers) and a limit on speed or amount, so that using it is still a real choice. Players should be able to over-use it and suffer for it.
karty.yr: Resources are called renewable, but they come back so fast or in such quantity that spending them has no cost.
karty.rk: what renews; renewal speed and conditions; maximum stock
karty.ik: <circle cx='32' cy='24' r='19' fill='#4fa83a'/><path d='M32 42v18M24 60h16'/><circle cx='24' cy='22' r='3.5' fill='#e85d4f' stroke='none'/><circle cx='40' cy='19' r='3.5' fill='#e85d4f' stroke='none'/><circle cx='33' cy='32' r='3.5' fill='#e85d4f' stroke='none'/>

karty.g: Combinations where the same action must be repeated a set number of times within a time limit.
karty.nz: The required count and time window must be tight enough to need effort or skill but reachable. The reward must be worth the effort, and progress should be visible so players feel the chain.
karty.yr: A combo counter that rewards nothing, or a window so generous that every ordinary play meets it without trying.
karty.rk: number of repeats; length of the time window; size of the reward
karty.ik: <circle cx='12' cy='44' r='7' fill='#e85d4f'/><circle cx='32' cy='44' r='7' fill='#e85d4f'/><circle cx='52' cy='44' r='7' fill='#e85d4f'/><path d='M12 32c6-18 34-18 40 0'/><path d='M44 22l8 10 4-12' stroke-width='3'/>

karty.g: If a position repeats during a game, the game ends in a draw.
karty.nz: The rules must define what counts as the same position and how many repeats end the game, and someone or something must track the history. The draw must be a real result that players can aim for or avoid.
karty.yr: A rule that is written down but never checked or enforced, so endless loops continue.
karty.rk: number of repeats that trigger the draw; what counts as identical state
karty.ik: <circle cx='32' cy='18' r='7' fill='#fff'/><path d='M26 26h12l4 22H22z' fill='#fff'/><path d='M18 56h28'/><path d='M8 30a24 24 0 0 1 10-18M12 6l6 6-8 2' stroke='#e85d4f' stroke-width='3'/><path d='M56 34a24 24 0 0 1-10 18M52 58l-6-6 8-2' stroke='#e85d4f' stroke-width='3'/>

karty.g: The player repeats the same actions or choices over and over.
karty.nz: The game's loop must offer few action types and the best choice must stay the same across rounds. Whether it feels like practice or tedium depends on the skill growth and rewards around it.
karty.yr: A game with many menus or content on offer, but the same few actions win every time, so variety exists only on paper.
karty.rk: variety of actions needed; how long one action type is demanded; how fast the best play changes
karty.ik: <path d='M4 58L58 22v36z'/><circle cx='34' cy='25' r='11' fill='#d5d9e0'/><path d='M30 22h8' stroke-width='2.5'/>

karty.g: How many new challenges, lessons, and experiences the game offers when played again.
karty.nz: Each playthrough needs different challenges or room to improve, through randomness, many routes, or goals that differ. Outcomes must stay uncertain and mastery must not run out quickly.
karty.yr: Randomness that changes only surface details, so every run plays out as the same solved sequence.
karty.rk: amount of variation between plays (randomness, content size); depth of mastery available
karty.ik: <path d='M52 32a20 20 0 1 1-6-14' stroke='#4fa83a'/><path d='M35 15l11 3-3-11' stroke='#4fa83a'/><rect x='22' y='22' width='20' height='20' rx='4' fill='#fff'/><circle cx='28' cy='28' r='2' fill='#2a2a2a' stroke='none'/><circle cx='36' cy='36' r='2' fill='#2a2a2a' stroke='none'/>

karty.g: Recordings of a past game that can be watched again.
karty.nz: The game must record enough state or input to replay faithfully, and players must be able to find and watch the result. Playback is only useful if there is something worth reviewing or sharing.
karty.yr: A replay button that records poorly, drifts from what happened, or cannot be viewed, shared or used for anything.
karty.rk: what is recorded; who controls recording; how long recordings are kept and how they are shared
karty.ik: <rect x='6' y='8' width='52' height='36' rx='4' fill='#fff'/><path d='M32 18L20 26l12 8zM46 18l-12 8 12 8z' fill='#e85d4f' stroke-width='3'/><path d='M32 44v12M18 58h28'/>

karty.g: Goal of freeing someone who is guarded or cannot move on their own.
karty.nz: There must be a held target, something that guards it, and means to overcome or avoid the guards. Rescuing must change the game state, such as progress or reward.
karty.yr: A captive mentioned in the story, but freeing it takes no effort or has no effect on play.
karty.rk: strength and number of guards; distance and obstacles to the target; reward for success

karty.g: Team members who wait outside the game because not everyone can play at once.
karty.nz: The active-slot limit must be lower than the team size, and swapping must be allowed with some cost or timing. Members must differ in skill or stamina so choosing who plays matters.
karty.yr: Bench players exist, but all members are identical and swaps never happen, so the bench changes nothing.
karty.rk: number of active slots versus team size; swap rules, timing and cost

karty.g: Limits on how many resources can be stored or spent.
karty.nz: The cap must be low enough that players actually reach it, so it forces them to spend or lose income. It also has to apply to a resource that matters.
karty.yr: A cap set so high that nobody ever reaches it, so it never affects a decision.
karty.rk: cap value per resource; whether caps can be raised
karty.ik: <rect x='18' y='16' width='28' height='42' rx='4' fill='#c9a24a'/><path d='M6 16h52' stroke='#e85d4f'/><path d='M22 8h20' stroke-width='3'/>

karty.g: Players compete for limited resources.
karty.nz: Resources must be scarce, shared and valuable, so one player's gain is another's loss. Players need to be able to interfere with or beat each other to it.
karty.yr: Each player has a private supply of the same resource, so they never actually compete.
karty.rk: total supply versus demand; how much is shared; how easily players can block each other
karty.ik: <circle cx='32' cy='32' r='10' fill='#c9a24a'/><path d='M4 32h14M12 25l7 7-7 7' stroke='#2f6b8f'/><path d='M60 32H46M52 25l-7 7 7 7' stroke='#e85d4f'/>

karty.g: Areas of the world where resources are located.
karty.nz: Locations must be placed so that getting there costs something, such as distance, risk or rivals. Resources must be useful enough to be worth the trip.
karty.yr: A resource node placed right at the start where everyone gets it with no effort or trade-off.
karty.rk: number, placement and richness of locations; access cost and who can take them
karty.ik: <path d='M4 58L32 8l28 50z'/><path d='M23 58V48a9 9 0 0 1 18 0v10z' fill='#2a2a2a'/><circle cx='32' cy='52' r='3' fill='#c9a24a' stroke='none'/><circle cx='50' cy='50' r='3' fill='#c9a24a' stroke='none'/>

karty.g: Allocating and spending available supplies wisely.
karty.nz: Resources must be limited, useful for several competing ends, and spending must have consequences later. Players need enough information to plan their use.
karty.yr: Resources are shown on screen but are so plentiful or so single-purpose that no real choices arise.
karty.rk: scarcity; number of competing uses; income versus spending rate
karty.ik: <rect x="8" y="8" width="48" height="48" rx="4"/><path d="M32 8v48M8 32h48"/><circle cx="20" cy="20" r="6" fill="#c9a24a"/><path d="M44 12c4 5 6 8 6 10a6 6 0 0 1-12 0c0-2 2-5 6-10z" fill="#2f6b8f" stroke-width="3"/><rect x="13" y="40" width="14" height="8" rx="4" fill="#c9a24a" stroke-width="3"/>

karty.g: Places, abstract or real, within the world where resources can be found or obtained.
karty.nz: Each source needs a clear way to obtain resources, with a cost, a limit or competition. Different sources should give different kinds or amounts so choosing among them matters.
karty.yr: A source that gives resources automatically with no action or limit, so it works like a number going up.
karty.rk: yield per source; cost or effort to use it; number of sources and their types

karty.g: Game elements that players spend to perform actions.
karty.nz: Resources must be required for actions and be limited enough that spending is a choice. They need visible quantities so players can plan with them.
karty.yr: A counter named like a resource that no action needs and no loss reduces, so it has no use in play.
karty.rk: what actions cost; starting amounts; income and loss rates
karty.ik: <rect x='6' y='44' width='26' height='10' rx='5' fill='#c9a24a'/><rect x='6' y='33' width='26' height='10' rx='5' fill='#c9a24a'/><rect x='6' y='22' width='26' height='10' rx='5' fill='#c9a24a'/><polygon points='38,32 56,32 60,40 47,56 34,40' fill='#2f6b8f'/>

karty.g: In trick-taking games: what to do if a player broke the rules of play.
karty.nz: The rule must say when a violation is detected, who decides, and what penalty applies. The penalty must be big enough to discourage breaking the rule yet allow play to continue.
karty.yr: A penalty written but never applied because violations are rarely checked, so breaking the rule costs nothing.
karty.rk: size of the penalty; time allowed to challenge; who checks
karty.ik: <rect x='14' y='6' width='28' height='42' rx='3' fill='#fff' transform='rotate(-8 28 27)'/><circle cx='27' cy='26' r='6' fill='#2a2a2a' stroke='none'/><path d='M38 36l20 20M58 36L38 56' stroke='#e85d4f' stroke-width='6'/>

karty.g: Rewards placed around the world even though, by the world's logic, they should not be there.
karty.nz: They must appear in the play area, be clickable or collectable, and be worth the effort of collecting. A time limit or auto-collect rule sets how much attention they demand.
karty.yr: A reward icon that pops up and gives nothing extra, or is collected automatically so that clicking is pointless.
karty.rk: how often widgets appear; time before they auto-collect; reward size

karty.g: What the player receives and experiences as pleasant.
karty.nz: Rewards must be tied to meaningful achievements and valued by players. Their size and timing should match the effort, so players feel they earned them.
karty.yr: Rewards given for anything, or of no practical or emotional value, like a badge that changes nothing.
karty.rk: reward size; how often they are given; what triggers them and how certain they are

karty.g: The action must be timed to a set rhythm.
karty.nz: A clear, perceivable rhythm must exist and failing to match it must have a cost. Timing windows need to be tuned so success is possible but demanding.
karty.yr: Beat visuals or music that play along, but timing is not checked, so any input works.
karty.rk: tempo; width of the timing window; penalty for missing the beat
karty.ik: <path d='M16 58L27 8h10l11 50z' fill='#c9a24a'/><path d='M32 52L42 16' stroke='#e85d4f'/><circle cx='39' cy='26' r='4.5' fill='#e85d4f'/><path d='M12 58h40'/>

karty.g: Real robots that take part in the game on equal terms with players.
karty.nz: The robot needs sensors, movement and an AI that can really act in the physical play space and follow the game's rules, as a human participant would. The game must be built so that physical actions by the robot count in the game state and other players can respond to them.
karty.yr: A robot sits on the table or moves along a fixed script while a person or a program secretly makes all the decisions, so it takes no real part in play and nothing depends on it.
karty.rk: how much the robot can sense and do; how skilled its AI is; how much the robot's physical actions affect the game state
karty.ik: <rect x='10' y='20' width='44' height='34' rx='6' fill='#d5d9e0'/><path d='M32 20V10'/><circle cx='32' cy='7' r='3' fill='#e85d4f'/><circle cx='22' cy='34' r='5' fill='#2f6b8f'/><circle cx='42' cy='34' r='5' fill='#2f6b8f'/><path d='M22 46h20'/>

karty.g: Goal of performing your role in the group well; it is frustrating if the group still loses.
karty.nz: Roles must be distinct, matter for the group's success, and be performable in ways players can see and recognise. Team results should depend on each role's contribution.
karty.yr: Roles that exist only as labels, with all players doing the same things and contributing the same way.
karty.rk: how different the roles are; how much the group result depends on each; how visible each player's contribution is

karty.g: The player chooses their abilities by picking one of a few ready-made roles.
karty.nz: The roles must differ in what they offer, so that choosing is a real decision with trade-offs. Rules must state who can choose what and when.
karty.yr: A choice among roles that are effectively identical or where one is clearly best, so selection does not matter.
karty.rk: number and difference of roles; whether roles are exclusive; when selection happens
karty.ik: <rect x='5' y='24' width='15' height='30' rx='3'/><rect x='24.5' y='8' width='15' height='34' rx='3' fill='#c9a24a'/><rect x='44' y='24' width='15' height='30' rx='3'/><circle cx='32' cy='25' r='3' fill='#2a2a2a' stroke='none'/><path d='M4 60h56'/>

karty.g: Players take on the goals and behavior of fictional characters.
karty.nz: Give players an agent-like character or faction with goals of its own, real freedom in how to pursue them, and some internal tension or hidden aims. Add a world with enough texture that staying in role has something to respond to.
karty.yr: A hero with a name and a portrait whose goals are just the player's own score, so nobody ever acts as the character would.
karty.rk: how much character goals are set by the game versus chosen by the player; how much freedom there is in pursuing them

karty.g: Places in the game world where game elements are safe from any threat.
karty.nz: The place must be truly shielded from traps, enemies and other players, by access rules or disabled hostile actions. It also needs a reason to go out again, such as risk and reward outside, or it just becomes a hiding spot.
karty.yr: A pretty calm-looking area that enemies can still walk into or that still damages you, so it protects nothing.
karty.rk: where havens are and how many; what they block; whether they expire or need a condition to enter
karty.ik: <path d='M5 30L32 7l27 23z' fill='#e85d4f'/><rect x='13' y='30' width='38' height='26' fill='#fff'/><rect x='27' y='38' width='10' height='18' fill='#c9a24a'/>

karty.g: Cheating that the rules allow or that other players consider acceptable.
karty.nz: Offer specific rule-bending actions, decide who may use them and what happens if caught, and keep them out of the normal action menu. In multiplayer, detection risk and some hidden information make it matter.
karty.yr: A cheat menu that nobody needs or that has no effect on goals, or a 'cheat' that other players are never able to notice or object to.
karty.rk: which cheats exist; who may use them; chance and penalty of being caught
karty.ik: <rect x='20' y='4' width='24' height='34' rx='3' fill='#fff' transform='rotate(-10 32 21)'/><path d='M28 18l5 6-5 6-5-6z' fill='#e85d4f' stroke-width='2.5' transform='rotate(-10 32 21)'/><path d='M6 34h40v24H6z' fill='#2f6b8f'/><path d='M46 38h8v16h-8' fill='#fff'/>

karty.g: Files with data that can be used to restore the state of the game.
karty.nz: Build real storage and loading of the full or partial state, and decide how saving is triggered and how many slots exist. Slot limits and where saving is allowed decide whether it supports pauses or invites abuse.
karty.yr: A save that only records progress through a password or level number, or loads into a state that immediately kills the player, so it does not truly restore the game.
karty.rk: number of slots; manual versus automatic saving; how much state is stored
karty.ik: <path d='M8 8h40l8 8v40H8z' fill='#2f6b8f'/><rect x='18' y='8' width='22' height='14' fill='#fff'/><rect x='16' y='34' width='32' height='22' rx='2' fill='#fff'/>

karty.g: Places in the world or between levels where the player can save the game.
karty.nz: Put saving at chosen locations or between levels, ideally in safe spots, and space them so retrying costs real effort. Decide whether saving is manual or automatic and how much state is stored.
karty.yr: Save points placed so densely, or saving allowed anywhere anyway, that they never limit anything or mark any progress.
karty.rk: distance between save points; manual versus automatic; how much state is saved

karty.g: The player keeps reloading a save and replaying a hard spot until they get lucky.
karty.nz: It shows up when saving is unlimited and cheap, retrying costs almost nothing, and outcomes are random or hidden. To prevent it, limit slots or saving, or make failure persistent.
karty.yr: A game that technically has a save limit but lets players copy or back up files, so reloading still costs nothing and the limit changes nothing.
karty.rk: how many save slots; where saving is allowed; how costly reloading is
karty.ik: <path d='M6 6h22l6 6v22H6z' fill='#2f6b8f'/><rect x='30' y='30' width='28' height='28' rx='6' fill='#e85d4f'/><circle cx='39' cy='39' r='2.5' fill='#fff' stroke='none'/><circle cx='49' cy='49' r='2.5' fill='#fff' stroke='none'/><circle cx='49' cy='39' r='2.5' fill='#fff' stroke='none'/><circle cx='39' cy='49' r='2.5' fill='#fff' stroke='none'/>

karty.g: The player saves and loads again and again until the game reaches the state they want.
karty.nz: Needs easy, fast saving and loading and challenges where a bad result can be undone by reloading. Restricting save timing or slots reduces how often it happens.
karty.yr: A save system that is so slow or restricted that players never use it to retry, so no cycles of save, try, and reload actually occur.
karty.rk: how fast and how often saving is allowed; how many slots; ironman-style limits
karty.ik: <path d='M52 32a20 20 0 1 1-6-14'/><path d='M35 15l11 3-3-11'/><path d='M23 23h14l5 5v14H23z' fill='#c9a24a' stroke-width='3'/><rect x='27' y='31' width='11' height='9' fill='#fff' stroke-width='2'/>

karty.g: A part of the game tied to a specific place and time within the game world.
karty.nz: Define each scene's location, who is present and how it ends, whether by a time limit, a condition, or a game master's call. Scenes must differ in setting or situation to feel like separate units.
karty.yr: Chapter labels over one continuous stretch of play where nothing about place, cast, or situation changes between them.
karty.rk: scene length; how scene ends are decided; how many characters and locations per scene

karty.g: A strip on which the players' points are marked.
karty.nz: Provide a track with enough spaces, a rule for overflow or shared spots, and public visibility. It gains meaning when it also affects turn order or tiebreaks.
karty.yr: A track that only mirrors a number kept elsewhere, is hidden or rarely consulted, so no one reacts to what it shows.
karty.rk: track length; what happens at the end or on shared spots; whether position affects turn order or ties
karty.ik: <rect x="4" y="24" width="56" height="16" rx="3"/><path d="M16 24v6M28 24v6M40 24v6M52 24v6" stroke-width="3"/><circle cx="22" cy="46" r="0"/><circle cx="34" cy="32" r="6" fill="#e85d4f"/><circle cx="14" cy="32" r="0"/><path d="M4 50h56" stroke-width="3"/>

karty.g: Numbers used in the game to decide who wins.
karty.nz: Define what raises or lowers the number, by how much, and what values trigger events or end the game. Players must see the score as tied to the actual goal for it to drive play.
karty.yr: A score shown on screen that does not determine winning, ranking, or any decision, so players ignore it.
karty.rk: points per action; end threshold; public versus hidden; penalties

karty.g: Moving through the world to learn about dangers while staying unseen.
karty.nz: Needs partial visibility of the world, a real chance of being detected, and a payoff for information such as threats or ambushes. Hiding places and routes make the activity richer.
karty.yr: Exploring the map with no enemies or no detection risk, so scouting is just walking around and nothing is learned or threatened.
karty.rk: detection range and chance; how much of the map is hidden; how many hiding places
karty.ik: <path d="M4 40h56"/><path d="M8 40c4-14 12-20 20-20" stroke-width="3"/><circle cx="20" cy="32" r="0"/><path d="M26 44c4-14 22-14 26-4" stroke-width="0"/><path d="M10 52c8-8 16-8 22-2s14 2 22-6" stroke-dasharray="1 7"/><path d="M36 8h14v12H36z" fill="#2f6b8f"/><path d="M36 8v-3" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M34 22l-4 8M52 22l4 8M43 22v10" stroke-width="3"/><circle cx="43" cy="14" r="3" fill="#fff" stroke-width="2"/>

karty.g: A preset chain of events plays out while the player can still act.
karty.nz: Place scripted events at particular points so players can still act, give reasons for them to watch, such as clues or threats, and decide how interruptible they are.
karty.yr: A cutscene in disguise, where the player is locked in place or the world is frozen, so there is no gameplay during the sequence.
karty.rk: how interruptible; trigger location; whether they threaten the player; clue content
karty.ik: <rect x="6" y="8" width="52" height="34" rx="3"/><path d="M26 17l14 8-14 8z" fill="#e85d4f"/><path d="M10 54h44M10 54v-4M26 54v-4M42 54v-4M54 54v-4" stroke-width="3"/>

karty.g: Knowing where sensors and connections work gives the player an advantage.
karty.nz: Needs location-sensing technology with real, learnable coverage gaps, and gameplay where being out of coverage helps, such as hiding. It does not work where coverage is everywhere.
karty.yr: Dead spots that exist but offer no advantage, or that players cannot find out about, so they are just glitches.
karty.rk: where and how large coverage gaps are; how much being unsensed helps players

karty.g: Screens with actions and data that add to the game's main interface.
karty.nz: Move actions and information that do not fit the main view into dedicated screens, such as inventory or character sheet, and make them quickly reachable. They matter when they hold real decisions.
karty.yr: A menu screen that only repeats what the main interface already shows and offers no extra actions.
karty.rk: which actions and information go on separate screens; how many screens; whether the game pauses when open
karty.ik: <rect x="4" y="8" width="38" height="30" rx="3" fill="#d5d9e0"/><rect x="30" y="26" width="30" height="28" rx="3" fill="#fff"/><path d="M36 34h18M36 42h12" stroke-width="3"/><circle cx="14" cy="18" r="3" fill="#2f6b8f"/>

karty.g: Parts of the game world that are hard to notice.
karty.nz: Hide areas behind obstacles or hidden triggers, give subtle clues, and put something worth finding inside. Players must be able to find them with effort.
karty.yr: An 'area' that is empty or trivially visible, or one that cannot actually be found, so searching earns nothing.
karty.rk: how well hidden; clue strength; reward inside; how many
karty.ik: <rect x="6" y="8" width="52" height="48" rx="3"/><path d="M6 36h20M38 36h20"/><path d="M26 36v20M38 36v20" stroke-dasharray="3 5"/><rect x="26" y="36" width="12" height="20" fill="#c9a24a" fill-opacity=".45" stroke="none"/><path d="M32 20c-3 0-5 2-5 5h3c0-1 1-2 2-2s2 1 2 2c0 2-4 2-4 6" stroke-width="3"/>

karty.g: A goal where a player has a task that the others do not know about.
karty.nz: Give players private goals that matter for winning, and keep them hidden through cards or a facilitator. Other players must have a reason and a way to guess or probe.
karty.yr: Hidden goals that all players have identical or that do not affect how anyone plays, so there is nothing to guess or hide.
karty.rk: how many secret goals; how different they are between players; whether they must be fulfilled to win
karty.ik: <rect x="10" y="24" width="44" height="32" rx="4" fill="#c9a24a"/><path d="M18 24v-6a14 14 0 0 1 28 0v6" stroke-width="0"/><path d="M18 24v-4a14 14 0 0 1 28 0v4"/><circle cx="32" cy="38" r="4" fill="#2a2a2a"/><path d="M32 40v8" stroke-width="3"/>

karty.g: Resources whose existence or properties at least one player does not know.
karty.nz: Hide resources through fog, hands, or unrevealed placement, and make finding or knowing them valuable. Players need a reason to search or infer.
karty.yr: A hidden resource that is irrelevant to play or that players can always see anyway, so hiding changes nothing.
karty.rk: how much is hidden; how many resources; how easy it is to discover them
karty.ik: <path d="M8 28c0-12 10-17 24-17s24 5 24 17"/><rect x="8" y="28" width="48" height="28" rx="3"/><path d="M8 38h48"/><rect x="26" y="33" width="12" height="12" rx="2" fill="#c9a24a" stroke-width="3"/>

karty.g: Ways to earn points that are revealed only when used or in the final count.
karty.nz: Offer hidden ways to score that are revealed only when used or at final count, and make them large enough to change who wins. It needs a multiplayer game with a visible leader to disturb.
karty.yr: Hidden points that are tiny or that everyone can already deduce, so the leader is still obvious.
karty.rk: size of hidden points; how many hidden scoring routes; when they are revealed
karty.ik: <rect x="8" y="24" width="26" height="34" rx="3" fill="#2f6b8f" transform="rotate(-8 21 41)"/><rect x="30" y="10" width="26" height="34" rx="3" fill="#fff" transform="rotate(10 43 27)"/><path d="M43 18l3 7 7 1-5 5 1 7-6-4-6 4 1-7-5-5 7-1z" fill="#c9a24a" stroke-width="2"/>

karty.g: A goal where the player chooses which goals to pursue from a set.
karty.nz: Offer several goals that really differ in risk, reward, or path, and make choosing among them matter, for example by excluding others. The set may change during play.
karty.yr: A list of goals where one is clearly best or all lead to the same result, so choosing is not a real decision.
karty.rk: how many goals are offered; whether the set changes; whether choices exclude each other
karty.ik: <path d="M8 12h10v10H8zM8 28h10v10H8zM8 44h10v10H8z"/><path d="M10 33l3 3 5-7" stroke="#4fa83a" stroke-width="4"/><path d="M26 17h28M26 33h28M26 49h28" stroke-width="4"/>

karty.g: The players themselves enforce the rules and keep all the records.
karty.nz: Rules must be clear and simple enough for players to apply and check themselves, with tokens or turn order lessening what must be remembered. Players also need to be able to agree on disputes.
karty.yr: A game that claims players run it but hides required calculations or rule enforcement in an app or referee, so players do none of the work.
karty.rk: how much bookkeeping players do; rule complexity; helper tokens
karty.ik: <rect x="6" y="24" width="52" height="30" rx="4" fill="#4fa83a" fill-opacity=".45"/><path d="M6 24h52"/><circle cx="20" cy="14" r="6"/><circle cx="44" cy="14" r="6"/><rect x="26" y="34" width="12" height="10" rx="2" fill="#fff"/>

karty.g: The player's physical location matters in the game, but the player reports it to the game themselves.
karty.nz: Players need a way to report their location, and the game should use that location for something. Trust or checks decide whether reports can be false.
karty.yr: A check-in button whose reported place has no effect on anything in the game.
karty.rk: how location is reported; how often; whether reports are checked

karty.g: Places in the game world where players make deals or get services themselves.
karty.nz: Place them at chosen spots with services that players actually need, such as trading, healing, or quests, and let their stock refill or limit it. Their location should shape movement.
karty.yr: A kiosk whose service is never needed or is available everywhere else, so no one has to go there.
karty.rk: what services; where placed; stock and refill rate; prices
karty.ik: <rect x="12" y="6" width="40" height="52" rx="4" fill="#2f6b8f"/><rect x="18" y="12" width="28" height="16" rx="2" fill="#fff"/><path d="M22 36h20v10H22z" fill="#c9a24a"/><path d="M18 54h28"/>

karty.g: A computer-controlled character reacts fittingly to events and to its own state.
karty.nz: The agent must react consistently to threats and to its own state, and remember earlier events. A single obvious failure breaks the impression.
karty.yr: A character that has health and a name but ignores danger or forgets what just happened to it.
karty.rk: how many situations it reacts to; how long it remembers; how consistent reactions are
karty.ik: <circle cx="32" cy="32" r="22"/><circle cx="24" cy="26" r="3" fill="#2a2a2a" stroke="none"/><circle cx="40" cy="26" r="3" fill="#2a2a2a" stroke="none"/><path d="M22 38c6 7 14 7 20 0"/><path d="M50 8l4 6 6-4" stroke="#e85d4f" stroke-width="3"/>

karty.g: A penalty forces the player to repeat past actions or go back over the same path.
karty.nz: Failure must send players back to redo something that cost real effort. It should not remove them from the game, and the size of the loss decides how sharply it hurts.
karty.yr: A 'setback' that costs almost nothing to redo, such as a respawn a few steps back.
karty.rk: how much progress is lost; how far back the player is sent
karty.ik: <path d="M6 56h14V42h14V28h14V14h10"/><path d="M52 8L44 16M44 8l8 8" stroke="none"/><path d="M46 30c10 0 12 16 2 20H30" stroke="#e85d4f"/><path d="M36 44l-7 6 7 6" stroke="#e85d4f"/>

karty.g: Groups of game elements that are worth more together than apart.
karty.nz: Define clear combinations that give a win, score, or bonus bigger than the parts, and make the parts available with enough chance and trade to work toward. Progress toward completing sets should be visible.
karty.yr: A set bonus so small, or pieces so easy to get, that players never go after the combination deliberately.
karty.rk: which combinations count; bonus size; how rarely pieces appear
karty.ik: <rect x="4" y="14" width="18" height="34" rx="3" fill="#e85d4f" transform="rotate(-10 13 31)"/><rect x="23" y="12" width="18" height="34" rx="3" fill="#c9a24a"/><rect x="42" y="14" width="18" height="34" rx="3" fill="#2f6b8f" transform="rotate(10 51 31)"/><path d="M6 58h52" stroke-width="3"/>

karty.g: A goal to meet a requirement, or else the penalty falls on several players at once.
karty.nz: A failure must hit a group or common pool, so that everyone has a stake in avoiding it. Decide how it is divided or whether players can negotiate it.
karty.yr: A penalty labelled as shared but hitting each player individually, or so mild that nobody cares to coordinate.
karty.rk: who shares it; its size; how it is split or negotiated

karty.g: Resources that several players can access during a game.
karty.nz: Several players must be able to use or change the same resource, and the resource must be scarce or important enough that sharing creates tension or cooperation.
karty.yr: A common pool so plentiful that nobody has to negotiate or compete for it.
karty.rk: who has access; how much is available; rate of use or refill

karty.g: A goal where the reward must be split among several players.
karty.nz: A reward must go to a group, with a clear rule on how it is divided or room to negotiate. Individual rewards on the side weaken it.
karty.yr: A reward everyone gets in full anyway, so there is nothing to share or argue about.
karty.rk: who shares; how it is divided; reward size

karty.g: The game world gets smaller and smaller as the game goes on.
karty.nz: Parts of the world must be permanently removed on a schedule or by player action, forcing players closer together. Shrinkage needs to be irreversible and fast enough to matter.
karty.yr: A map whose edges close only cosmetically or so slowly that the game ends before anyone feels it.
karty.rk: how fast and in what order the world shrinks; what triggers it
karty.ik: <rect x="4" y="4" width="56" height="56" rx="3" stroke-dasharray="3 5"/><rect x="16" y="16" width="32" height="32" rx="2" fill="#e85d4f" fill-opacity=".25"/><path d="M10 10l8 8M54 10l-8 8M10 54l8-8M54 54l-8-8" stroke-width="3"/>

karty.g: Item improvements that help only in certain situations, not in general.
karty.nz: Each option must give a gain in some situations and a loss in others, balanced so no option is best everywhere. Players need to be able to tell when each is useful.
karty.yr: A 'sidegrade' that is strictly better than the base item, or whose downside never matters, so it is just an upgrade.
karty.rk: size of gain versus loss; how specialized; how it is unlocked
karty.ik: <path d="M10 46L38 18" stroke-width="6"/><path d="M38 18l10-10 8 8-10 10z" fill="#d5d9e0"/><path d="M6 54l8-8" stroke-width="6"/><path d="M10 14h20M24 8l6 6-6 6M54 50H34M40 44l-6 6 6 6" stroke="#4fa83a" stroke-width="3"/>

karty.g: A goal made of tasks that can be skipped when completing the main story.
karty.nz: Side quests need their own goals and rewards that are worth the detour, and a main quest they can be skipped from without breaking it. Some should lead to different outcomes or exclude each other so that choosing between them matters.
karty.yr: A fetch-and-return errand marked as optional whose reward is trivial or duplicated by the main path, so skipping it costs nothing and doing it adds nothing.
karty.rk: how many side quests there are; how big their rewards are; how many exclude each other
karty.ik: <path d="M6 34h22"/><path d="M28 34l12-14h20"/><path d="M28 34l12 14h6" stroke-dasharray="1 7"/><path d="M46 40v18" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M46 40h12l-4 5 4 5H46z" fill="#e85d4f" stroke-width="2.5"/><circle cx="10" cy="34" r="4" fill="#2a2a2a"/>

karty.g: Only one player can take part in each game session.
