karty.nz: Without other people to push back, the game must supply its own opposition through puzzles, scripted enemies or time pressure. It also needs a clear decision on whether the game can be won at all.
karty.yr: A multiplayer-style game that is simply played alone, with no automated opposition or puzzle to replace the missing opponents, so nothing resists the player.
karty.rk: strength and behaviour of automated opposition; whether the game can be won; time limits

karty.g: A measure of how likely a character is to succeed at a task; it grows with experience.
karty.nz: Skill values must visibly change the odds or the outcomes of actions, and different skills must matter in different situations. Players need some way to raise them and to see the effect.
karty.yr: A skill list on the character sheet whose values barely move the success chance, or a skill that nobody ever has reason to check or improve.
karty.rk: number of skills; how strongly a skill value shifts success odds; how fast skills grow
karty.ik: <path d="M10 56V40M24 56V28M38 56V16" stroke-width="8" stroke="#4fa83a"/><path d="M6 58h52"/><path d="M50 6l3 7 7 1-5 5 1 7-6-4-6 4 1-7-5-5 7-1z" fill="#c9a24a" stroke-width="2"/>

karty.g: Places in the game world that are good for shooting from far away.
karty.nz: The spot needs a long sightline over a useful area and relative safety, for instance through height, cover or hard access. Counterplay such as flanking routes or kill replays keeps it from dominating.
karty.yr: A high ledge with a nice view that is exposed from every side or overlooks nothing worth shooting at, so nobody gains from using it.
karty.rk: sightline length; amount of cover; how hard it is to reach; how many counter-routes exist
karty.ik: <path d="M6 58V34h12v-8h14v32" fill="#d5d9e0"/><circle cx="46" cy="26" r="14"/><circle cx="46" cy="26" r="4" fill="#e85d4f"/><path d="M46 8v10M46 34v10M28 26h10M54 26h8" stroke-width="3"/>

karty.g: The game easily adjusts to different groups of people and circumstances.
karty.nz: The design must offer real options such as pausing, drop-in/out, adjustable length or location, and players or a facilitator must have the power to use them.
karty.yr: A rulebook line saying you may adapt the game to your group, while the rules give no practical way to pause, shorten or change anything.
karty.rk: how easily play can be paused or joined; how adjustable session length is; who may change the rules

karty.g: A choice between benefiting yourself and benefiting another player or your group.
karty.nz: Selfish choices must truly pay in the short term while hurting the group, and players must be unsure what the others will do. They also need other human participants who can be trusted or betrayed.
karty.yr: A shared-pool choice where cooperating is plainly best for everyone, or where the selfish option gives no real advantage, so there is nothing to agonize over.
karty.rk: size of individual vs. shared payoff; how hidden or delayed others' choices are; group size

karty.g: Rewards that raise a player's standing among people rather than giving an in-game benefit.
karty.nz: The reward must be visible to other players, through lists, titles or shown achievements, and must be something that others actually respect. It should not change the in-game balance.
karty.yr: A badge that only the owner ever sees, or one handed out for trivial actions so that it earns no recognition from anyone.
karty.rk: how visible rewards are to others; how hard they are to earn; how many kinds exist

karty.g: Roles that people receive or take toward one another because of the game.
karty.nz: There must be several players with different abilities or tasks, a way to communicate, and enough gameplay differences that people fall into distinct positions. Anonymity and cut communication weaken it.
karty.yr: Named roles listed in the game that players never actually take on, because everyone does the same things and has the same standing.
karty.rk: how different player abilities are; how strong group structures are; how much players can communicate

karty.g: Success in the game depends on the players' ability to communicate and persuade.
karty.nz: Outcomes must depend on how players deal with each other, through bluffing, trading, negotiation or alliances, and the interaction must not be fully mediated away by rules.
karty.yr: A game with a negotiation phase where the best move is always the same calculated trade, so charm or bluffing never changes anything.
karty.rk: how many social actions affect outcomes; how open communication is; how much information is hidden

karty.g: Slots in an item where upgrades, such as gems, are inserted.
karty.nz: Socket counts must be limited and the upgrades must offer meaningfully different benefits, so that choosing what goes where is a real decision. Whether upgrades can be removed changes how risky the choice feels.
karty.yr: Sockets that always take the same single best upgrade, or are so plentiful that nothing needs to be chosen.
karty.rk: sockets per item; types of sockets; whether upgrades are removable; how upgrades are obtained
karty.ik: <path d="M10 42L32 6l22 36-22 14z" fill="#d5d9e0"/><circle cx="32" cy="32" r="9" fill="#fff"/><path d="M32 4l-5 8h10z" fill="#2f6b8f" stroke-width="2.5"/>

karty.g: The player does not know whether a solution to the task exists, which creates uncertainty.
karty.nz: The challenge must be complex or information-poor enough that players cannot tell the answer at once, and the answer must not be easily learned from earlier plays. Players must believe a solution may exist.
karty.yr: A puzzle with an obvious answer or one that can be brute-forced by trying every option, or a puzzle whose solution is copied from a guide.
karty.rk: amount of hidden information; size of the option space; how much feedback hints at the answer
karty.ik: <path d="M6 32h18v-12h16v24h18"/><path d="M6 32v-8M58 44v10" stroke="none"/><path d="M26 14c0-8 14-8 14 0 0 6-8 6-8 14" stroke="#2f6b8f" stroke-width="5"/><circle cx="32" cy="38" r="3" fill="#2f6b8f" stroke="none"/><rect x="10" y="44" width="16" height="14" rx="2" fill="#c9a24a"/><path d="M26 52h8" stroke="none"/>

karty.g: Places where characters, units, or enemies appear.
karty.nz: Placement must take safety, fairness between sides and strategic value into account, since spawn locations draw camping and attacks. Safe zones or protection are often needed.
karty.yr: A marked point that all elements simply appear from with no influence on fighting, routes or balance, or one placed so far from anything that nobody cares about it.
karty.rk: where they are placed; how many there are; whether they are fixed or moving; protection around them
karty.ik: <ellipse cx="32" cy="50" rx="22" ry="7" fill="#2f6b8f"/><path d="M32 44V14" stroke-dasharray="2 6"/><circle cx="32" cy="14" r="6" fill="#fff"/><path d="M18 28l-8-6M46 28l8-6" stroke="#c9a24a" stroke-width="3"/>

karty.g: The moment an avatar, unit, or other element appears in the game world.
karty.nz: The rules must say what appears, when, where and with what advantages or penalties. It must fit the pace of the game, such as reviving players or refilling enemies and resources.
karty.yr: Elements that reappear instantly in the same state with no cost or delay, so removal and death carry no consequence.
karty.rk: what spawns; how often; delay before respawn; where it can happen; penalties on respawn

karty.g: Enjoyment from losing or making a mistake in a loud and dramatic way.
karty.nz: Failure must be dramatic, visible and slow enough to watch, and the game must be hard enough for mistakes to snowball. Players must be willing to take the stakes lightly.
karty.yr: A plain game over screen or quiet elimination, or failure that is punishing and silent so nobody laughs or retells it.
karty.rk: difficulty level; how much mistakes cascade; how visible failures are; how fast failure unfolds

karty.g: People who watch the players' actions but do not affect the game.
karty.nz: Public information must be available to outsiders in a form they can follow, such as a view of the game or replays. Players eliminated early also need a way to keep watching.
karty.yr: Watching is allowed in theory, but the information shown is unreadable, hidden or too fast to follow, so spectators learn nothing.
karty.rk: how much information spectators see; delay of the view; whether they can talk to players

karty.g: A player sure of the lead tries to end the game as fast as possible.
karty.nz: Players must be able to estimate who is ahead, and must have actions that bring the end closer, such as emptying a shared supply. The winner must be decided after play ends, not by an instant win.
karty.yr: A game-end condition that is nominally reachable but that nobody can judge or trigger in time, so players play on and the ending is never rushed.
karty.rk: how clear the score standings are; what triggers the end; how fast end triggers can be depleted
karty.ik: <circle cx="26" cy="34" r="20"/><path d="M26 34V20M26 34l8 4" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M20 8h12"/><path d="M46 14l14 0M50 26h10M46 38h14" stroke="#e85d4f" stroke-width="3"/>

karty.g: A goal to finish the game or part of it as fast as possible.
karty.nz: The game needs a real-time structure, a trustworthy time measure and a way to compare or share results, ideally with replays. Routes should be learnable and improvable so there is room to get faster.
karty.yr: A built-in timer shown on screen that nobody tracks or compares, with no record, so there is no reason to try again faster.
karty.rk: time limit or par times; whether records are stored and shared; how many shortcuts exist
karty.ik: <path d="M14 58V6"/><path d="M14 8h30l-6 8 6 8H14" fill="#fff"/><path d="M14 8h10v8H14zM24 16h10v8H24z" fill="#2a2a2a" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M20 40h40M26 50h34" stroke="#e85d4f" stroke-width="4"/>

karty.g: The screen is divided into parts, each constantly showing its own view of the game.
karty.nz: The game must run on a shared screen with real-time play, with a layout that gives each view enough space to be readable. It should adapt when the number of players changes.
karty.yr: A divided screen where the views are so small or the same that players cannot play independently, or one view is only a static picture.
karty.rk: number of views; layout; size of each view; whether it changes with joining players
karty.ik: <rect x="6" y="8" width="52" height="48" rx="3"/><path d="M32 8v48M6 32h52"/><rect x="10" y="12" width="18" height="16" fill="#2f6b8f" stroke="none"/><rect x="36" y="36" width="18" height="16" fill="#e85d4f" stroke="none"/>

karty.g: Chosen cards are placed in set parts of the deck beforehand to steer random draws.
karty.nz: The game needs drawing stacks and a rule that places certain cards in certain positions, at setup or in play. The seeding must be strong enough to shape what happens, not just reshuffled away.
karty.yr: A rule that places key cards but then shuffles the whole stack again, so the seeding has no effect on what is drawn.
karty.rk: which cards are placed; how deep in the stack; when seeding happens (setup or during play)
karty.ik: <rect x="14" y="40" width="36" height="10" rx="2" fill="#fff"/><rect x="14" y="28" width="36" height="10" rx="2" fill="#c9a24a"/><rect x="14" y="16" width="36" height="10" rx="2" fill="#fff"/><path d="M54 34h-8M50 30l-4 4 4 4" stroke="#e85d4f" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M14 56h36"/>

karty.g: The first stage in games that have clearly separated stages.
karty.nz: The opening needs few options and distinct goals from later phases, and starting conditions must be fair. A following phase must be clearly different so the structure is noticeable.
karty.yr: A section called the opening that plays exactly like the rest of the game, so players never notice a phase.
karty.rk: how many actions are available at the start; how long the phase lasts; how much starting positions differ
karty.ik: <path d="M6 54h52"/><path d="M10 54V34M10 34h14" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M32 54V34" stroke="none"/><path d="M14 14v28"/><path d="M14 14h28l-6 7 6 7H14" fill="#4fa83a"/><path d="M50 30l8 8-8 8" stroke-width="4"/>

karty.g: A supply that inevitably shrinks as the game goes on.
karty.nz: There must be no way to generate or refill the resource, and players must have a reason or requirement to use it. The depletion rate sets how long the game can last.
karty.yr: A resource meter that goes down but is refilled by pick-ups or regeneration, so it never really runs out.
karty.rk: starting amount; consumption rate; whether anything can restore it
karty.ik: <rect x="8" y="12" width="12" height="42" rx="2" fill="#c9a24a"/><rect x="26" y="27" width="12" height="27" rx="2" fill="#c9a24a"/><rect x="44" y="42" width="12" height="12" rx="2" fill="#c9a24a"/><path d="M4 58h56"/>

karty.g: A goal to move and act so that you are not detected.
karty.nz: Enemies or opponents must detect and punish being seen, and the player must have cover, routes and the time to move carefully. Waiting or slow movement must be a real option.
karty.yr: A stealth label on a game where enemies barely notice you or where running through everything works just as well, so hiding is pointless.
karty.rk: enemy sight range and awareness; penalty for detection; amount of cover; noise from movement
karty.ik: <path d='M32 6c-12 0-18 10-18 22v30h36V28C50 16 44 6 32 6z' fill='#2f6b8f'/><path d='M21 30c0-7 22-7 22 0s-22 8-22 0z' fill='#2a2a2a'/><circle cx='27' cy='30' r='2' fill='#fff' stroke='none'/><circle cx='37' cy='30' r='2' fill='#fff' stroke='none'/>

karty.g: The game's design pushes players to think through their actions ahead of time.
karty.nz: Results of actions must be predictable enough for plans to be trusted, and there must be goals that need several steps. The option space should be large enough to need planning but not so large that it is hopeless.
karty.yr: A game that lets you plan but where randomness or a single obvious move makes any plan pointless.
karty.rk: predictability of outcomes; number of steps to goals; number of options per turn

karty.g: Stories that are told inside the game itself.
karty.nz: The game needs agents, places and conflicts that carry a story, and a way to deliver it that does not break the game's own world. Choose between a fixed story and one that follows what players do.
karty.yr: A story told only in a manual or intro that has no connection to actions in play, so it could be removed without changing anything.
karty.rk: fixed vs. adaptive story; how it is delivered (cutscenes, environment, facilitator); how often it appears

karty.g: Knowing the rules, possible actions, and value of moves apart from any specific situation.
karty.nz: The game must have stable rules and structures that carry across sessions, and hidden or deep parts worth learning. Playing must give feedback that shows what works.
karty.yr: A game that changes so much each time, or is so shallow, that nothing learned in one session helps in the next.
karty.rk: how much stays the same between sessions; amount of hidden rules; how much depth rewards learning

karty.g: Parts of the world where control or access gives an advantage.
karty.nz: The location must give a real advantage, such as resources, safety or access, and be noticeable to players. The advantage must be balanced between sides or contested.
karty.yr: A prominent landmark that gives no advantage when held, so players ignore it.
karty.rk: size of the advantage; how many such places; how visible they are; how evenly they are distributed

karty.g: Planning based only on knowing the rules and what other players can do.
karty.nz: The game needs learnable general structures and real strategic choices, plus replays so players can try and refine strategies. Outcomes should be predictable enough to reward a plan.
karty.yr: Several listed strategies that all lead to the same result, so choosing a plan changes nothing.
karty.rk: number of viable strategies; predictability of results; how much replay is encouraged
karty.ik: <path d='M32 14L16 34M32 14L48 34M16 34L8 54M16 34L24 54'/><path d='M32 14L48 34L56 54' stroke='#e85d4f'/><circle cx='32' cy='12' r='6' fill='#c9a24a'/><circle cx='16' cy='34' r='5' fill='#fff'/><circle cx='48' cy='34' r='5' fill='#e85d4f'/><circle cx='8' cy='54' r='4' fill='#fff'/><circle cx='24' cy='54' r='4' fill='#fff'/><circle cx='56' cy='54' r='4' fill='#e85d4f'/>

karty.g: One action stands in for another, as if replacing it.
karty.nz: The replacement action should keep as much meaning as the original, and players must be told and have a chance to practice it. Without a shared understanding it does not work.
karty.yr: A named stand-in action that nobody has been told about or that resembles nothing of the original, so people stop and explain what it means.
karty.rk: how closely the action resembles the original; how much briefing and practice is given
karty.ik: <g transform='rotate(45 32 32)'><rect x='27' y='4' width='10' height='34' rx='5' fill='#e85d4f'/><path d='M20 42h24'/><rect x='29' y='44' width='6' height='14' rx='2' fill='#c9a24a'/></g>

karty.g: A recap of events before or after the game itself to bring the player up to speed.
karty.nz: The summary must give players what they need to know about the setting or the consequences, at the right time and in short enough form to be read. It fits games with a planned story.
karty.yr: A recap screen that repeats what the player already knows, or one so long that it is skipped without being read.
karty.rk: when it appears; how long it is; how much information it contains
karty.ik: <path d='M18 8h34v44a6 6 0 0 1-6 6H12a6 6 0 0 0 6-6z' fill='#fff'/><path d='M25 20h20M25 28h20M25 36h10'/><circle cx='44' cy='47' r='5' fill='#c9a24a' stroke-width='3'/>

karty.g: A goal to complete a task that mainly helps reach the game's other goals.
karty.nz: The reward must really make the main goal easier, and the link must be visible to players. Whether the goal is required or optional decides if players weigh trade-offs.
karty.yr: A side goal whose reward has no effect on the main goal, so it only looks like it helps.
karty.rk: size of the help given to the main goal; whether the goal is required or optional; cost to complete

karty.g: Attacks that the target did not expect.
karty.nz: Combat must exist alongside hidden information (fog, stealth, hiding spots, traps), and attackers need a real way to approach unseen. Defenders must be able to be caught unprepared, with a cost for being caught.
karty.yr: Enemies pop out of nowhere on a script, or the player is warned so clearly that it is just an ordinary fight with a jump-scare sound.
karty.rk: how much each side can see; how many hiding or flanking routes exist; damage bonus for striking unseen
karty.ik: <path d='M32 58L24 26h16z' fill='#d5d9e0'/><path d='M32 58l-3-12h6z' fill='#e85d4f' stroke='none'/><path d='M18 26h28'/><rect x='29' y='6' width='6' height='16' rx='2' fill='#c9a24a'/>

karty.g: A player stops the game, admitting defeat.
karty.nz: The game needs a visible losing position and a cheap way to quit, and the rest of the session should survive someone leaving. How readable the standings are decides how early people give up.
karty.yr: A 'concede' button exists but nobody ever uses it, or using it ruins the game for everyone else so it is effectively unavailable.
karty.rk: how clearly standings show who is losing; how easy it is to quit; what happens to the others afterwards

karty.g: A goal to keep your game elements from being destroyed or removed.
karty.nz: There must be a real threat (enemies, hazards, draining resources) and a real loss when the thing dies. Players must be able to act to prevent that loss.
karty.yr: The thing to protect cannot realistically die, or dying costs nothing, so 'survive' is only a label on the screen.
karty.rk: threat strength and frequency; how fast resources drain; how many lives or how much health

karty.g: A reward that refills something constantly used up, such as health or fuel.
karty.nz: Something must be constantly draining so the refill matters, and the refills must arrive at a pace that keeps players near, but not at, running out. Timing and placement of supplies is the main design work.
karty.yr: Pickups that top up a resource nobody ever runs short of, so collecting them is pointless.
karty.rk: drain rate; amount per pickup; how often and where supplies appear

karty.g: World elements that players use to trigger events or actions.
karty.nz: The activation must change something that matters (open a path, alter hazards, change rules), and players must be able to find the switch and guess roughly what it does. Position and state handling are the main choices.
karty.yr: A lever that only plays an animation, or whose effect was already available some other way.
karty.rk: number and placement of switches; what each does; whether reusable, timed, or one-shot
karty.ik: <rect x='6' y='22' width='52' height='22' rx='11' fill='#d5d9e0'/><circle cx='47' cy='33' r='8' fill='#4fa83a'/><path d='M32 8v6M18 12l3 5M46 12l-3 5' stroke='#c9a24a' stroke-width='3'/>

karty.g: One player's success or failure affects the other player in the same way.
karty.nz: Players' outcomes must be genuinely linked (shared goals, shared enemies, or helpful actions that benefit others), so helping is in their own interest. Helping must also be possible through actual actions.
karty.yr: Players are put on a 'team' by name, but their results are independent and nothing one does changes another's outcome.
karty.rk: how much one player's results spread to others; shared versus individual rewards; availability of helping actions
karty.ik: <rect x='4' y='20' width='34' height='24' rx='12' stroke='#2f6b8f' stroke-width='5'/><rect x='26' y='20' width='34' height='24' rx='12' stroke='#c9a24a' stroke-width='5'/>

karty.g: A goal where the sides have essentially the same tasks and the same rewards for them.
karty.nz: All sides must have the same objective with the same requirements and rewards, and the means to pursue it must be comparable. Differences in start or tools quietly break the symmetry.
karty.yr: Everyone has the same stated goal, but different starting powers or rewards make it effectively different goals.
karty.rk: sameness of objectives and rewards; how equal starting conditions are
karty.ik: <path d='M32 6v52' stroke-dasharray='2 6'/><path d='M14 10v48'/><path d='M14 10l14 7-14 7z' fill='#2f6b8f'/><path d='M50 10v48'/><path d='M50 10l-14 7 14 7z' fill='#e85d4f'/>

karty.g: All players receive resources in equal amounts and on equal terms.
karty.nz: Each player must start with, and have access to, equal amounts and kinds of resources. Equal sharing must also hold up over time.
karty.yr: The totals are equal on paper, but the resources are placed so some players can reach or use them more easily.
karty.rk: amount and kind of starting resources; placement of resource sources
karty.ik: <rect x='6' y='44' width='22' height='9' rx='4.5' fill='#c9a24a'/><rect x='6' y='35' width='22' height='9' rx='4.5' fill='#c9a24a'/><rect x='6' y='26' width='22' height='9' rx='4.5' fill='#c9a24a'/><rect x='36' y='44' width='22' height='9' rx='4.5' fill='#c9a24a'/><rect x='36' y='35' width='22' height='9' rx='4.5' fill='#c9a24a'/><rect x='36' y='26' width='22' height='9' rx='4.5' fill='#c9a24a'/><path d='M4 58h56'/>

karty.g: All players' game sessions run at the same time and overlap.
karty.nz: The game needs ways to get everyone present together and a pace that suits shared time, with breaks handled. Communication and waiting rules matter.
karty.yr: Players are online together but each plays alone and never has to react to anyone else's timing.
karty.rk: turn or real-time structure; how long sessions last; how breaks and late joiners are handled
karty.ik: <path d='M6 8h52'/><path d='M20 8l-8 36M44 8l-8 36'/><circle cx='12' cy='44' r='7' fill='#2f6b8f'/><circle cx='36' cy='44' r='7' fill='#c9a24a'/>

karty.g: Planning based on what is known about the current state of the game.
karty.nz: Players need several meaningful options whose value depends on the current situation, plus enough time and information to weigh them. Costs or trade-offs must make the choice matter.
karty.yr: One option is always clearly best, or there is too little time or information to compare, so choosing is just habit.
karty.rk: number of options; how much outcomes depend on local state; time to decide; amount of hidden information

karty.g: The satisfaction of achieving something together with a group.
karty.nz: The task must truly need several players' contributions and be hard enough that success feels earned. Credit for the result must feel shared rather than attributed to one star.
karty.yr: A group completes the goal, but one player could have done it alone, so nobody feels it was joint.
karty.rk: how much each task depends on all members; difficulty; how success is shown to the group

karty.g: Competing teams have about equal chances of success and victory.
karty.nz: Team makeup and rules must offset advantages, with some correction for teams that fall behind. Features that snowball or cause lopsided numbers must be controlled.
karty.yr: Teams have equal member counts, but skill spread, roles, or snowballing make one side win most of the time.
karty.rk: team composition rules; handicap strength; strength of catch-up effects
karty.ik: <path d='M32 40l-9 16h18z' fill='#d5d9e0'/><path d='M6 40h52'/><circle cx='16' cy='32' r='8' fill='#2f6b8f'/><circle cx='48' cy='32' r='8' fill='#e85d4f'/>

karty.g: Coordinated actions by several players trigger an extra effect they would not have alone.
karty.nz: The extra effect must be big enough to justify coordinating, and players need to be able to notice or learn how to trigger it. Roles that differ, or timing windows, make it truly require several people.
karty.yr: Players acting near each other get a small bonus that they would almost as easily get alone, so no one coordinates.
karty.rk: size of the combo bonus; timing window; how many players and which abilities are required
karty.ik: <path d='M6 18h22v10a6 6 0 0 1 0 12v10H6z' fill='#2f6b8f'/><path d='M34 18h22v32H34V40a6 6 0 0 1 0-12z' fill='#c9a24a'/><path d='M32 4v6M20 8l3 4M44 8l-3 4' stroke='#e85d4f' stroke-width='3'/>

karty.g: Teams change over time because of the game's progress and the players' growing skills.
karty.nz: There must be real improvement options that cost resources and change what the team can do. Improvements should be visible and should shape later play.
karty.yr: The team has a level or rank that goes up, but it changes nothing in what the team can do.
karty.rk: cost and speed of improvement; what can be improved; caps on growth

karty.g: Removing all members of the opposing team from the game.
karty.nz: Teams must be able to lose all their members for good, with no endless respawning. Eliminating members must be possible and worth pursuing.
karty.yr: Members come back immediately, so 'wiping the team' never ends anything.
karty.rk: how hard members are to eliminate; respawn rules; team size

karty.g: A team finds and picks a shared strategy, often based on a mix of strengths.
karty.nz: Players need complementary abilities or synergies to find, a reason to work together (common threat or goal), and room to talk. The game must not hand them one obvious best plan.
karty.yr: Roles are clearly labelled and the optimal team plan is spelled out, so there is nothing to discover.
karty.rk: how varied and hidden synergies are; how different the roles are; communication options
karty.ik: <rect x='10' y='10' width='44' height='48' rx='4' fill='#fff'/><rect x='22' y='4' width='20' height='10' rx='3' fill='#c9a24a'/><circle cx='20' cy='28' r='5' fill='#2f6b8f'/><path d='M26 31c10 2 14 6 14 14'/><path d='M40 44l8 8M48 44l-8 8' stroke='#e85d4f'/>

karty.g: Agents or game elements acting toward one shared goal.
karty.nz: Members must share rewards and penalties so their interests align. Some actions should benefit or depend on teammates.
karty.yr: Players wear the same colour but are scored individually, so teams have no effect on decisions.
karty.rk: team size; which rewards and penalties are shared; friendly-fire rules
karty.ik: <circle cx='32' cy='34' r='27' stroke-dasharray='2 6'/><circle cx='32' cy='22' r='6' fill='#2f6b8f'/><circle cx='20' cy='42' r='6' fill='#2f6b8f'/><circle cx='44' cy='42' r='6' fill='#2f6b8f'/>

karty.g: The order of events in the game matches the order of events in the game world.
karty.nz: The design must remove or limit saving, reloading and free retries, so events stay as played. Lives or pauses must not let players erase outcomes.
karty.yr: The story claims events are final, but players can reload a save and redo any moment freely.
karty.rk: whether and when saves are allowed; number of retries; how events are permanent
karty.ik: <path d='M14 20v26M30 20v26M44 20v26' stroke-dasharray='1 6'/><path d='M4 20h50M4 46h50'/><path d='M50 15l6 5-6 5M50 41l6 5-6 5'/><circle cx='14' cy='20' r='4' fill='#c9a24a'/><circle cx='30' cy='20' r='4' fill='#c9a24a'/><circle cx='44' cy='20' r='4' fill='#c9a24a'/><circle cx='14' cy='46' r='4' fill='#c9a24a'/><circle cx='30' cy='46' r='4' fill='#c9a24a'/><circle cx='44' cy='46' r='4' fill='#c9a24a'/>

karty.g: Abilities available only for a limited stretch of game time.
karty.nz: The ability must be strong enough to change what players do and must truly expire. Players should face a choice about when to use it.
karty.yr: A 'temporary' power lasts so long, or recurs so often, that it is effectively permanent.
karty.rk: duration or number of uses; power level; how often it can be gained
karty.ik: <circle cx='32' cy='32' r='27' stroke-dasharray='3 7'/><path d='M36 6L16 36h14l-4 22 22-32H34z' fill='#c9a24a'/>

karty.g: Worry about the outcome when you cannot fully control it.
karty.nz: Players must care about the result and not control it fully, with real stakes for losing. Uncertainty has to be real and not too easy to see through.
karty.yr: Dramatic music and a countdown, but failure costs nothing and the outcome is certain.
karty.rk: size of stakes; amount of randomness or hidden information; closeness of outcomes
karty.ik: <ellipse cx="25" cy="28" rx="15" ry="18" fill="#e85d4f"/><path d="M22 46h6l-3 4z" fill="#e85d4f" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M25 50c-3 4 3 7 0 12" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M58 6L44 20" stroke-width="3"/><circle cx="57" cy="7" r="4" fill="#c9a24a"/>

karty.g: Parts of the world that belong to one of the inhabitants of the game world.
karty.nz: Ownership must be clearly marked and able to change hands, and owning a territory must bring a benefit. Players need means to take or defend them.
karty.yr: Regions have names and colours but owning them gives nothing, so nobody fights over them.
karty.rk: number and size of territories; benefits of owning; cost of capturing

karty.g: A reward for the player simply trying out some action.
karty.nz: The tested activities should be optional ones players might otherwise skip, and trying should be cheap. The reward should be noticeable enough to nudge behavior.
karty.yr: The achievement is for something every player does anyway, so it never changes what anyone tries.
karty.rk: which activities are included; how easy the trigger is; how visible the reward is
karty.ik: <path d='M22 4l10 20M42 4L32 24' stroke='#e85d4f' stroke-width='6'/><circle cx='32' cy='42' r='16' fill='#c9a24a'/><path d='M24 42l6 6 11-12'/>

karty.g: Characters, items, and their behavior fit together with the theme of the world.
karty.nz: Characters, objects, rules and behavior must all follow the same set of expectations, and features that break the theme must be avoided or explained. Rules should plausibly follow from the fiction.
karty.yr: The art matches a theme, but rules and behavior contradict it, so the setting is only decoration.
karty.rk: how strictly rules follow the fiction; level of detail in setting; how many off-theme features are allowed

karty.g: The camera follows a chosen object and moves with it, rather than seeing through the hero's eyes.
karty.nz: The camera must follow a chosen entity smoothly and show enough surroundings to play. Controls must fit the camera angle.
karty.yr: The camera sits behind the character but is so fixed or so cramped that it gives no extra view of surroundings.
karty.rk: camera distance and angle; follow smoothness; which entity is followed
karty.ik: <rect x='4' y='6' width='22' height='14' rx='3' fill='#d5d9e0'/><circle cx='15' cy='13' r='4' fill='#c9a24a' stroke-width='3'/><path d='M18 22l14 6' stroke-dasharray='1 6'/><circle cx='42' cy='32' r='7'/><path d='M30 60c0-12 5-16 12-16s12 4 12 16z' fill='#2f6b8f'/>

karty.g: Real-time games with long pauses between updates, leaving time to think.
karty.nz: Ticks must be long enough to plan within and must cap actions per tick. Someone or something must enforce the schedule.
karty.yr: Updates happen so fast or so freely that players act continuously, so it is simply real-time.
karty.rk: tick length; actions allowed per tick; how unused actions are handled
karty.ik: <path d='M26 8h12l12 48H14z' fill='#c9a24a'/><path d='M32 52L36 8' stroke-width='3'/><circle cx='35' cy='22' r='4' fill='#e85d4f' stroke-width='3'/><path d='M8 58h48'/>

karty.g: Rules for separating results that would otherwise be equal.
karty.nz: The secondary rule must be clear in advance and rarely tie itself. It should feel fair to players.
karty.yr: A tiebreaker rule exists but ties on it are just as common, so ties remain.
karty.rk: which secondary criteria are used and in what order
karty.ik: <rect x='8' y='28' width='20' height='30' fill='#2f6b8f'/><rect x='36' y='28' width='20' height='30' fill='#2f6b8f'/><circle cx='46' cy='20' r='7' fill='#c9a24a'/>

karty.g: Two or more results are counted as equal and have the same consequences.
karty.nz: Results must be coarse enough that equal values can happen, and the rules must say that equal means equal. The game needs several competitors to compare.
karty.yr: Scores are so fine-grained that ties essentially never happen, so tie rules are never used.
karty.rk: scoring granularity; whether ties share rewards or are broken

karty.g: The game offers different ways to take part, differing in time and kind of actions.
karty.nz: Each tier must have a real, distinct role and requirements, and tiers must stay meaningfully connected to the same game. Players should be able to choose or move between tiers.
karty.yr: Tiers are only labels for how much someone plays, with no different game roles.
karty.rk: number of tiers; time and activity required per tier; ease of moving between tiers
karty.ik: <path d='M32 6l12 16H20z' fill='#c9a24a'/><path d='M18 26h28l7 14H11z' fill='#d5d9e0'/><path d='M8 44h48l4 14H4z' fill='#fff'/>

karty.g: Placing pieces where their position relative to those already laid matters.
karty.nz: Where a piece goes must matter for what follows, with relations to neighbors affecting play. Placement must vary between games.
karty.yr: Tiles are laid down but position has no effect, so it is decoration.
karty.rk: placement rules; who places; how many tile types and how drawn
karty.ik: <rect x='6' y='38' width='16' height='16' fill='#fff'/><rect x='22' y='38' width='16' height='16' fill='#fff'/><rect x='38' y='38' width='16' height='16' stroke-dasharray='2 5'/><rect x='38' y='6' width='16' height='16' fill='#e85d4f' transform='rotate(12 46 14)'/><path d='M46 27v5M43 29l3 4 3-4'/>

karty.g: Pieces used to hand out resources without showing beforehand what is where.
karty.nz: Tile types and counts must be chosen so they distribute resources or build the world in a way that matters. Hidden or randomised tiles need a known distribution.
karty.yr: Tiles are all identical in effect, so which one you get changes nothing.
karty.rk: number of tiles; mix of types; hidden or shown

karty.g: The game's rules themselves limit how long a single game can last.
karty.nz: A clock or a turn/action count must be built in so the session truly ends at a known point, with end and scoring rules that work when time runs out. The cap should be clear to players before they start.
karty.yr: A timer shown on screen that never ends the session or changes who wins, so players can ignore it.
karty.rk: length of the session cap; whether players can choose it

karty.g: Time allowed for an action, a goal, a game mode, or the whole game.
karty.nz: The timer must be tied to a real consequence (failure, loss, elimination) and be short enough relative to the task that players must skip or trade off something. It must also be visible or otherwise noticed.
karty.yr: A generous timer that nearly everyone beats with room to spare, or one with no penalty when it runs out.
karty.rk: how much time is given; what happens at zero; how time can be gained or lost

karty.g: The game creates a feeling that you must act and reach goals quickly.
karty.nz: A real deadline or a race against others, committed goals, and a time budget that is tight for the players' skill level. Players must be able to sense the clock through indicators or alarms.
karty.yr: A visible timer that is so loose, or so lightly penalised, that nobody feels hurried or changes how they act.
karty.rk: time budget relative to task difficulty; severity of failure; how visible the clock is

karty.g: The feeling that you are playing with others, not alone.
karty.nz: Players must share a space or a goal over time and have chances for shared experience, such as joint success, shared failure, or moments to socialise. Group symbols and a sense of team identity help.
karty.yr: A team label or a multiplayer lobby where players act separately and never rely on or notice each other.
karty.rk: team size and stability; how much players depend on each other; room for social downtime

karty.g: Players choose future actions by placing their tokens on them.
karty.nz: Action slots must be fewer than the demand for them, so placing a token blocks others, and each player needs only a few tokens. A clear turn order for placement is required.
karty.yr: Every action slot is unlimited or open to everyone, so placing a token is just a bookkeeping step that blocks nobody.
karty.rk: tokens per player; number and capacity of action slots; placement turn order
karty.ik: <rect x='6' y='32' width='52' height='26' rx='4'/><circle cx='18' cy='45' r='5'/><circle cx='32' cy='45' r='5' stroke-dasharray='2 4'/><circle cx='46' cy='45' r='5' fill='#2f6b8f'/><circle cx='32' cy='14' r='8' fill='#c9a24a'/><path d='M32 25v6'/>

karty.g: Elements that give actions in the world or make them easier to do.
karty.nz: A tool must open up a new action or clearly improve one, and players must have a reason to want it and a way to obtain and use it. Scarcity or wear makes the choice of tool matter.
karty.yr: A named item that only gives a cosmetic change or a tiny bonus nobody notices, or one that every character has from the start.
karty.rk: which actions it enables or boosts; how common it is; whether it wears out
karty.ik: <path d="M44 6l10 10-8 8-10-10z" fill="#c9a24a"/><path d="M40 20L10 50" stroke-width="6"/><path d="M8 48l8 8" stroke-width="6"/><path d="M36 10l-6 6" stroke-width="3"/>

karty.g: An explanation shown when the player pays attention to a game element.
karty.nz: The text must contain information that actually helps decisions, appear at the right moment and with the right delay, and not flood the player. It should cover the elements players are likely to be unsure about.
karty.yr: A popup that merely repeats the item's name or flavour text and teaches nothing about how it works.
karty.rk: which elements get tips; how much detail; hover delay before showing
karty.ik: <rect x="6" y="6" width="52" height="34" rx="5" fill="#fff"/><path d="M18 40v8l10-8" fill="#fff"/><path d="M16 18h32M16 28h20" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M40 50l6 12 3-6 6-3z" fill="#2f6b8f" stroke-width="3"/>

karty.g: A goal to win a series of matches arranged as a competition.
karty.nz: Matches must be linked by a bracket or standings so that earlier results shape later play, and there must be enough players and a schedule to run it. Players need a reason to care about the overall result.
karty.yr: A list of unconnected games with a 'tournament' label, where results never feed into a ranking or later matches.
karty.rk: format (elimination vs. round-robin); number of rounds; length of each match

karty.g: World elements that lead the player to places that matter in the game.
karty.nz: The marks must be noticeable but not obvious, and reliably (or deliberately unreliably) connect to something in play such as enemies, loot or traps. Players must be able to read them and act on them.
karty.yr: Decorative marks that sit in the world but correspond to nothing, so following them gets players nowhere.
karty.rk: how visible they are; how reliable they are; how long they last; whether players can alter them
karty.ik: <path d="M6 52c10 0 14-12 26-12s14-14 26-14" stroke-dasharray="1 8"/><ellipse cx="14" cy="34" rx="5" ry="8" fill="#2f6b8f" transform="rotate(-20 14 34)"/><ellipse cx="32" cy="20" rx="5" ry="8" fill="#2f6b8f" transform="rotate(-20 32 20)"/><ellipse cx="50" cy="8" rx="4" ry="6" fill="#2f6b8f" fill-opacity=".4" transform="rotate(-20 50 8)"/>

karty.g: The player chooses among several options and weighs what can be given up for what.
karty.nz: Options must have genuinely different, comparable costs and benefits, with no choice that is better in every way. Players must understand the consequences well enough to weigh them.
karty.yr: A choice between options where one is clearly best, so the 'decision' is obvious and players never hesitate.
karty.rk: relative size of the gains and costs of each option; how well the effects are shown to the player

karty.g: Players exchange resources with each other.
karty.nz: Players must hold different things of different value to them, be allowed to exchange them, and have a way to find and talk to each other. Needs must differ enough that swaps benefit both sides.
karty.yr: A trade menu in a game where everyone has the same needs and goods, so nobody ever gains from using it.
karty.rk: how unequal the holdings are; which items can be traded; trade limits or fees

karty.g: Items that can be passed from one character to another.
karty.nz: There must be an action to give, drop or swap items, and a clear set of limits about which items and to whom. Items must have value to other players or characters to make transfers worthwhile.
karty.yr: An option to hand over items that is blocked for nearly everything useful, or covers items nobody wants.
karty.rk: which items can be transferred; to whom; what limits apply (binding, class restrictions)
karty.ik: <circle cx="12" cy="20" r="6"/><path d="M2 44c0-8 4-12 10-12s10 4 10 12z"/><circle cx="52" cy="20" r="6"/><path d="M42 44c0-8 4-12 10-12s10 4 10 12z"/><path d="M24 14c4-6 12-6 16 0" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M26 54h12v8H26z" fill="#c9a24a" stroke-width="3" transform="translate(0 -8)"/>

karty.g: A path that must be traveled to reach certain places in the game world.
karty.nz: Routes must be the actual way between key places, with no free shortcut, and take meaningful time or effort. Something on or about the journey, such as hazards, choices or waiting, makes the travel matter.
karty.yr: A corridor that players can bypass or skip with instant travel, so it adds only a loading pause.
karty.rk: route length; number of alternative routes; whether shortcuts or fast travel exist
karty.ik: <path d="M24 4L10 60M40 4l14 56"/><path d="M32 8v8M32 24v8M32 40v8" stroke="#c9a24a"/><path d="M20 22h24M16 40h32" stroke-width="3"/>

karty.g: Elements or events that kill or wound characters.
karty.nz: The hazard must be able to hurt the player in a way that matters, and be fair, either learnable by observation or memory or spotted by clues. The penalty has to be real for players to change their movement.
karty.yr: A hazard that does so little harm, or is so telegraphed, that players walk through it without any change in behaviour.
karty.rk: damage or penalty; how well hidden it is; how often it triggers; whether it resets

karty.g: A goal to move a game element from one point in the world to another.
karty.nz: A clear start and end point with a route that holds obstacles, choices or opposition, so the journey is not trivial. Progress should be readable to the player, for example through checkpoints.
karty.yr: A destination marker reached by simply holding a key down, with nothing to cross or avoid.
karty.rk: distance; obstacles along the way; number of checkpoints
karty.ik: <path d="M6 52h20v-14h14v-14h18"/><circle cx="12" cy="42" r="4" fill="#2f6b8f"/><path d="M46 8v18"/><path d="M46 8l12 5-12 5z" fill="#e85d4f" stroke-width="2.5"/>

karty.g: The solution is found by simply trying all the possible options.
karty.nz: The set of possible solutions must be small and visible, and trying a wrong one must be cheap enough that testing is possible. The solution should be found only by testing.
karty.yr: A puzzle with so many options, or such heavy penalties for a wrong try, that testing is unrealistic, or whose answer is obvious.
karty.rk: number of candidate solutions; cost of a wrong attempt; whether the answer changes between plays
karty.ik: <rect x="6" y="10" width="16" height="16" rx="3"/><rect x="24" y="10" width="16" height="16" rx="3"/><rect x="42" y="10" width="16" height="16" rx="3" fill="#4fa83a"/><path d="M10 40l8 8M18 40l-8 8M28 44h8" stroke="#e85d4f"/><path d="M46 44l4 5 8-9" stroke="#4fa83a"/>

karty.g: Several players play cards, and one of them wins that round.
karty.nz: Cards need ranked values with rules for following suit, a winner-determination rule, and a clear scoring goal (most, fewest, exact). A turn order must exist.
karty.yr: Players play cards in a round but the winner is picked at random or the result changes nothing in scoring.
karty.rk: goal (most, fewest or exact tricks); suit-following rules; trump use
karty.ik: <rect x="6" y="14" width="24" height="34" rx="3" fill="#fff" transform="rotate(-14 18 31)"/><rect x="22" y="10" width="24" height="34" rx="3" fill="#fff"/><rect x="36" y="18" width="24" height="34" rx="3" fill="#fff" transform="rotate(14 48 35)"/><path d="M34 20c-4 4-6 6 0 10 6-4 4-6 0-10z" fill="#e85d4f" stroke-width="2"/>

karty.g: In trick-taking card games, a suit that beats the cards of all other suits.
karty.nz: The trump suit must really override normal ranking and must be chosen in a way that matters, such as being fixed, random or bid. There must be a trick-taking game for it to modify.
karty.yr: A named trump suit that happens to rank the same as normal, or is so rare it almost never decides a trick.
karty.rk: fixed vs. changing trump; how trump is chosen (random or bid)
karty.ik: <rect x="10" y="14" width="22" height="32" rx="3" fill="#fff" transform="rotate(-10 21 30)"/><rect x="26" y="12" width="26" height="38" rx="3" fill="#fff"/><path d="M10 4l4 5 5-4 3 8H6z" fill="#c9a24a" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M39 24l9 10-9 10-9-10z" fill="#e85d4f" stroke-width="3"/>

karty.g: One player takes actions, then the turn passes to the next players.
karty.nz: A clear order and clear conditions for when a turn starts and ends, enforced by the rules or system. Designers should also deal with the first player's advantage and with waiting time.
karty.yr: Nominal turns that nobody enforces, so players act whenever they like.
karty.rk: turn order; what ends a turn; whether there are extra turns or time limits
karty.ik: <circle cx="32" cy="32" r="22"/><path d="M32 10a22 22 0 0 1 19 11" stroke="#c9a24a" stroke-width="6"/><path d="M54 14l-3 9-9-4" fill="#c9a24a" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="32" cy="32" r="5" fill="#2f6b8f"/>

karty.g: The game is split into clear parts where the player can think and choose an action.
karty.nz: The rules must clearly mark when planning and acting are allowed and when not, with a clear end of turn. Decisions need to reward the time spent thinking.
karty.yr: A game described as turn-based where actions are really continuous and the turns do not limit anything.
karty.rk: how long a turn lasts; actions per turn; whether turns are simultaneous or alternating
karty.ik: <rect x="8" y="8" width="48" height="48" rx="3"/><path d="M8 24h48M8 40h48M24 8v48M40 8v48" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="16" cy="16" r="5" fill="#2f6b8f"/><circle cx="48" cy="48" r="5" fill="#e85d4f"/>

karty.g: A game event ends one player's turn and immediately passes the turn to another.
karty.nz: Actions must carry a real chance of failure, and failure must end the turn immediately and cost the player their remaining actions. Players need to see that risk before they act.
karty.yr: A failure that is called a turnover but the player keeps acting or loses nothing meaningful.
karty.rk: chance of failure per action; which failures end the turn

karty.g: Games where teams compete against each other.
karty.nz: Fixed teams with shared goals and a scoring rule that compares teams, plus attention to team balance and to players leaving or joining. Teams must be able to affect each other.
karty.yr: Players wear team colours but score and win individually, so team membership changes nothing.
karty.rk: team size; balancing methods; how team results are scored

karty.g: You can play almost any time and in most places with little preparation.
karty.nz: The game must need little setup or equipment, work without a fixed place or simultaneous players (for example asynchronous play), and allow short interruptible sessions.
karty.yr: A mobile app that needs a constant connection, a long session or a quiet setting, so it still can't be played at most times and places.
karty.rk: required equipment and connection; whether play is asynchronous; session length
karty.ik: <rect x="20" y="6" width="24" height="44" rx="4" fill="#fff"/><path d="M28 44h8"/><circle cx="32" cy="24" r="6" fill="#4fa83a"/><path d="M10 18c-4 6-4 12 0 18M54 18c4 6 4 12 0 18" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M4 58h56"/>

karty.g: Events that players cannot influence in any way.
karty.nz: The event must really be beyond player action and have a visible effect on play. Players should know about it in advance if you want planning around it.
karty.yr: An event shown as unstoppable that players can in fact prevent or ignore with little effort.
karty.rk: when and how often it occurs; how large its effect is; whether it is announced

karty.g: The player is unsure whether the information they have can be trusted.
karty.nz: Some relevant information must be hidden, noisy or possibly false, and players must need that information to decide. It should not be so extreme that decisions become pure guesses.
karty.yr: Hidden information that does not matter for any decision, or that players can easily look up elsewhere.
karty.rk: how much is hidden; how reliable the information is; available sources of clarification

karty.g: Before the game starts, it is hard to say reliably how it will end.
karty.nz: There must be real sources of variance, such as chance, deep strategy or unpredictable players, and no dominant strategy or runaway leader. Skill should still matter.
karty.yr: A game with random elements that rarely change who wins, so the result is clear well in advance.
karty.rk: amount of randomness; balance between players; strategic depth
karty.ik: <path d="M12 12h40l4 12-24 32L8 24z" fill="#fff" transform="translate(0 -2)"/><path d="M8 22h48" stroke-width="3"/><circle cx="22" cy="34" r="3" fill="#e85d4f"/><circle cx="42" cy="34" r="3" fill="#e85d4f"/><circle cx="32" cy="46" r="3" fill="#e85d4f"/>

karty.g: Expendable pieces controlled by a player or the game, usually faceless and acting in groups.
karty.nz: There must be many similar controllable or opposing elements whose individual loss does not decide the game, with actions that matter at a group level. Counts and costs should make losing units meaningful as a resource.
karty.yr: A single unit renamed as a group, or many units so identical and disposable that no one cares about losing them.
karty.rk: number of units; their cost and strength; how much autonomy they have
karty.ik: <circle cx="14" cy="14" r="6" fill="#2f6b8f"/><circle cx="32" cy="14" r="6" fill="#2f6b8f"/><circle cx="50" cy="14" r="6" fill="#2f6b8f"/><path d="M6 34h16v8H6zM24 34h16v8H24zM42 34h16v8H42z" fill="#2f6b8f" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M6 54h52"/>

karty.g: A goal that is unknown to the player at first, and sometimes later too.
karty.nz: Goals must be genuinely hidden from the player at first and revealed later through play or clues. Hints should exist so players know something is there.
karty.yr: Goals that are labelled hidden but are listed in the menu or manual, or that can be guessed from the start.
karty.rk: when and how goals get revealed; how many hints are given
karty.ik: <path d="M10 56V8h8l8 8h26l-6 8 6 8H26l-8-8" fill="#d5d9e0" stroke="none"/><path d="M16 58V6"/><path d="M16 8h38l-8 10 8 10H16z" fill="#d5d9e0"/><path d="M30 14c0-5 10-5 10 0 0 4-5 4-5 8" stroke-width="3"/>

karty.g: Gaining access to new abilities or game content.
karty.nz: Content must be truly withheld until a clear requirement is met, and players should know it exists. The unlocked item should be worth the effort.
karty.yr: An 'unlock' that gives something trivial or that was available all along, or a requirement so easy it is never felt.
karty.rk: what is gated; the unlock requirement; how visible the locked content is

karty.g: Characters are capable of unexpected actions.
karty.nz: Agents need real variation, through randomness, complex rules or human control, while still staying within sensible limits. Players should not be able to learn and exploit a fixed script.
karty.yr: Agents that follow a fixed script with a bit of random flavour that never changes what they do.
karty.rk: amount of randomness in agent decisions; complexity of agent rules
karty.ik: <circle cx="32" cy="34" r="14" fill="#fff"/><path d="M24 30h2M38 30h2M25 40c4-3 10 3 14 0" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M6 10c6 6 0 10 6 16M58 10c-6 6 0 10-6 16M32 4v8" stroke="#e85d4f" stroke-width="3"/>

karty.g: The starts and ends of different players' game sessions do not line up in time.
karty.nz: The game must let people join, leave, quit or be eliminated at different moments, and the server or facilitator must keep play going for those who remain. Without free entry and exit, everyone ends up starting and finishing together.
karty.yr: A lobby with a join button that in practice always waits for a full group and ends for everyone at once, so sessions stay aligned.
karty.rk: how freely players may join or leave mid-game; how elimination and surrender are handled
karty.ik: <path d="M6 14h30" stroke="#2f6b8f" stroke-width="6"/><path d="M20 32h36" stroke="#c9a24a" stroke-width="6"/><path d="M10 50h24" stroke="#e85d4f" stroke-width="6"/><path d="M6 4v56M58 4v56" stroke-width="2"/>

karty.g: States from which no actions can lead to a win anymore.
karty.nz: The rules need irreversible actions, dominant strategies or kingmaking that can lock a player (or everyone) out of any route to victory, and the player must be able to notice or suspect this. Hidden scoring or a late-revealed winner can mask it.
karty.yr: A game that merely feels hard or a player who is far behind but still has a clear comeback path; nothing is actually closed off.
karty.rk: how reversible actions are; strength of catch-up mechanisms; how visible the score is
karty.ik: <path d="M10 58V6"/><path d="M10 8h34l-8 10 8 10H10z" fill="#d5d9e0"/><path d="M32 38h24v20H32z" fill="#e85d4f"/><path d="M38 44l12 8M50 44l-12 8" stroke="#fff" stroke-width="3"/>

karty.g: Games that have no winning conditions at all.
karty.nz: The system needs no reachable winning state, plus something that guarantees play ends, such as rising difficulty, a survive goal or a time limit, and some way to compare results like scores. Otherwise players have no reason to continue.
karty.yr: A game that calls itself endless but actually has a final boss, a victory screen or a reachable completion state.
karty.rk: how fast difficulty rises; length of time limit or resource drain; presence of score tables
karty.ik: <path d="M32 56V8"/><path d="M32 10l22 8-22 8" fill="#d5d9e0"/><path d="M10 10l44 44" stroke="#e85d4f" stroke-width="6"/><path d="M18 58h28"/>

karty.g: Changes to items that make them more effective.
karty.nz: Upgrades must measurably improve an ability of existing equipment and cost players something, like scarce materials or an irreversible choice, so selection matters. Slots and acquisition rules must be clear.
karty.yr: A cosmetic or tiny numeric bump that no one can feel, or one upgrade so obviously best that every player takes it.
karty.rk: size of the boost; cost and scarcity; number of upgrade slots; whether installing is reversible

karty.g: The feeling that the effort put into the game is worth something.
karty.nz: Players need real agency, visible feedback that links their actions to outcomes, and some permanence of results, such as persistent worlds, self-set goals or measurable improvement. Effort that gets overwritten or ignored kills it.
karty.yr: Reward screens and numbers pop up regardless of what the player did, so effort and outcome are unrelated.
karty.rk: how permanent results are; clarity of feedback on actions; proportion of outcome that depends on player choices
karty.ik: <path d="M6 56h52"/><path d="M10 56l12-14 10 8 14-24" stroke="#4fa83a" stroke-width="5"/><circle cx="50" cy="20" r="10" fill="#c9a24a"/><path d="M50 15v10" stroke-width="3"/>

karty.g: A mechanic that imitates how hitting a target is sometimes easier and sometimes harder.
karty.nz: Shots must actually miss based on understandable factors the player can influence, and the current accuracy should be shown to them. The effect must be big enough to alter how they position and fire.
karty.yr: A crosshair that wiggles for show while every shot still lands exactly where aimed.
karty.rk: spread size; penalty from moving or taking damage; time to aim; effect of skills and upgrades
karty.ik: <circle cx="32" cy="32" r="24"/><circle cx="32" cy="32" r="12"/><circle cx="32" cy="32" r="3" fill="#e85d4f"/><circle cx="44" cy="20" r="3" fill="#2a2a2a"/><circle cx="17" cy="40" r="3" fill="#2a2a2a"/>

karty.g: Gameplay changes within one game or from game to game.
karty.nz: Choices have to lead to meaningfully different situations, supported by changing rules, random elements or generated worlds, and by feedback that discourages repeating one approach. Differences must affect how play develops, not just surface details.
karty.yr: Many options or levels that all play the same, so players settle into one routine within minutes.
karty.rk: amount of randomness; number of distinct viable goals or strategies; how often rules or content change

karty.g: The game's rules change over time, but within a preset collection.
karty.nz: Clear triggers must change the active rules during play, such as random cards, locations, switches or new abilities, and players must be told about the changes. The shifts must alter what good play looks like.
karty.yr: A rule list that technically has conditional clauses which never trigger in practice, so play stays the same throughout.
karty.rk: how often rules change; trigger type (random, location, progress); how many rules can change at once

karty.g: The order of turns changes during the game, by itself or by the players' choice.
karty.nz: Order must really change between rounds by rotation, score-based ranking or player choice, and the first slot must carry a real advantage or disadvantage for the variation to matter. Limit player-driven changes so they do not dominate.
karty.yr: A rotating order in a game where acting first or last makes no difference, so the rotation changes nothing.
karty.rk: how order is determined (rotation, score, bidding); how big the first-player advantage is; how many changes players may make

karty.g: Game areas designed for driving or flying a vehicle.
karty.nz: The terrain scale, obstacles and routes must suit vehicle speed and abilities, and vehicles must be available there. Walking through should be clearly worse than driving.
karty.yr: A big open area with a car parked in it where walking is just as fast and the layout is the same.
karty.rk: size of area; vehicle availability; density of obstacles and choke points; speed difference versus walking

karty.g: Elements that let you move faster or differently than usual.
karty.nz: Vehicles must provide clearly different movement, speed, protection or weapons from walking, and be reachable at set places or buildable. The world must be shaped so the difference matters.
karty.yr: A model you sit in that moves like the avatar at the same speed and gives no new access or power.
karty.rk: speed; terrain access (air, water); armor and weapons; spawn locations and numbers

karty.g: The same view of the world is shown in different ways, such as thermal vision.
karty.nz: Each mode must reveal information the normal view hides, such as hidden objects or clues, and have a cost, limit or tradeoff so switching is a real decision. Otherwise one mode wins permanently.
karty.yr: A colored filter that shows exactly the same information as the normal view.
karty.rk: what each mode reveals; energy or duration limits; how many modes exist; how they are unlocked

karty.g: A temporary stay in a part of the world controlled by another player.
karty.nz: There must be private player spaces, a way to be allowed in (friends or neighbors), and a small set of allowed actions, preferably helpful ones. The visit should also leave the owner something to see or gain.
karty.yr: A view-only gallery of another player's space where the visitor can do nothing and nobody notices the visit.
karty.rk: who can visit; which actions visitors have; daily action caps; benefits to host and visitor

karty.g: Weak points that others can take advantage of.
karty.nz: Weaknesses must change damage or effects noticeably, differ between enemies or situations, and be discoverable or hideable so players adapt their choices. Counter options must exist.
karty.yr: A listed weakness with a negligible bonus, or one that applies to every enemy equally, so there is nothing to exploit.
karty.rk: damage multiplier; which entities have which weakness; how obvious the weakness is; availability of exploiting weapons

karty.g: Exercises before the game that help players get into their roles.
karty.nz: Exercises must target the specific roleplay skills the game demands, be short and low-pressure, and be done right before play with everyone participating. They should also teach any special rules used.
karty.yr: A generic icebreaker listed in the rulebook that people skip or that has nothing to do with the roles in the game.
karty.rk: length; type of exercise; amount of group interaction; relevance to the game's roleplay demands

karty.g: Links between distant places in the world that make them neighbors.
karty.nz: Entrances and exits must connect distant places with clear activation rules, and the shortcuts must matter for travel, loops or map topology. Their effect on obstacles and exploration should be considered.
karty.yr: A portal between two spots that are already next to each other, or one used only for cutscenes.
karty.rk: number and placement; destinations; activation conditions; one-way or two-way; who can create them

karty.g: Attacks at set times by a large number of identical enemies.
karty.nz: Groups of enemies must arrive on a schedule with pauses between, with escalating size or type, and defeat must threaten the player. Rests need to be long enough to prepare.
karty.yr: A steady trickle of enemies labeled as waves, with no clear groups, pauses or growth.
karty.rk: wave size; time between waves; growth rate; enemy mix and resistances

karty.g: Items used to cause death and destruction in the game world.
karty.nz: Weapons must differ in damage, range, speed, ammo or special effects so choosing one matters, and the world must offer situations where each is better. Acquisition should feel earned.
karty.yr: Several weapons with different names and models but identical stats and handling.
karty.rk: damage; range; rate of fire; ammo limits; accuracy; special effects and unlock timing

karty.g: The winners are decided only after the gameplay has finished.
karty.nz: The game needs a clear end trigger and a scoring or comparison step afterward, and the standings must stay hard to calculate during play, through hidden scores or complexity. Otherwise the result is known early.
karty.yr: A final tally that merely confirms a leader who was obvious and uncatchable long before the end.
karty.rk: end trigger; how visible scores are; scoring formula; hidden versus open information

karty.g: The player who reaches a state that itself ends the game wins.
karty.nz: There must be a specific achievable end condition that declares a winner at once, plus rules for simultaneous achievement or ties. The goal must be within reach of competing players.
karty.yr: A goal that exists on paper but the game ends by timer anyway, or the winner is decided by a later count.
karty.rk: threshold needed (score, targets, survivors); tiebreaker rules; time cap

karty.g: Techniques used before the game: building the world together or preparing for the game.
karty.nz: Sessions must have defined techniques to create characters, relationships and setting together, with enough time and facilitation for everyone to take part. The output must feed into play.
karty.yr: A group discussion that produces nothing used in the game, or a handout read silently.
karty.rk: length; techniques used; how much is created collectively; facilitator involvement

karty.g: People make no direct decisions during play; the game runs by itself.
karty.nz: The rules must run by themselves, with any player influence confined to setup, programming or rule creation, and be rich enough for interesting outcomes to emerge. Observers need a way to watch and compare.
karty.yr: A game where a player presses a button now and then but the outcome never depends on it, billed as a zero-player game with no real setup choices either.
karty.rk: how much freedom the setup phase gives; complexity of rules; how agents are programmed; observation options

karty.g: A game element affects how the elements next to it can act.
karty.nz: Units must project effects onto neighboring spaces, such as forced stops, extra movement cost or attack penalties, strong enough to shape movement and positioning. Terrain and choke points should make it matter.
karty.yr: A highlighted area around units that has no effect on movement or combat.
karty.rk: radius; effect strength (stop, extra cost, free attacks); which units generate it; exceptions
